lessons.title: Greetings and numbers 0–100
vocab: ありがとうございます
よろしくお願[ねが]いします
nice to meet you; please treat me kindly

points.title: Everyday greetings
points.pattern: おはようございます · こんにちは · こんばんは
points.gist: pick the greeting by the time of day
points.explain: Japanese greetings are **fixed blocks**: learn each one whole, like a single word. Choose by the clock: **おはようございます** in the morning, **こんにちは** during the day, **こんばんは** in the evening. **おやすみなさい** is only for going to bed, and **さようなら** is a fairly formal goodbye.
points.tip: こんばんは is a hello, never a goodbye. Also, the final は in こんにちは and こんばんは is read **wa**.
points.yt: Japanese greetings ohayou gozaimasu konnichiwa konbanwa beginners

s.en: Good morning.
Hello. / Good afternoon.
Good evening.
Good night.
Goodbye.

points.title: Thanks, sorry, excuse me
points.pattern: (どうも) ありがとうございます · すみません
points.gist: thanking, apologizing and getting attention
points.explain: **ありがとうございます** is the polite thank-you; with friends, **ありがとう** is enough. **すみません** does three jobs: “excuse me”, “I'm sorry” and a humble “thanks for the trouble”. **どうも** alone is a quick “thanks”, and in front of another phrase it adds **very much**.
points.tip: When someone thanks you, reply with a light **いいえ** (“not at all”), not はい.
points.yt: Japanese arigatou sumimasen doumo difference

s.en: Thank you very much.

c.w: ありがとうございます

s.en: Excuse me. / I'm sorry.
Thanks! (casual)
Not at all. (reply to thanks)
Thank you so much, sorry for the trouble.

points.title: First introductions
points.pattern: はじめまして。 Name です。 よろしくお願いします。
points.gist: the three-step formula for meeting someone
points.explain: Meeting someone for the first time follows a recipe: **はじめまして** (“how do you do”), then your name + **です**, then **よろしくおねがいします** (“please treat me kindly”). Put **どうぞ** in front for extra politeness. If someone greets you first, answer **こちらこそ** (“likewise”).
points.tip: Never put さん after your own name: ミラージュです, not ミラージュさんです.
points.yt: Japanese self introduction hajimemashite yoroshiku onegaishimasu

s.en: How do you do?
I'm Mirage.
Nice to meet you. (lit. please treat me kindly)
It's a real pleasure to meet you.
Likewise, nice to meet you.

points.title: Numbers 0–100
points.pattern: tens + じゅう + ones
points.gist: build any number like blocks: 4 × 10 + 7 = よんじゅうなな
points.explain: Learn 1 to 10 and you can build everything up to 99: **tens digit + じゅう + ones digit**. So 14 is じゅうよん, 40 is よんじゅう and 47 is よんじゅうなな. 100 is simply **ひゃく**, and zero is **ゼロ** (or れい).
points.tip: 4, 7 and 9 each have two readings. For counting and for the tens, use **よん, なな, きゅう**: よんじゅう, ななじゅう, きゅうじゅう.
points.yt: Japanese numbers 1 to 100 for beginners

s.en: It's 14.
It's 29.

c.w: 二十九[にじゅうきゅう]です

s.en: It's 47.

c.w: 四十七[よんじゅうなな]です

s.en: It's 73.

c.w: 七十三[ななじゅうさん]です

lessons.title: I am…
vocab: 留学生[りゅうがくせい]

points.title: X は Y です — X is Y
points.pattern: X は Y です
points.gist: the basic “X is Y” sentence
points.explain: **は** marks the topic: what you are talking about (read it **wa**). **です** closes the sentence and means “is / am / are”. There is no “a / the” and no plural, so がくせいです can mean “I'm a student” or “they're students”.
points.tip: Once the topic is clear, Japanese drops it. Saying わたしは in every sentence sounds unnatural; often がくせいです alone is enough.
points.yt: Genki lesson 1 X wa Y desu grammar

s.en: I'm a student.
Mirage is Brazilian.
Tanaka-san is a teacher.
Ana is an international student.

c.w: 留学生[りゅうがくせい]です

s.en: Kimura-san is Japanese.

c.w: 日本人[にほんじん]です

points.title: 〜か — asking a question
points.pattern: X は Y ですか
points.gist: put か at the end to make a question
points.explain: For a yes/no question, just add **か** to the end: no change in word order, no question mark needed. For “what?”, put **なん** exactly where the answer will go: せんこうは なんですか → せんこうは れきしです.
points.tip: あなた (“you”) can sound blunt. Use the person's name + さん instead: アナさんは がくせいですか.
points.yt: Japanese question particle ka nan desu ka

s.en: Tanaka-san, are you Japanese?

c.w: 日本人[にほんじん]ですか

s.en: What's your major?
Ana, are you a student?
What's your name?
Kimura-san, are you a college student?

c.w: 大学生[だいがくせい]ですか

points.title: N の N — linking two nouns
points.pattern: N₁ の N₂
points.gist: the first noun describes the second: my name, a Japanese teacher
points.explain: **の** joins two nouns. The noun **after** の is the main thing; the noun before it narrows it down: わたしの なまえ = my name, にほんごの せんせい = a Japanese teacher. It covers English “'s”, “of”, “at” and more.
points.tip: English order often flips: “a student **at** Tokyo University” is とうきょうだいがくの がくせい. The main noun always comes last.
points.yt: Japanese particle no possessive Genki lesson 1

s.en: My name is Mirage.
Ana is a student at the University of Tokyo.

c.w: 東京大学[とうきょうだいがく]

s.en: Tanaka-san is a Japanese teacher.
Kimura-san's major is history.
Mirage is a college student in Brazil.

c.w: 大学生[だいがくせい]です

lessons.title: Time, phone numbers and age
vocab: 電話番号[でんわばんごう]

points.title: 〜じ / 〜じはん — telling the time
points.pattern: (ごぜん / ごご) number + じ (+ はん)
points.gist: o'clock and half past
points.explain: Add **じ** to a number for o'clock: さんじ = 3:00. Add **はん** for half past: さんじはん = 3:30. **ごぜん** (a.m.) and **ごご** (p.m.) go **in front** of the time: ごご よじ = 4 p.m.
points.tip: Three hours are irregular: **よじ** (4), **しちじ** (7) and **くじ** (9). Never よんじ or きゅうじ.
points.yt: Japanese telling time ji han gozen gogo

s.en: It's three o'clock now.
It's nine thirty now.
It's 4 p.m. now.

c.w: 午後[ごご]四時[よじ]です

s.en: It's 7 a.m. now.

c.w: 午前[ごぜん]七時[しちじ]です

s.en: Japanese class is at 10:30.

c.w: 十時半[じゅうじはん]です

points.title: Phone numbers
points.pattern: digits の digits の digits
points.gist: read digit by digit; each dash becomes の
points.explain: Phone numbers are read **one digit at a time**, and each dash is spoken as **の**: 03-3721 = ゼロさんの さんななにいち. Ask with でんわばんごうは なんばんですか.
points.tip: Use the clearest readings for digits: **よん, なな, きゅう** (not し, しち, く), and ゼロ for 0.
points.yt: how to say phone numbers in Japanese

s.en: My phone number is 090-8135-2647.

c.w: 電話番号[でんわばんごう]
ゼロきゅうゼロのはちいちさんごのにろくよんななです

s.en: What's Tanaka-san's phone number?

c.w: 電話番号[でんわばんごう]

s.en: The school's phone number is 03-3721-4689.

c.w: 電話番号[でんわばんごう]
ゼロさんのさんななにいちのよんろくはちきゅうです

s.en: Is Ana's phone number 080-4462-9310?

c.w: 電話番号[でんわばんごう]
ゼロはちゼロのよんよんろくにのきゅうさんいちゼロですか

points.title: 〜さい — age
points.pattern: number + さい です
points.gist: how old someone is
points.explain: Age is a number + **さい**: じゅうきゅうさい = 19 years old. Ask with **なんさいですか**. A softer, politer way to ask an adult is おいくつですか.
points.tip: Watch the sound changes: **いっさい** (1, 21, 31…), **はっさい** (8), **じゅっさい** (10), and 20 is the special word **はたち**.
points.yt: Japanese age counter sai hatachi

s.en: I'm twenty.
Tanaka-san, how old are you?
Ana is nineteen.

c.w: 十九歳[じゅうきゅうさい]です

s.en: Tanaka-san is forty-one.

c.w: 四十一歳[よんじゅういっさい]です

s.en: My cat is eight.

points.title: 〜ねんせい — year in school
points.pattern: (school の) number + ねんせい です
points.gist: first-year, second-year student…
points.explain: **ねんせい** means “student in year …”: いちねんせい is a first-year. To name the school, put it in front with **の**: だいがくの にねんせい = a second-year college student. Ask with **なんねんせいですか**.
points.tip: Fourth year is **よねんせい**, not よんねんせい.
points.yt: Japanese nensei school year Genki lesson 1

s.en: I'm a second-year college student.

c.w: 二年生[にねんせい]です

s.en: Ana, what year are you in?

c.w: 何年生[なんねんせい]ですか

s.en: Ana is a first-year.

c.w: 一年生[いちねんせい]です

s.en: Kimura-san is a fourth-year at the University of Tokyo.

c.w: 東京大学[とうきょうだいがく]
四年生[よねんせい]です

s.en: My friend is a third-year in high school.

c.w: 三年生[さんねんせい]です

points.title: いま なんじですか — asking the time
points.pattern: いま なんじですか
points.gist: “what time is it (now)?”
points.explain: **なんじ** (“what time”) sits exactly where the answer will go: いま なんじですか → いま くじです. **いま** (“now”) is a time word, so it takes **no particle**. Put a place first to ask about another city: とうきょうは いま なんじですか.
points.tip: In the answer you can drop いま and just say the time: くじはんです.
points.yt: Japanese ima nanji desu ka what time is it

s.en: What time is it now?
What time is it in Tokyo now?
What time is the party?
Is it four o'clock now?
In São Paulo it's 10 p.m. now.

c.w: 午後[ごご]十時[じゅうじ]です

lessons.title: This, that, that over there
vocab: 郵便局[ゆうびんきょく]

points.title: これ・それ・あれ・どれ
points.pattern: これ / それ / あれ は N です
points.gist: this one, that one, that one over there, which one
points.explain: Japanese splits space into three zones: **これ** is near me, **それ** is near you, **あれ** is far from both of us. **どれ** asks “which one?” among three or more. They stand alone, like nouns: これは じしょです.
points.tip: どれ is a question word, so it never takes は. Say かさは どれですか, not どれは….
points.yt: Genki lesson 2 kore sore are dore

s.en: This is a dictionary.
What's that?
That over there is the library.

c.w: 図書館[としょかん]です

s.en: Mirage, which one is your umbrella?
Is that a Japanese book?

points.title: この・その・あの・どの + noun
points.pattern: この / その / あの / どの + N
points.gist: this ~, that ~, which ~ (always followed by a noun)
points.explain: **この, その, あの, どの** use the same three zones as これ/それ/あれ/どれ, but they **must** be followed by a noun: この とけい = this watch. The first sound tells the distance: こ near me, そ near you, あ over there, ど which?
points.tip: この can't stand alone. Say これは… or この + noun + は, never このは.
points.yt: Japanese kono sono ano dono explained

s.en: That person over there is a teacher.
Is that book a dictionary?
This bicycle is Tanaka-san's.

c.w: 自転車[じてんしゃ]です

s.en: Which person is Kimura-san?
Is that a Japanese watch?

points.title: ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ
points.pattern: N は ここ / そこ / あそこ / どこ です
points.gist: here, there, over there, where
points.explain: The same こ・そ・あ・ど family, now for **places**: ここ (here), そこ (there, near you), あそこ (over there), どこ (where?). The easiest way to ask for a place is **X は どこですか**; to answer, swap どこ for the place word.
points.tip: It's あ**そ**こ, not あこ: the one irregular member of the family.
points.yt: Japanese koko soko asoko doko

s.en: Where is the restroom?
The post office is over there.

c.w: 郵便局[ゆうびんきょく]

s.en: This is the library. (We are in it.)

c.w: 図書館[としょかん]です

s.en: The café is right there, near you.
Where am I? (lit. Where is here?)

points.title: だれの — whose?
points.pattern: だれ の N ですか
points.gist: asking who something belongs to
points.explain: **だれ** means “who”, so **だれの** means “whose”: これは だれの かさですか. To answer, put the owner before の. If the thing is obvious, drop it: わたしのです = it's mine.
points.tip: The noun after の can disappear, but の stays: アナさんのです (it's Ana's). アナさんです would mean “it's Ana”.
points.yt: Japanese dare no whose Genki lesson 2

s.en: Whose umbrella is this?
That's mine.
Whose is that umbrella over there?
That dictionary is the teacher's.
Is this bag Kimura-san's?

c.w: 木村[きむら]さんのですか

points.title: 〜えん — yen
points.pattern: number + えん
points.gist: prices in yen
points.explain: A price is a number + **えん**: ひゃくえん = ¥100. In a sentence it's just **X は 〜えん です**: コーヒーは にひゃくえんです. Note that Japanese says **えん**, not “yen”.
points.tip: 4 yen is **よえん**, not よんえん.
points.yt: Japanese yen prices en hyaku en

s.en: This book is 500 yen.

c.w: 五百円[ごひゃくえん]です

s.en: Coffee is 200 yen.

c.w: 二百円[にひゃくえん]です

s.en: That umbrella is 100 yen.
This tea is 90 yen.

c.w: 九十円[きゅうじゅうえん]です

s.en: Water is 110 yen.

c.w: 百十円[ひゃくじゅうえん]です

points.title: いくら — how much?
points.pattern: N は いくらですか
points.gist: asking the price
points.explain: **いくら** means “how much (money)?”. Like every question word, it sits where the answer will go: これは いくらですか → ごひゃくえんです. Point at the item with これ/それ/あれ or この/その/あの + noun.
points.tip: いくら is only for price. To ask someone's age you need なんさい, not いくら.
points.yt: Japanese shopping ikura desu ka

s.en: How much is this?
How much is that bag?
How much is that watch over there?
How much are these shoes?
How much is the sushi?

points.title: Numbers up to 100,000
points.pattern: まん → せん → ひゃく → じゅう → ones
points.gist: hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands: ひゃく · せん · まん
points.explain: Big numbers are built **largest unit first**: にまん ごせん = 25,000. **まん** (10,000) is its own unit, so 100,000 is じゅうまん, “ten ten-thousands”. 1,000 is just **せん**, but 10,000 is **いちまん**.
points.tip: Learn the sound changes: **さんびゃく, ろっぴゃく, はっぴゃく** (300, 600, 800) and **さんぜん, はっせん** (3,000, 8,000).
points.yt: Japanese big numbers hyaku sen man

s.en: This watch is 3,000 yen.

c.w: 三千円[さんぜんえん]です

s.en: That bag is 8,000 yen.

c.w: 八千円[はっせんえん]です

s.en: That bicycle over there is 25,000 yen.

c.w: 二万五千円[にまんごせんえん]です

s.en: This hat is 600 yen.

c.w: 六百円[ろっぴゃくえん]です

s.en: This camera is 98,000 yen.

c.w: 九万八千円[きゅうまんはっせんえん]です

points.title: 〜を ください — please give me
points.pattern: N を ください
points.gist: asking for something: “N, please”
points.explain: **ください** means “please give me”. Put what you want in front, marked with **を**: みずを ください. In a shop, これを ください (“I'll take this”) is all you need to buy something.
points.tip: ください asks for a thing to be handed to you. It is not a general “please” you can add to any sentence.
points.yt: Japanese wo kudasai shopping phrases

s.en: This one, please.
Water, please.
I'll take that umbrella, please.
Can I have the menu, please?
This hat, please.

points.title: 〜を おねがいします — N, please
points.pattern: N を おねがいします
points.gist: a softer request, perfect for ordering
points.explain: **おねがいします** (“I request”) is a softer, more polite way to ask. It is the natural choice when **ordering** food or asking staff for a service: コーヒーを おねがいします. In quick speech the を often drops: おかいけい おねがいします.
points.tip: Both work in shops, but おねがいします sounds gentler. With waiters and strangers, it is the safe choice.
points.yt: kudasai vs onegaishimasu difference

s.en: Coffee, please.
The check, please.
Tonkatsu, please.
Tea, please.
Ramen, please.

lessons.title: Also, is not, right?
lessons.titleJp: も・じゃないです・ね・よ

points.title: N も — also, too
points.pattern: N も Y です
points.gist: “N too”: も takes the place of は
points.explain: **も** means “too / also”, and it **replaces** は: わたしは がくせいです → わたしも がくせいです (“I'm a student too”). Put も right after the thing that is “also” the same.
points.tip: Never stack them: はも and もは are both wrong. も simply takes は's seat.
points.yt: Japanese particle mo also too

s.en: I'm a student too.
Ana is Brazilian too.
Is Kimura-san a college student too?

c.w: 大学生[だいがくせい]ですか

s.en: This umbrella is also 1,000 yen.
Tanaka-san is a teacher too.

points.title: N じゃないです — is not
points.pattern: X は N じゃないです
points.gist: the negative of です
points.explain: To say “X is **not** N”, swap です for **じゃないです**: にほんじんです → にほんじんじゃないです. **じゃありません** means exactly the same and sounds a bit more formal.
points.tip: In writing you'll also meet ではありません: it is just the full, careful form of じゃありません.
points.yt: Japanese ja nai desu ja arimasen noun negative

s.en: I'm not Japanese.

c.w: 日本人[にほんじん]じゃないです

s.en: That's not my umbrella.
Tanaka-san isn't a doctor.

c.w: 医者[いしゃ]じゃないです

s.en: Kimura-san isn't an office worker.

c.w: 会社員[かいしゃいん]じゃないです

s.en: That building over there isn't the library.

c.w: 図書館[としょかん]じゃないです

points.title: 〜ね / 〜よ — right? / you know
points.pattern: sentence + ね · sentence + よ
points.gist: ね looks for agreement, よ gives new information
points.explain: Add **ね** when you expect the listener to agree or want to check: おいしいですね (“it's tasty, isn't it?”). Add **よ** when you tell them something they don't know yet: わたしの かばんですよ (“it's my bag, you know”).
points.tip: Too much よ can sound pushy. ね is softer and keeps a conversation friendly.
points.yt: Japanese sentence ending particles ne yo

s.en: This ramen is delicious, isn't it?
That's my bag, you know.
Tanaka-san, you're a teacher, right?
That person over there is Ana's friend, you know.
That watch over there is expensive, isn't it?

lessons.title: Verbs: the polite present
vocab: to sleep, to go to bed (る-verb)

points.title: Three verb groups
points.pattern: る-verb · う-verb · irregular
points.gist: every verb belongs to one of three groups
points.explain: Dictionary forms all end in an **-u** sound. **る-verbs** end in -iru or -eru (たべる, ねる, みる): drop る and add ます. **う-verbs** are everything else (いく, のむ): change the last -u to -i and add ます, so のむ → のみます. Only two verbs are **irregular**: する → します and くる → きます.
points.tip: Some -eru/-iru verbs are secretly う-verbs: **かえる** → かえります, **はいる** → はいります. Learn them as exceptions.
points.yt: Japanese ru verbs u verbs irregular verbs Genki lesson 3

s.en: I'm going to bed.
Ana is going tomorrow.
Kimura-san is coming tomorrow.
I study every day.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]します

s.en: Tanaka-san, are you going home too?

points.title: 〜ます / 〜ません — do / don't
points.pattern: V-ます · V-ません
points.gist: polite present: “do / will” and “don't / won't”
points.explain: **ます** is the polite verb ending and **ません** is its negative. The same form covers habits (“I study every day”) and the future (“I'll go tomorrow”). Add **か** for a question: きますか (“are you coming?”).
points.tip: The verb comes **last**, so yes or no arrives only with the final word. Keep listening until the end of the sentence.
points.yt: Japanese masu masen polite form

s.en: I'm not studying today.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]しません

s.en: Tanaka-san, are you coming tomorrow?
I don't drink coffee.
Kimura-san isn't going home tonight.
I don't watch TV.
I'll go too.

points.title: を — the direct object
points.pattern: N を V
points.gist: marks the thing the action is done to
points.explain: **を** (read **o**) points at what the verb acts on. It answers “**what?**”: さかなを たべます (eat what? fish). It goes right after the object, and the verb usually follows soon after.
points.tip: Movement verbs like いく and くる don't take を for the destination. Going somewhere uses に or へ.
points.yt: Japanese particle wo direct object Genki lesson 3

s.en: I eat fish.
Ana listens to music.
Tanaka-san reads magazines.
What will you drink?
Kimura-san is watching a movie tonight.

points.title: で — where the action happens
points.pattern: Place で V
points.gist: the stage where an action takes place
points.explain: **で** marks the **place where an action happens**, like “at / in”: としょかんで べんきょうします. Picture で as the stage and the verb as the show on it.
points.tip: で needs an action. For simply going somewhere, use に/へ: としょかんに いきます.
points.yt: Japanese particle de place of action

s.en: I study at the library.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]します

s.en: I drink coffee at a café.
Ana watches movies at home.
Where do you eat lunch?
Tanaka-san plays tennis at school.

points.title: に / へ — the destination
points.pattern: Place に / へ いきます・きます・かえります
points.gist: the place you are moving toward
points.explain: With movement verbs (**いく, くる, かえる**), **に** or **へ** marks where you are going: がっこうに いきます. へ (read **e**) stresses the direction “toward”, に the arrival point, but for going places they are interchangeable.
points.tip: As a particle, へ is read **e**, just as は is read wa and を is read o.
points.yt: Japanese particles ni vs e direction

s.en: I go to school.
Ana is going to Kyoto.
Tanaka-san goes home.
Is Kimura-san coming to the university tomorrow?
Where are you going?

points.title: は — topic and contrast
points.pattern: X は …
points.gist: sets the frame of the sentence; can also contrast it
points.explain: **は** says “as for X…” and frames the whole sentence. It can take over almost any block: a time word, or even the object (then を disappears). When it does, it often adds **contrast**: おさけは のみません = “alcohol, I don't drink (other things, maybe)”.
points.tip: は replaces を, so never say をは. Contrast は is especially common in negative sentences.
points.yt: Japanese wa topic and contrast particle

s.en: On weekends I watch movies at home.
Alcohol, I don't drink.
Fish, I do eat.
Today I'm not studying.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]しません

s.en: Japanese, I study every day.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]します

points.title: Word order
points.pattern: Topic は · time · place で · object を · verb
points.gist: the verb is locked at the end; the rest can move
points.explain: Japanese has one strict rule: **the verb goes last**. The blocks before it can move, because each particle already says what job its block does. The most natural order is **topic → time → place → object → verb**.
points.tip: Lost in a long sentence? Read the verb first, then ask who, when, where and what: each particle answers one question.
points.yt: Japanese sentence word order explained beginner

s.en: I'm studying Japanese at the library today.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]します

s.en: Ana watches a movie at home on weekends.
Tanaka-san is going to Kyoto tomorrow.
Kimura-san drinks coffee at a café every day.
I'm having dinner at home tonight.

lessons.title: When and how often
lessons.titleJp: いつ・よく・〜ませんか

points.title: に with clock times and days
points.pattern: Time に V
points.gist: “at 7 o'clock”, “on Saturday”
points.explain: Points you can find on a clock or a calendar take **に**: しちじに おきます (at 7), どようびに (on Saturday). Ask with **なんじに** (“at what time?”).
points.tip: Add **ごろ** for “around”: ろくじごろ. After ごろ the に is optional.
points.yt: Japanese particle ni time days of the week

s.en: I get up at seven.
Ana plays tennis on Saturday.
Tanaka-san goes to bed at eleven.
What time do you go home?
Kimura-san eats dinner around six.

points.title: Time words without に
points.pattern: きょう / あした / まいにち + … V
points.gist: relative time words take no particle
points.explain: Words measured **from today**, like きょう, あした, こんばん, まいにち, いま and いつ, stand alone with **no particle**: あした だいがくに いきます. They usually come near the start of the sentence.
points.tip: あしたに is a classic learner mistake. If the meaning changes depending on today's date, it takes no に.
points.yt: Japanese time expressions with and without ni

s.en: I study Japanese every day.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]します

s.en: Are you going to the university tomorrow?
Ana is watching a movie at home tonight.
Tanaka-san drinks coffee every morning.
When are you going to Kyoto?

points.title: How often: frequency adverbs
points.pattern: Topic は + いつも / よく / ときどき + … V
points.gist: always, often, sometimes, not much, never
points.explain: Frequency words usually sit right after the topic, before the rest of the sentence: **いつも** (always), **よく** (often), **ときどき** (sometimes). **あまり** (not much) and **ぜんぜん** (not at all) must pair with a **negative** verb.
points.tip: ぜんぜん たべます is wrong: ぜんぜん and あまり need 〜ません.
points.yt: Japanese frequency adverbs itsumo yoku tokidoki amari zenzen

s.en: I often go to cafés.
Ana sometimes eats ramen.
Tanaka-san doesn't watch TV much.
Kimura-san always studies at the library.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]します

s.en: I don't drink alcohol at all.

points.title: 〜ませんか — invitations
points.pattern: V-ませんか
points.gist: “won't you…?”: a polite invitation
points.explain: To invite someone, ask in the **negative**: えいがを みませんか (“won't you watch a movie (with me)?”). It sounds polite because it leaves room to say no. Add **いっしょに** (“together”) to make it warmer.
points.tip: To decline gently, Japanese avoids a flat “no”: すみません、ちょっと… (“sorry, that's a bit…”) is enough.
points.yt: Japanese masen ka invitation

s.en: Would you like to watch a movie together?
Do you want to play tennis on Saturday?
Shall we have ramen tonight?
Would you like to study together at the library tomorrow?

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]しませんか

s.en: Why don't we have coffee at a café on Sunday?

points.title: あります / います — there is
points.pattern: Place に N が あります / います
points.gist: saying that something or someone exists
points.explain: **います** is for living things that move on their own (people, animals); **あります** is for everything else (things, buildings, plants, events). The place takes **に** and the thing that exists takes **が**: こうえんに いぬが います.
points.tip: Trees are あります: alive, but they don't move. あります also means “to have” plans: あした クラスが あります.
points.yt: Japanese arimasu vs imasu

s.en: There's a dog in the park.
There's a convenience store over there.
Is there a library at the university?
We have a cat at home.
I have class tomorrow.

points.title: Location words
points.pattern: A の うえ / した / なか / まえ … に
points.gist: on, under, inside, in front of, next to…
points.explain: Position words are **nouns**, linked to the reference object with **の**: つくえの うえ = “the desk's top”, so “on the desk”. Then add **に** for where something is: つくえの うえに ほんが あります. The main ones: うえ, した, なか, まえ, うしろ, みぎ, ひだり, となり, ちかく.
points.tip: English order flips: “**on** the desk” is つくえの うえ. The reference object comes first, the position word second.
points.yt: Japanese location words ue shita naka mae ushiro

s.en: There's a book on the desk.
There's a cat under the chair.
There's a convenience store next to the bank.
What's in the bag?
There's a park in front of the station.

points.title: N は 〜に あります — where is it?
points.pattern: N は Place に あります / います
points.gist: telling where something already known is
points.explain: When the thing is already the **topic** (you ask or tell where it is), it takes **は** and comes first: ぎんこうは えきの ちかくに あります. Compare: 〜に 〜が あります introduces something new; 〜は 〜に あります locates something you both know about.
points.tip: A handy shortcut: X は Place です also works. ぎんこうは あそこです.
points.yt: Japanese wa ni arimasu location sentences

s.en: Where is the library?
The cat is under the desk.
The bank is near the station.
Tanaka-san is behind the tree.
My bag is to the right of the chair.
The restroom is on the left.

points.title: でした / じゃなかったです — was / was not
points.pattern: X は N でした · X は N じゃなかったです
points.gist: the past of です and じゃないです
points.explain: The past of です is **でした** (“was”). The past of じゃないです is **じゃなかったです** (“was not”); a more formal version is じゃありませんでした. Only the very end of the sentence changes.
points.tip: Don't try to put the past on the time word: きのうは にちようびでした. Only the ending carries the tense.
points.yt: Japanese deshita ja nakatta desu past tense nouns

s.en: Yesterday was Sunday.

c.w: 日曜日[にちようび]でした

s.en: The test wasn't on Monday.

c.w: 月曜日[げつようび]じゃなかったです

s.en: Last year Kimura-san was a third-year.

c.w: 三年生[さんねんせい]でした

s.en: Was the party on Saturday?

c.w: 土曜日[どようび]でしたか

s.en: Yesterday's dinner was ramen.
Last week wasn't a holiday.

c.w: 休[やす]みじゃなかったです

points.title: 〜ました / 〜ませんでした — did / didn't
points.pattern: V-ました · V-ませんでした
points.gist: the polite past of verbs
points.explain: Swap **ます** for **ました** (did) and **ません** for **ませんでした** (didn't): たべます → たべました → たべませんでした. The part before ます never changes, so if you know the ます form, you already know the past.
points.tip: Questions just add か: なにを しましたか (“what did you do?”).
points.yt: Japanese mashita masen deshita past tense verbs

s.en: I studied at the library yesterday.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]しました

s.en: I didn't eat breakfast this morning.
Ana took photos in Kyoto.
What did you do on the weekend?
Kimura-san didn't come to the party.
Tanaka-san waited for a friend at the station.

lessons.title: And, with, also, a lot
lessons.titleJp: と・も・じかん・たくさん

points.title: N と N — and
points.pattern: N と N + particle
points.gist: joining nouns: “A and B”
points.explain: **と** ties nouns into one block: パンと みずを かいました. The block's own particle (を, は, に…) comes only **after the last noun**.
points.tip: と joins **nouns** only. Don't use it to join sentences like “I ate and slept”: that needs different grammar later.
points.yt: Japanese particle to and with

s.en: I bought bread and water.
My father and mother are teachers.
Ana speaks Japanese and English.
Yesterday I bought shoes and a bag at the department store.
I have Japanese class on Mondays and Wednesdays.

points.title: N と — together with
points.pattern: Person と V
points.gist: doing something with someone
points.explain: After a person, **と** means “with”: ともだちと えいがを みました. Add **いっしょに** (“together”) for emphasis, or say **ひとりで** for “alone”.
points.tip: と is for company, not for tools: “with chopsticks” uses a different particle you'll meet later.
points.yt: Japanese to together with issho ni

s.en: I watched a movie with a friend.
Ana went to Kyoto with Kimura-san.
I had lunch with my mother.
Who did you talk with?
On the weekend I went shopping by myself.

points.title: も after other particles
points.pattern: に・で・と + も → にも・でも・とも
points.gist: adding “too” to a place, time or person
points.explain: **も** replaces は, が and を: コーヒーも のみました. But with **に, で, へ and と** it stacks **after** them: きょうとにも (to Kyoto too), としょかんでも (at the library too), アナさんとも (with Ana too).
points.tip: をも and がも don't exist: those two particles always disappear before も.
points.yt: Japanese mo with other particles nimo demo tomo

s.en: I also study at the library.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]します

s.en: Ana went to Kyoto too.
Tanaka-san talked with Kimura-san too.
I drank coffee too.
Are you coming on Saturday too?

points.title: 〜じかん — for X hours
points.pattern: number + じかん (ぐらい) V
points.gist: how long something lasts
points.explain: **じかん** counts hours of duration: にじかん = for two hours. Add **はん** for “and a half” (いちじかんはん) and **ぐらい** for “about”. Ask with **なんじかん**. A length of time takes **no に**.
points.tip: Don't mix them up: にじ = 2 o'clock (a point in time), にじかん = two hours (a length of time).
points.yt: Japanese jikan duration hours

s.en: I study Japanese for an hour every day.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]します

s.en: Yesterday I talked with Ana for two hours.
How many hours did you sleep?
Kimura-san played video games for about three hours.

c.w: 三時間[さんじかん]ぐらい

s.en: I waited at the station for an hour and a half.

c.w: 一時間半[いちじかんはん]

points.title: たくさん — a lot
points.pattern: N を / が たくさん V
points.gist: a lot, many
points.explain: **たくさん** (“a lot”) usually goes **right before the verb**, after the noun and its particle: しゃしんを たくさん とりました. It can also come before a noun with の: たくさんの ひと (a lot of people).
points.tip: たくさん is never used with a negative to mean “not much”. For that, use あまり 〜ません.
points.yt: Japanese takusan a lot many

s.en: I took a lot of photos in Kyoto.
There are a lot of books in the library.
Ana bought a lot of bread yesterday.
There were a lot of people in the park.
Lots of friends came to the party.

points.title: い-adjectives
points.pattern: N は Adj-い です
points.gist: describing words that end in い
points.explain: An **い-adjective** describes something and always ends in い: たかい, あたらしい, おもしろい. Put it before **です** and it becomes the predicate: "this camera **is expensive**". The adjective already means "is expensive" — です just adds politeness.
points.tip: The い belongs to the word: it is たかいです, never たかです. Nothing goes between the adjective and です.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 5 i-adjectives

s.en: This camera is expensive.
Tanaka's room is big.
It's cold today, isn't it?
This game is fun, you know.
Is that restaurant cheap?

points.title: な-adjectives
points.pattern: N は Adj です
points.gist: adjectives that act like nouns
points.explain: **な-adjectives** behave like nouns: before です they stand bare — しずかです, ゆうめいです. They are named after the **な** they need in front of a noun (see "Adjective + noun"). Learn each new adjective together with its type.
points.tip: きれい, ゆうめい and きらい end in い but are な-adjectives. The い is part of the word, not an ending.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 5 na-adjectives

s.en: This town is quiet.
Mt. Fuji is famous.
Ana's room is clean, isn't it?
I'm free today.
Is Tanaka doing well?

points.title: Present affirmative and negative
points.pattern: Adj-い → 〜くないです · Adj-な → 〜じゃないです
points.gist: い→くない for い-adjectives; じゃない for な-adjectives
points.explain: To say "is **not**", an **い-adjective** swaps its final い for **くない**: たかい → たか**くない**です. A **な-adjective** works like a noun and adds **じゃない**: しずか**じゃない**です. One irregular: いい (good) becomes **よくない**.
points.tip: きれい is a な-adjective, so it is きれいじゃないです — not きれくないです. And never say いくないです.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 5 adjectives negative kunai janai

s.en: This book isn't expensive.
My town isn't quiet.

c.w: 静[しず]かじゃないです

s.en: This hotel isn't good.
Japanese isn't difficult, you know.

c.w: 難[むずか]しくないですよ

s.en: Kimura isn't free today.

points.title: Adjective + noun
points.pattern: Adj-い N · Adj-な な N
points.gist: put the adjective right before the noun
points.explain: To describe a noun directly, place the adjective **in front of it**. い-adjectives go in as they are: あたらしい スマホ. な-adjectives add **な**: しずか**な** まち. The adjective + noun block then acts like one noun and takes any particle. To ask "what kind of…?", use **どんな**.
points.tip: No の between adjective and noun: おもしろい ほん, not おもしろいの ほん.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 5 adjectives before nouns donna

s.en: This is a new smartphone.
Kyoto is a beautiful city.
I bought a big bag.
I read a book at a quiet café.
What kind of person is Tanaka?

points.title: Past tense of adjectives
points.pattern: Adj-い → 〜かったです / 〜くなかったです · Adj-な → 〜でした / 〜じゃなかったです
points.gist: い-adjectives change their own ending; な-adjectives change です
points.explain: An **い-adjective** carries the tense itself: たかい → たか**かった**です (was expensive), たかくない → たかく**なかった**です (wasn't). A **な-adjective** works like a noun: しずか**でした**, しずか**じゃなかった**です. いい again switches to よ: **よかった**です.
points.tip: たかいでした is the classic mistake. With い-adjectives the past goes on the adjective, and です stays です.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 5 adjectives past tense

s.en: Hokkaido was cold.
Last week's homework was easy.
That movie wasn't interesting.

c.w: おもしろくなかったです

s.en: Ana's room wasn't quiet.

c.w: 静[しず]かじゃなかったです

s.en: The weather in Kyoto was good.

points.title: すき(な) / きらい(な)
points.pattern: N は X が すきです
points.gist: what you like takes が, because すき is an adjective
points.explain: **すき** (liked) and **きらい** (disliked) are **な-adjectives**, not verbs. So the thing you like is marked with **が**, not を: ねこ**が** すきです — literally "cats are likable (to me)". Add だい for a strong version: **だいすき** (love). Before a noun they take な: すきな いろ (favorite color).
points.tip: ねこを すきです is wrong — すき is not a verb. For "not really", use あまり + negative: あまり すきじゃないです, softer than きらいです.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 5 suki kirai

s.en: I like cats.
Kimura hates bugs.
Mirage loves video games.
What is your favorite color?
Tanaka doesn't like fish very much.

points.title: 〜ましょう / 〜ましょうか
points.pattern: V-ましょう · V-ましょうか
points.gist: "let's…!" and "shall we…?"
points.explain: Swap ます for **ましょう** and you are proposing to do something together: いき**ましょう** (let's go!). Add か — **ましょうか** — for a softer "shall we…?" that leaves the choice open. With a question word it asks for a plan: なにを しましょうか (what shall we do?).
points.tip: ましょう assumes you will do it together. To invite someone first, use ませんか; once they say yes, carry on with ましょう.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 5 mashou mashouka

s.en: Let's have lunch together.
Shall we meet at the station?
What shall we do on the weekend?
Let's play tennis in the park tomorrow.
Shall we go home by taxi?

points.title: ひとつ, ふたつ… and counters
points.pattern: N を [number + counter] V
points.gist: the number goes after the noun and its particle, right before the verb
points.explain: Japanese counts with **counters** stuck to the number. For general things use the native set: **ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ, いつつ…** up to **とお** (10). Flat things use **〜まい** (いちまい, にまい) and long things **〜ほん** (いっぽん, にほん, さんぼん). The usual order is noun + particle + number + verb: りんごを みっつ かいました. Ask with **いくつ** (how many?).
points.tip: The number does not need a particle of its own: みっつ かいました, not みっつを かいました.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 5 counting hitotsu futatsu counters

s.en: I bought three apples.
Two coffees, please.
Please give me one sheet of paper.
There are five pens on the desk.
How many mandarin oranges did you eat?

points.title: Degree words: とても, ちょっと, ぜんぜん
points.pattern: とても Adj · ちょっと Adj · ぜんぜん + negative
points.gist: turn the volume up or down
points.explain: Put a degree word right **before** the adjective or verb it measures. **とても** = very. **ちょっと** = a little. **ぜんぜん** = not at all, and it needs a **negative** ending (like あまり, "not very").
points.tip: ぜんぜん with an affirmative ending sounds wrong in standard Japanese. Pair it with ない or ません: ぜんぜん たかくないです.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 5 totemo chotto zenzen

s.en: This ramen is very tasty.
It's a little cold today.
I don't drink alcohol at all.
The Japanese homework wasn't difficult at all.

c.w: 難[むずか]しくなかったです

s.en: I studied a little yesterday.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]しました

lessons.title: The て-form
lessons.titleJp: たべて・のんで・して
vocab: 写真[しゃしん]を撮[と]る

points.title: Forming it: る-verbs
points.pattern: V-る → V-て
points.gist: drop る, add て
points.explain: The **て-form** is a connector: it has no tense of its own, and whatever follows it decides the meaning. For **る-verbs** it is easy: drop る and add **て** — たべる → たべ**て**, みる → み**て**. From the ます-form, just swap ます for て: ねます → ねて. In these examples the て-form links two actions ("…and then…"); you will practice that use in the next lesson.
points.tip: The て-form is not a past tense: たべて alone never means "ate". The last verb of the sentence carries the tense.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 6 te form ru verbs

s.en: I get up at seven and take a shower.
I eat dinner and watch TV.
I opened the window and looked outside.
I watched a movie and went to bed at eleven.
I borrowed a book at the library and went home.

points.title: Forming it: う-verbs
points.pattern: う・つ・る → って · む・ぶ・ぬ → んで · く → いて · ぐ → いで · す → して
points.gist: the ending depends on the last sound of the verb
points.explain: **う-verbs** change by their last sound, in five groups: う・つ・る → **って** (かう → かって); む・ぶ・ぬ → **んで** (のむ → のんで); く → **いて** (かく → かいて); ぐ → **いで** (およぐ → およいで); す → **して** (はなす → はなして). Chanting the groups (or singing one of the many "te-form songs") is the fastest way to lock them in.
points.tip: Some verbs that end in -eru/-iru are う-verbs: かえる → かえって (not かえて), はいる → はいって.
points.yt: Japanese te form song u verbs

s.en: I bought bread at the convenience store and ate it.
I drank coffee at a café and read the newspaper.
I wrote an email to a friend and went to sleep.
I went home and made dinner.
I talked with my teacher and went to the library.

points.title: Irregulars: して / きて / いって
points.pattern: する → して · くる → きて · いく → いって
points.gist: three forms to memorize
points.explain: **する** becomes **して**, and so does every する-verb: べんきょうする → べんきょう**して**. **くる** becomes **きて**. **いく** is a normal う-verb everywhere except here: its て-form is **いって**, not いいて.
points.tip: きて can be "come" (くる) or "wear" (きる). The kanji tells them apart: 来て vs 着て.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 6 te form irregular verbs iku

s.en: I did my homework and then played video games.
I went to Tokyo and met a friend.
Ana came to school and studied Japanese.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]しました

s.en: I went to Kyoto and took lots of photos.
On the weekend I cleaned my room and did the laundry.

c.w: 洗濯[せんたく]しました

points.title: 〜てください
points.pattern: V-て ください
points.gist: a polite request: "please do…"
points.explain: Put **ください** after a て-form to ask someone to do something: みて**ください** (please look). Everything else in the sentence stays the same; only the ending changes. You will hear it from teachers, shop staff and station announcements all the time.
points.tip: Use it to ask, not to offer. After a plain noun, ください means "please give me": みずを ください.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 6 te kudasai

s.en: Please write your name here.
Please wait a moment.
Please speak in Japanese.
Please say it once more.
Please close the window.

points.title: Action て action (and then)
points.pattern: V1-て V2-て V3-ます
points.gist: line up actions in order; only the last verb shows tense
points.explain: Chain actions with the て-form to say "I did A, and then B". You can link two, three or more. **Only the last verb** carries the tense and politeness, so the whole chain is past if it ends in ました, and a request if it ends in てください.
points.tip: Actions are listed in the order they happen. Keep the last verb in a full form — a sentence cannot end on a bare て-form in polite speech.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 6 te form and then

s.en: I eat breakfast and go to school.
Yesterday I met a friend in Shibuya and ate ramen.
I went home, took a shower and went to bed.
On the weekend I went shopping with friends and then to karaoke.
Please get off the train at the station and take the bus.

lessons.title: May I / must not
lessons.titleJp: 〜てもいいです・〜てはいけません

points.title: 〜てもいいです
points.pattern: V-て も いいです(か)
points.gist: permission: "you may…" / "may I…?"
points.explain: **てもいいです** literally says "even if you do it, it's good" — that is, "it's OK to…". Add **か** to ask for permission: とって**もいいですか** (may I take one?). Typical answers: はい、どうぞ (sure, go ahead) or すみません、ちょっと… (sorry, that's a bit…).
points.tip: Keep the も in polite speech. The shorter とっていい？ exists, but it is casual.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 6 te mo ii desu

s.en: May I take photos here?

c.w: 撮[と]ってもいいですか

s.en: May I use this computer?

c.w: 使[つか]ってもいいですか

s.en: May I open the window?

c.w: 開[あ]けてもいいですか

s.en: You can drink water in the classroom.

c.w: 飲[の]んでもいいですよ

s.en: May I go to your house tomorrow, Ana?

c.w: 行[い]ってもいいですか

points.title: 〜てはいけません
points.pattern: V-て は いけません
points.gist: prohibition: "you must not…"
points.explain: **てはいけません** means "it won't do if you…" — a firm "you must not". It states **rules**: signs, school, parents. The は here is pronounced **wa**.
points.tip: It sounds strict, so it is not for asking a favor. For "please don't…" you will learn 〜ないでください in lesson 8.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 6 te wa ikemasen

s.en: You must not take photos here.

c.w: 撮[と]ってはいけません

s.en: You must not play video games in the classroom.
You must not enter the temple with your shoes on.

c.w: 入[はい]ってはいけません

s.en: Children must not drink alcohol.

c.w: 飲[の]んではいけません

s.en: You must not smoke in the park.

c.w: 吸[す]ってはいけません

points.title: 〜から (because)
points.pattern: [reason] から、[result]
points.gist: から after the reason: "…, so…"
points.explain: Say the **reason first**, add **から**, then the result: しごとが あります**から**、のみません ("I have work, so I won't drink"). English often puts "because" later; Japanese builds up to the main point at the end. In polite speech the reason keeps です/ます: 〜ですから, 〜ますから.
points.tip: から goes right after the reason, never before it. When you answer "why?" (どうしてですか), you can give only the reason and end with から.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 6 kara because

s.en: I have work tomorrow, so I won't drink tonight.
It's hot, so let's open the window.
Today is Sunday, so the bank is closed.

c.w: 日曜日[にちようび]です

s.en: I don't have money, so I won't go on a trip.
This shop is cheap, so I come here often.

points.title: 〜ましょうか (offering help)
points.pattern: V-ましょうか
points.gist: offer to do something for someone: "shall I…?"
points.explain: In lesson 5, ましょうか meant "shall **we**…?". The same form also **offers help**: "shall **I**…?". Context decides: if only you will do it, it is an offer. Reply with ありがとうございます。おねがいします (yes, please) or いいえ、だいじょうぶです (no, I'm fine).
points.tip: Don't offer with てください — that asks the other person to act. Offers use ましょうか.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 6 mashou ka offering help

s.en: Shall I carry that bag?
Shall I take a picture (for you)?
It's cold, so shall I close the window?
Shall I help with the cooking?

c.w: 手伝[てつだ]いましょうか

s.en: Shall I call Tanaka (for you)?

c.w: 電話[でんわ]しましょうか

lessons.title: 〜ている
vocab: 電話番号[でんわばんごう]

points.title: Action in progress
points.pattern: V-て います
points.gist: "is doing" — an action going on right now
points.explain: て-form + **います** describes an action **in progress**: いま テレビを みて**います** (I'm watching TV now). It also covers ongoing habits: まいにち べんきょうしています (I study every day, these days). Only います changes for tense and negation: みていました, みていません.
points.tip: This いる is the same "to exist" いる, so it conjugates like a る-verb: います, いません, いました.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 7 te iru

s.en: I'm watching TV now.
Kimura is cooking in the kitchen.
What is Tanaka doing now?
It's raining outside.
Last night Mirage was playing video games.

points.title: Resulting state
points.pattern: V-て います (state)
points.gist: a change happened and its result is still true
points.explain: With verbs of **change**, ている describes the **state left behind**, not an action in motion. けっこんしています = got married and still is → "**is married**". Likewise しっています (knows), すんでいます (lives in), めがねを かけています (wears glasses). Ask yourself: is it moving, or is it a result that stays?
points.tip: "I don't know" is しりません, not しっていません — the one odd negative. And すむ takes に: おおさかに すんでいます.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 7 te iru resulting state

s.en: My older sister is married.

c.w: 結婚[けっこん]しています

s.en: Ana lives in Osaka now.
Do you know Tanaka's phone number?

c.w: 電話番号[でんわばんごう]

s.en: My father wears glasses.
I don't know that person's name.

lessons.title: Describing people
lessons.titleJp: かみが ながい・〜くて
vocab: height, back (せが たかい = tall)

points.title: N は X が Adj
points.pattern: N は X が Adj
points.gist: "as for N, X is…" — describe someone by a feature
points.explain: To describe a feature, Japanese uses two layers: **は** marks who you are talking about, **が** marks the feature, and the adjective describes it. アナさんは かみが ながいです = "As for Ana, the hair is long" → "Ana has long hair". There is no verb "have": the adjective does the work.
points.tip: "Tall" for a person is せが たかい (literally "the back is high"); "short" is せが ひくい — みじかい is for hair or things.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 7 describing people wa ga

s.en: Ana has long hair.
Tanaka is tall.
This dog has big ears, doesn't it?
Tokyo has a lot of people.
Mirage has a deep voice.

points.title: Joining descriptions with くて / で
points.pattern: Adj-い → 〜くて · Adj-な / N → 〜で
points.gist: link two descriptions: "X and Y"
points.explain: To say two things about the same topic, put the first one in its **て-form**. い-adjectives drop い and add **くて**: やすい → やす**くて**. な-adjectives and nouns add **で**: しずか**で**, がくせい**で**. The tense lives in the **last** part: にぎやかで たのし**かった**です (it was lively and fun).
points.tip: いい becomes よくて. And don't join adjectives with と — と only links nouns.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 7 kute de adjectives

s.en: This place is cheap and tasty.
My room is quiet and bright.
Tanaka is a student, and he is twenty.
Kimura is smart and kind.
Yesterday's party was lively and fun.

lessons.title: Going to do · counting people
lessons.titleJp: 〜に いく・ひとり、ふたり

points.title: Verb stem + に いく / くる / かえる
points.pattern: [place] に [V-stem] に いきます
points.gist: go / come / go back somewhere in order to do something
points.explain: Take the ます-form and drop ます — that is the **stem** (かいます → かい). Add **に** and a movement verb: かい**に** いきます (go to buy). Stem + に is the **purpose** of the trip. The destination keeps its own に or へ: デパートへ ふくを かいに いきます.
points.tip: With する-verbs you can also use the noun alone: べんきょうに いきます. Only movement verbs (いく, くる, かえる) fit this pattern.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 7 verb stem ni iku purpose

s.en: I'm going to the department store to buy clothes.
Ana came to Japan to study Japanese.
I went home to get my wallet.
Let's go to the beach to swim this weekend.
Kimura goes to the park to run every week.

points.title: ひとり, ふたり, 〜にん
points.pattern: N が [number]にん います
points.gist: counting people
points.explain: People have their own counter. The first two are special: **ひとり** (1) and **ふたり** (2). From three on, it is number + **にん**: さんにん, ごにん, じゅうにん — but 4 is **よにん** and 7 is **しちにん** (or ななにん). Ask with **なんにん**. Like other counters, it sits right before the verb. ひとりで means "alone, by oneself".
points.tip: Never いちにん or ににん. And "four people" is よにん, not よんにん.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 7 counting people hitori futari

s.en: There are four people in my family.
I have two younger sisters.
How many students are in the Japanese class?
Seven people came to the party.
I went to Kyoto by myself.

points.title: Dictionary form and ない
points.pattern: のみます → のむ / のまない · たべます → たべる / たべない
points.gist: the plain present: dictionary form ("do") and ない form ("don't")
points.explain: Every ます-form has a **short (plain) form** with the same meaning, minus the politeness. Affirmative = the **dictionary form**: たべる, のむ, する. Negative = the **ない form**: る-verbs drop る + **ない** (たべない); う-verbs change -u to -a + **ない** (のむ → のまない, かえる → かえらない). Irregulars: する → しない, くる → **こない**, and ある → just **ない**.
points.tip: Verbs ending in う take わ, not あ: かう → かわない, あう → あわない. The negative of ある is ない, never あらない.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 8 short form dictionary nai

s.en: I study Japanese every day.
I don't watch TV much.
Are you going to school tomorrow?
Tanaka isn't coming today.
We don't have a car at home.

points.title: Adjectives and nouns in short form
points.pattern: たかい / たかくない · ひまだ / ひまじゃない · がくせいだ / がくせいじゃない
points.gist: drop です; な-adjectives and nouns use だ
points.explain: For **い-adjectives**, just drop です: たかいです → **たかい**, たかくないです → **たかくない**. **な-adjectives and nouns** swap です for **だ**: ひまだ, がくせいだ, and the negative drops です: ひま**じゃない**. In casual questions だ disappears completely: ひま？ (are you free?).
points.tip: Never add だ to an い-adjective: たかいだ is wrong.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 8 short form adjectives nouns da

s.en: This manga is fun!
I'm free today.
That person isn't a teacher.

c.w: 先生[せんせい]じゃないよ

s.en: This room isn't very big.
Is tomorrow a day off?

points.title: Casual speech
points.pattern: short form (+ よ / ね), rising tone for questions
points.gist: talking with friends: short forms, no か, fewer particles
points.explain: With friends and family, Japanese uses **short forms** instead of です/ます. Questions usually drop **か** and simply rise in tone: いく？ Particles like は and を are often left out, and 〜ない？ makes a casual invitation (like ませんか). Keep it for people close to you, not teachers or strangers.
points.tip: うん (yeah) and ううん (nope) replace はい and いいえ. A bare だ at the end can sound blunt, so people often add よ or ね.
points.yt: Japanese casual speech plain form Genki lesson 8

s.en: What are you doing today?
Want to watch a movie together?
This game is really fun, huh.
Is Mirage coming tomorrow?
I'm going too.

lessons.title: Quoting and giving opinions
lessons.titleJp: 〜と おもいます・〜と いっていました

points.title: 〜と おもいます
points.pattern: [short form] と おもいます
points.gist: "I think (that)…"
points.explain: To give an opinion or a guess, put a **short-form** sentence before **と おもいます**: あめが ふる**と おもいます** (I think it will rain). **と** works like quotation marks around the thought. Nouns and な-adjectives need **だ**: いい ひと**だ**と おもいます. For "I don't think…", make the quoted part negative: こないと おもいます.
points.tip: No です/ます inside the quote: たかいと おもいます, not たかいですと. And don't forget だ after nouns and な-adjectives.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 8 to omoimasu

s.en: I think it will rain tomorrow.
I think Tanaka is a good person.
I don't think that restaurant is expensive.
I don't think Kimura eats meat.
I think Japanese trains are convenient.

points.title: 〜と いっていました
points.pattern: [person] は [short form] と いっていました
points.gist: report what someone said: "X said that…"
points.explain: To pass on what someone told you, use **[short form] と いっていました** — "they were saying that…". The quote is in short form, exactly as with おもいます. The person who said it usually comes first with **は**.
points.tip: The quote is marked with と, not を. いいました also works, but いっていました sounds more natural when relaying a message.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 8 to itte imashita

s.en: Tanaka said he's busy tomorrow.
Ana said she's going to Japan next month.
The teacher said Friday is a day off.
Kimura said he isn't free this weekend.
My mother said she'll make sushi tonight.

lessons.title: Don't · I like doing · something/nothing
lessons.titleJp: 〜ないで・〜のが すき・なにか

points.title: 〜ないでください
points.pattern: V-ない で ください
points.gist: "please don't…"
points.explain: Take the **ない form** and add **でください** to ask someone **not** to do something: みない**でください** (please don't look). It is the negative partner of 〜てください. Among friends, just 〜ないで: いかないで！
points.tip: It is ないで, not なくて, in requests. For general rules (signs, school), 〜てはいけません fits better.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 8 naide kudasai

s.en: Please don't park your bicycle here.

c.w: 止[と]めないでください

s.en: Please don't forget your homework.

c.w: 忘[わす]れないでください

s.en: Please don't talk loudly in the library.

c.w: 話[はな]さないでください

s.en: Please don't eat this cake, OK?

c.w: 食[た]べないでくださいね

s.en: Please don't go home yet.

c.w: 帰[かえ]らないでください

points.title: Verb + のが すき / じょうず
points.pattern: V-dict の が すきです / じょうずです
points.gist: の turns a verb into a noun: "doing X"
points.explain: すき, きらい, じょうず and へた describe **nouns**. To use a **verb** there, add **の** to its dictionary form: およぐ → およぐ**の** ("swimming"). Now it is a noun and takes **が**: およぐのが すきです (I like swimming). The verb can keep its object: えを かくのが じょうずです (is good at drawing).
points.tip: Use the dictionary form before の, never the ます-form: みるのが すき, not みますのが. And じょうず praises others — about yourself it sounds like bragging.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 8 no ga suki nominalizer

s.en: I like playing video games.
Ana is good at drawing.
Mirage hates getting up in the morning.
Tanaka is bad at cooking.
What do you like doing on weekends?

points.title: が (subject particle)
points.pattern: question word が … · answer が …
points.gist: が points at exactly who or what
points.explain: **は** sets the topic ("as for…"); **が** points at the subject and puts a spotlight on it. Question words can never be the topic, so they always take **が**: だれ**が** きましたか (who came?). The answer keeps が: たなかさん**が** きました. Think of が as "it's **this one**".
points.tip: Never だれは or なには. If the question uses が, the answer uses が too.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 8 ga particle wa vs ga

s.en: Who came yesterday?
Tanaka came.
What does Ana like?
Which one is your bag, Mirage?
I'll go. (I'm the one who'll go.)

points.title: なにか / なにも
points.pattern: なにか + affirmative · なにも + negative
points.gist: "something" vs "nothing"
points.explain: **なにか** = "something", used in affirmative sentences and questions: なにか たべましたか (did you eat anything?). **なにも** + a **negative** verb = "nothing": なにも たべませんでした. が and を usually disappear after them. The same pattern works for people: だれか (someone), だれも (no one).
points.tip: なにも needs a negative ending: なにも たべました is wrong — say なにも たべませんでした.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki lesson 8 nanika nanimo

s.en: Did you eat anything this morning?
I didn't eat anything yesterday.
Did you do anything on the weekend?
There's nothing in the fridge.
No one came to the party.

points.title: た / なかった — short past forms
points.pattern: V-た · V-なかった · A-かった · N / na-A だった
points.gist: the plain past: did / didn't, was / wasn't
points.explain: Short past forms are the casual twins of 〜ました and 〜でした. If you know the **て-form**, you already know the past: swap て→**た** and で→**だ** (食べて→食べた, 読んで→読んだ). For "didn't", take the ない form and change it to **なかった**. い-adjectives end in **かった** (高かった); nouns and な-adjectives use **だった / じゃなかった**.
points.tip: いい is irregular: "was good" is よかった and "wasn't good" is よくなかった — never いかった.
points.yt: Genki lesson 9 short form past tense Japanese

s.en: I ate ramen with Ana yesterday.
I didn't go to school today.
The weather was nice on Sunday.
The kanji test was really hard.
The library wasn't quiet.

c.w: 静[しず]かじゃなかった

points.title: Casual speech in the past
points.pattern: 〜た？ · 〜たよ · 〜たね
points.gist: how friends talk about what happened
points.explain: With friends and family, the short past form **is** the whole sentence. A question is just the short form said with a **rising voice** — no か: 楽しかった？ Statements often end with **よ** ("I'm telling you") or **ね** ("right?").
points.tip: Don't add か to a casual question — 食べたか？ sounds rough. Say 食べた？ Friends also drop は and を a lot (映画見た？), but keeping them is never wrong.
points.yt: Japanese casual speech past tense with friends

s.en: What did you do yesterday?
The movie was really fun!
Did you see Tanaka-san at the party?
Kimura-san wasn't at school today, huh.
Was the test easy?

points.title: と思う / と言っていた with the past
points.pattern: [short past] と思います · [short past] と言っていました
points.gist: I think (it) happened / (someone) said (it) happened
points.explain: Whatever comes before と思います or と言っていました is in **short form** — and now that includes the past. "I think it was expensive" is 高かった**と思います**: the quote is past, but 思います stays present because you think it **now**. To report someone's words, use と言っていました: 田中さんは疲れた**と言っていました**.
points.tip: Don't make 思う past to show a past event: "I think he went" is 行ったと思います, not 行くと思いました.
points.yt: Japanese と思う past tense と言っていました

s.en: I think Tanaka-san went home.
Ana said the exam was easy.
I think the concert was great.
Kimura-san said he didn't eat breakfast.
I think Mirage wasn't sick.

c.w: 病気[びょうき]じゃなかった

lessons.title: Sentences that describe nouns
lessons.titleJp: めがねをかけている人

points.title: Clause + noun — a whole sentence describing a noun
points.pattern: [short-form clause] + N
points.gist: a sentence placed before a noun tells you which one
points.explain: In Japanese, **everything that describes a noun comes before it** — even a whole sentence: **めがねをかけている人** = "the person who is wearing glasses". The verb touching the noun is in **short form**, and a subject inside the description takes **が**, not は (母**が**作ったケーキ). Read it **from the end**: 人 "a person" → which person? → かけている "wearing" → wearing what? → めがね "glasses". English says "person ← who wears glasses"; Japanese says "glasses-wearing → person".
points.tip: Japanese has no word for "who / that / which". When a short-form verb sits right before a noun, everything in front of it is a description of that noun.
points.yt: Japanese relative clauses noun modifying clauses explained

s.en: Who is the person wearing glasses?
This is the cake my mother made.
I'm reading the book I bought yesterday.
Mirage has a friend who speaks Japanese.

c.w: 日本語[にほんご]を話[はな]す

s.en: Mirage met the person who took this photo.

c.w: この写真[しゃしん]を撮[と]った

points.title: もう 〜ました — already
points.pattern: もう V-ました
points.gist: the action is already done
points.explain: Put **もう** in front of a past verb to say something is **already** done: もう食べました "I've already eaten." In a question, もう means **yet**: もう宿題をしましたか "Have you done your homework yet?"
points.tip: もう with a negative verb means "not anymore", not "not yet": もう食べません = "I won't eat any more."
points.yt: Japanese もう already まだ not yet Genki lesson 9

s.en: I've already eaten lunch.
Have you bought the ticket yet?
Tanaka-san has already gone home.
I've already read this book.
The movie has already started.

points.title: まだ 〜ていません — not yet
points.pattern: まだ V-ていません
points.gist: it hasn't happened yet (but it probably will)
points.explain: For **not yet**, use **まだ** + the negative **ている** form: まだ食べていません. Think of it as "I'm still in the state of not having eaten." The short answer to a もう question is simply **まだです** — "Not yet."
points.tip: Don't use the past negative: まだ食べませんでした is wrong. "Not yet" describes your situation now, so use 〜ていません.
points.yt: Japanese まだ ていません not yet grammar

s.en: I haven't done my homework yet.
Ana hasn't come yet.
I haven't bought souvenirs yet.
Kimura-san hasn't read my email yet.
I haven't seen that movie yet.

points.title: 〜から with short forms
points.pattern: [short form] から、〜
points.gist: because …, (so) …
points.explain: You already know から "because". The reason before から can be in **short form** — very common, even inside a polite sentence: 雨が降っている**から**、出かけません. Only the reason part is short; the end of the sentence stays polite. Nouns and な-adjectives add **だ**: 休み**だから**.
points.tip: Order matters: reason first, から glued to its end, result last. "I'm tired because I worked" = 働いたから、疲れました.
points.yt: Japanese から because short form Genki lesson 9

s.en: It's raining, so I won't go out.
Tomorrow is a day off, so let's watch a movie.
I didn't sleep last night, so I'm sleepy.
This shop is cheap, so I come here often.
Ana is good at Japanese, so please ask her.

lessons.title: Comparing
lessons.titleJp: より・どちら・いちばん

points.title: A のほうが B より — comparing two things
points.pattern: A のほうが B より Adj
points.gist: A is more … than B
points.explain: Japanese adjectives have no "-er / more" form. Instead you point at the winner with **のほうが** ("the side of A") and at the other one with **より** ("than B"): 電車**のほうが**バス**より**速いです "The train is faster than the bus." The adjective itself never changes.
points.tip: より always marks the one that is LESS. Read it as "compared to". バスより電車のほうが速い means the same thing — the order can swap, the particles can't.
points.yt: Japanese comparison のほうが より Genki lesson 10

s.en: The train is faster than the bus.
Games are more fun than homework.
Japanese is more difficult than English.

c.w: 日本語[にほんご]のほう

s.en: I like cats more than dogs.
Kyoto is quieter than Tokyo.

points.title: どちらが — which of the two?
points.pattern: A と B と どちらが Adj ですか
points.gist: asking which of two things is more …
points.explain: To compare two things in a question, list them with **と … と** and ask **どちらが** "which one?": 夏と冬と**どちらが**好きですか. Answer with のほうが — 冬のほうが好きです — or say **どちらも** "both". In casual speech, どちら becomes **どっち**.
points.tip: どちら is only for TWO choices. For three or more you need 何が / だれが / どこが with の中で (next point).
points.yt: Japanese どちら どっち comparison question Genki 10

s.en: Which do you like better, summer or winter?
I like winter better.
Which is cheaper, the bus or the train?
Which is better, ramen or udon?
I like both.

points.title: 〜の中で 〜が いちばん — the most
points.pattern: [group] の中で X が いちばん Adj
points.gist: the most … in a group of three or more
points.explain: For "the most", first name the group with **の中で** ("among"), then the winner with **が**, then **いちばん** ("number one") before the adjective: 果物の中でりんごがいちばん好きです. In a question, pick the question word that fits: **何が** (things), **だれが** (people), **どこが** (places), **いつが** (times).
points.tip: The winner takes が, never は — and so does the question word: 何がいちばん好きですか, not 何はいちばん….
points.yt: Japanese の中で いちばん superlative Genki lesson 10

s.en: Of all fruits, I like apples the most.

c.w: 果物[くだもの]の中[なか]

s.en: Who is the youngest in your family?
What Japanese food do you like the most?

c.w: 日本料理[にほんりょうり]の中[なか]

s.en: Where is the most beautiful place in Japan?
Of the three, this game is the most interesting.

points.title: Adjective / noun + の — "the … one"
points.pattern: Adj + の · N + の
points.gist: の stands in for a noun you don't want to repeat
points.explain: When it's obvious what you're talking about, Japanese swaps the noun for **の**, like English "one": 赤い**の** "the red one", 安い**の** "a cheap one". After a person, it means "…'s (one)": 田中さん**の**です "It's Tanaka-san's." な-adjectives keep their な: きれい**な**の.
points.tip: Don't drop な: "the quiet one" is 静かなの, not 静かの. And の only works when the thing was already mentioned or is right in front of you.
points.yt: Japanese の as pronoun the red one 赤いの Genki 10

s.en: The red one, please.
This umbrella is Tanaka-san's.

c.w: 田中[たなか]さんのです

s.en: Do you have a cheaper one?
Kimura-san bought the blue one.
For the room, I'd prefer a quiet one.

points.title: 〜つもりだ — I intend to
points.pattern: V (dictionary) つもりです · V-ない つもりです
points.gist: a plan you have already decided on
points.explain: Put **つもりです** after a verb in dictionary form to say what you **plan** to do: 来年日本へ行く**つもりです**. For "I plan not to", use the ない form: ゲームをしない**つもりです**. It shows a decision already made in your head — stronger than a vague "maybe".
points.tip: つもり follows the short form, never the ます form: 行くつもり, not 行きますつもり.
points.yt: Japanese つもり intention grammar Genki lesson 10

s.en: I plan to go to Japan next year.
I don't intend to play games today.
What are you planning to do over winter break?
Ana said she plans to study Japanese in Kyoto.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]するつもりだ

s.en: I'm planning to buy a new computer this weekend.

lessons.title: Change · somewhere · by means of
lessons.titleJp: 〜くなる・どこか・で・かかる

points.title: 〜くなる / 〜になる — to become
points.pattern: A-い → A-くなる · N / na-A + になる
points.gist: describes a change: get colder, become a doctor
points.explain: **なる** means "to become". い-adjectives drop い and add **くなる**: 寒い → 寒**く**なる "get cold". Nouns and な-adjectives take **になる**: 上手**に**なる, 医者**に**なる. The past なりました says the change has happened: 寒くなりました "It's gotten cold."
points.tip: いい becomes よくなる, not いくなる. And keep the two groups apart: "become quiet" is 静かになる, never 静かくなる.
points.yt: Japanese くなる になる become Genki lesson 10

s.en: It's gotten cold in the mornings.
Ana has become good at Japanese.

c.w: 上手[じょうず]になりました

s.en: My older brother became a doctor.

c.w: 医者[いしゃ]になりました

s.en: I cleaned the room, so it got clean.
The weather got better in the afternoon.

points.title: どこかに / どこにも — somewhere / nowhere
points.pattern: どこか (へ) + positive · どこ (に/へ) も + negative
points.gist: question word + か = some-; question word + も + negative = no-
points.explain: Add **か** to a question word and it becomes "some-": どこ**か** "somewhere", だれ**か** "someone", いつ**か** "someday". Add **も** and use a **negative** verb and it becomes "no-": どこ**にも**行きません "I don't go anywhere." Notice where the particle goes: after どこか (どこか**へ**), but between どこ and も (どこ**に**も).
points.tip: どこにも needs a negative verb: どこにも行きませんでした. If the verb is positive, you want どこか.
points.yt: Japanese どこか どこにも question word か も Genki 10

s.en: Did you go somewhere over winter break?
I didn't go anywhere on the weekend.
Let's eat lunch somewhere.
My glasses are nowhere to be found.
Is someone in the room?

points.title: で — by (means of transport)
points.pattern: [vehicle] で 行く / 来る / 帰る
points.gist: で marks how you travel: by bus, by train
points.explain: **で** marks the tool or method you use — and that includes vehicles: バス**で**行きます "I go by bus." The vehicle takes で; the destination still takes に or へ. To ask "how?", use **何で** — read なにで, since なんで can also mean "why" — or どうやって.
points.tip: "On foot" is not 足で — say 歩いて行きます ("go walking"). And で goes on the vehicle, never on the destination.
points.yt: Japanese particle で means of transportation Genki 10

s.en: I go to school by bus.
Tanaka-san comes to the office by bike.
How did you get here today?
We went from Tokyo to Kyoto by bullet train.
It was raining, so I went home by taxi.

points.title: 〜かかります — it takes (time / money)
points.pattern: [amount] かかります
points.gist: how much time or money something takes
points.explain: **かかる** means "to take" (time) or "to cost" (money). Put the amount right before it: 一時間**かかります** "It takes an hour." Ask with **どのくらい** "how long / how much": 駅までどのくらいかかりますか. The route (から … まで) and the means (で) fit in front.
points.tip: The amount takes no particle: 三十分かかります, not 三十分をかかります. Add ぐらい for "about": 二時間ぐらい.
points.yt: Japanese かかる how long does it take どのくらい

s.en: It takes thirty minutes by bus.

c.w: 三十分[さんじゅっぷん]

s.en: How long does it take from here to the station?
From Tokyo to Kyoto takes about two hours by bullet train.
Walking from school to my house took an hour.
The trip cost 50,000 yen.

lessons.title: Wanting to · listing actions
vocab: all along, for a long time

points.title: 〜たい — want to
points.pattern: V-stem + たいです
points.gist: says what you want to do
points.explain: Take the ます-stem (食べます → 食べ) and add **たい**: 食べ**たい** "want to eat". The result behaves like an **い-adjective**: 食べたく**ない** (don't want to), 食べた**かった** (wanted to), plus です to be polite. The object can take を or **が**: すし**が**食べたいです.
points.tip: Use たい for yourself, or to ask "you". For someone else, report it instead: 田中さんは行きたいと言っていました.
points.yt: Japanese たい want to do grammar Genki lesson 11

s.en: Someday I want to go to Japan.
What do you want to eat?
I don't want to work tomorrow.

c.w: 働[はたら]きたくないです

s.en: I've always wanted to see Mt. Fuji.
Tanaka-san said she wants to go to the beach.

points.title: 〜たり〜たりする — things like A and B
points.pattern: V-たり V-たり する
points.gist: gives a few example activities, not the full list
points.explain: To give **examples** of what you do, take each verb's **た-form** and add **り**: 見た → 見たり. List two (or more), then finish with **する**, which carries the tense and politeness: 映画を見**たり**、買い物をし**たり**しました "I did things like watching a movie and shopping." There may have been other activities too.
points.tip: Don't forget the final する: 見たり食べたりしました. The tense goes on する, not on the たり verbs.
points.yt: Japanese たり たり する grammar Genki lesson 11

s.en: On weekends I do things like watch movies and play games.
In Kyoto I did things like see temples and drink tea.
Yesterday I cleaned, did the laundry, and so on.

c.w: 洗濯[せんたく]したりしました

s.en: At the party we sang songs and danced.

c.w: 踊[おど]ったりしました

s.en: You must not eat or drink in the library.

c.w: 飲[の]んだりしてはいけません

points.title: 〜ことがある — have done before
points.pattern: V-た ことが あります
points.gist: talks about experience: I have (ever) done …
points.explain: **こと** turns a verb into a noun ("the act of"), so 富士山に登った**ことがあります** literally says "the experience of having climbed Mt. Fuji exists" — that's how Japanese says "I have climbed Mt. Fuji." The verb before こと is always the **past short form**. For "I've never…", use ことが**ありません**.
points.tip: Use the た-form: 食べたことがあります. With the dictionary form (食べることがあります) it means "I sometimes eat" — a different idea.
points.yt: Japanese たことがある experience grammar Genki 11

s.en: I have climbed Mt. Fuji.
Have you ever eaten natto?
I've never been to Okinawa.
Kimura-san has worked in America.
Have you ever met a famous person?

points.title: A や B — A, B, and so on
points.pattern: N や N (など)
points.gist: lists some examples from a longer list
points.explain: **と** gives the complete list: りんご**と**バナナ = "apples and bananas (that's all)". **や** gives only examples: りんご**や**バナナ = "apples, bananas and such". The last item takes whatever particle the sentence needs — が, を, に… Add など after it to stress "and so on".
points.tip: や joins nouns only. For lists of actions, use the たり form: 見たり食べたりしました.
points.yt: Japanese particle や vs と listing Genki lesson 11

s.en: There are books, notebooks and such in my bag.
I bought apples, bananas and so on at the supermarket.
I've been to places like Kyoto and Nara.
In Japan I want to eat things like sushi and tempura.
Tanaka-san, Ana and others came to the party.

points.title: 〜んです — explaining
points.pattern: [short form] んです
points.gist: gives or asks for an explanation, the story behind something
points.explain: **んです** adds the feeling of **"the thing is…"**. Use it to explain a situation — 頭が痛い**んです** "I have a headache, you see" — or to ask about one you noticed: どうした**んですか** "What happened?" It follows short forms; nouns and な-adjectives add **な**: 誕生日**な**んです.
points.tip: Don't put it on every sentence. A plain fact needs no んです; save it for explaining, or for reacting to something you see.
points.yt: Japanese んです explanation grammar Genki lesson 12

s.en: I have a headache, you see.
Why didn't you come yesterday?

c.w: 来[こ]なかったんですか

s.en: Oh, are you going somewhere today?
The thing is, I don't have any money.
Tomorrow is my birthday, you see.

c.w: 誕生日[たんじょうび]なんです

points.title: 〜すぎる — too much
points.pattern: V-stem / A(-い) / na-A + すぎる
points.gist: too much, too … (more than is good)
points.explain: **すぎる** means "to go past the limit". Attach it to a verb stem — 食べ**すぎる** "eat too much" — or to an adjective without its い / な: 高**すぎる** "too expensive", 静か**すぎる** "too quiet". It then works as a normal る-verb: 飲みすぎました "I drank too much."
points.tip: すぎる always sounds like a complaint ("more than is good"). For a neutral "very", use とても. いい becomes よすぎる.
points.yt: Japanese すぎる too much grammar Genki lesson 12

s.en: I ate too much yesterday.
This bag is too expensive.
The test was too difficult.

c.w: 難[むずか]しすぎました

s.en: I drank too much coffee, so I'm not sleepy.
This town is too quiet.

lessons.title: Advice · because
vocab: to rest; to take a day off
to be late, to be delayed

points.title: 〜ほうがいいです — you'd better
points.pattern: V-た ほうがいい · V-ない ほうがいい
points.gist: strong advice: you should / you shouldn't
points.explain: To give advice, use the **past short form + ほうがいいです**: 薬を飲ん**だほうがいいですよ** "You'd better take some medicine." To advise against something, use the **ない form**: 出かけ**ないほうがいいです** "You shouldn't go out." Literally: "that side is better."
points.tip: The positive uses た, but the negative uses ない — not なかった: 行ったほうがいい / 行かないほうがいい. It's quite direct, so be careful with people above you.
points.yt: Japanese ほうがいい advice grammar Genki lesson 12

s.en: You'd better take some medicine.

c.w: 飲[の]んだほうがいいですよ

s.en: You shouldn't go out today.

c.w: 出[で]かけないほうがいいです

s.en: You should go to the hospital soon.

c.w: 行[い]ったほうがいいですよ

s.en: You shouldn't eat too much at night.

c.w: 食[た]べすぎないほうがいいです

s.en: You have a fever, so you should rest.

c.w: 休[やす]んだほうがいいです

points.title: 〜ので — because (softer)
points.pattern: [short form] ので、〜
points.gist: gives a reason in a softer, more polite way
points.explain: **ので** means "because, so", just like から, but it sounds **softer and more objective** — perfect for explaining yourself to a teacher or at work. It follows short forms, but nouns and な-adjectives use **な** instead of だ: 日曜日**なので**, 静か**なので**.
points.tip: Before ので it's な (病気なので); before から it's だ (病気だから). 病気だので is a common slip.
points.yt: Japanese ので vs から because Genki lesson 12

s.en: I've caught a cold, so I'll take today off.
It's Sunday, so the bank is closed.
The train was delayed, so I was late.
My throat hurts, so I'll go home early.
This park is quiet, so I come here often.

lessons.title: Obligation · probably
lessons.titleJp: 〜なければいけません・〜でしょう

points.title: 〜なければいけません / 〜なきゃ — must
points.pattern: V-ない → V-なければいけません · casual: V-なきゃ
points.gist: must, have to (literally "if I don't, it won't do")
points.explain: Take the **ない form**, drop the い, and add **ければいけません**: 行かない → 行かな**ければいけません** "I have to go." Literally: "if I don't go, it's no good." Among friends it shrinks to **なきゃ**: 帰ら**なきゃ** "I gotta go home."
points.tip: For "had to", change only the very end: 行かなければいけませんでした. なきゃ is for friends — use the full form with teachers and at work.
points.yt: Japanese なければいけない なきゃ must Genki lesson 12

s.en: I have to get up at six tomorrow.

c.w: 起[お]きなければいけません

s.en: I've gotta do my homework.
Yesterday I had to work until ten.

c.w: 働[はたら]かなければいけませんでした

s.en: You have to take this medicine every day.

c.w: 飲[の]まなければいけません

s.en: It's already late, so I've gotta go home.

points.title: 〜でしょう — probably
points.pattern: [short form] でしょう · N / na-A でしょう
points.gist: a guess (probably …); with a rising voice, "right?"
points.explain: **でしょう** after a short form turns it into a **guess**: 明日は雨が降る**でしょう** "It will probably rain tomorrow" — the classic weather-forecast phrase. Nouns and な-adjectives drop だ: 先生**でしょう**. Said with a rising voice, **でしょう？** checks that the listener agrees: "…, right?"
points.tip: No だ before でしょう: 静かでしょう, not 静かだでしょう. With verbs and い-adjectives, just attach it: 高いでしょう.
points.yt: Japanese でしょう probably grammar Genki lesson 12

s.en: It will probably rain tomorrow.
Tanaka-san is probably at home now.
Kyoto was beautiful, wasn't it?

c.w: きれいだったでしょう

s.en: That person is probably a teacher.

c.w: 先生[せんせい]でしょう

s.en: Tomorrow's test will probably be difficult.

c.w: 難[むずか]しいでしょう

points.title: Potential verbs — can / be able to
points.pattern: る-verb → 〜られる · う-verb → 〜える · する → できる · 来る → 来られる
points.gist: says what someone can or can't do
points.explain: The potential form says what you **can** do. **る-verbs** swap る for **られる**: 食べる → 食べ**られる**. **う-verbs** change the last u-sound to its **e-sound + る**: 読む → 読**める**, 泳ぐ → 泳**げる**, 行く → 行**ける**. Irregulars: する → **できる**, 来る → **来られる** (こられる). The result is a normal る-verb: 読めます, 読めません, 読めませんでした.
points.tip: The object often switches from を to **が**: 漢字**が**読めます. And "can't" is the potential in the negative — 泳げません — not the plain negative 泳ぎません ("I don't swim").
points.yt: Tokini Andy Genki 2 lesson 13 potential verbs

s.en: I can read a little kanji.
Mirage, can you eat natto?
I can't swim.
Kimura-san can ski.
I had a fever, so I couldn't come yesterday.

c.w: 来[こ]られませんでした

points.title: 〜し〜し — and what's more
points.pattern: [short form] し、[short form] し、〜
points.gist: stacks up several reasons that point the same way
points.explain: **し** piles up reasons: "it's A, and B too, so…". Put it after a **short form**: 安い**し**、おいしい**し**、よく来ます. The conclusion usually comes at the end, but it can be left unsaid when it's obvious. Nouns and な-adjectives use **だし**: きれい**だし**.
points.tip: Use し for reasons that point the same way (all good, or all bad). To simply list actions in order ("I ate and slept"), use the て-form.
points.yt: Japanese し grammar listing reasons Genki 13

s.en: This restaurant is cheap and tasty, so I come here often.
Today I have homework and my part-time job too, so I'm busy.
Kyoto is beautiful and the food is good too, so I love it.
It's raining and I'm tired, so I won't go.
Ana is kind and funny, so she's popular.

points.title: 〜そうです — looks …
points.pattern: A(-い) / na-A + そうです · そうな + N
points.gist: says how something looks to you
points.explain: Add **そう** to an adjective to say how something **looks**: おいし**そう**です "It looks delicious." い-adjectives drop the い (高い → 高**そう**); な-adjectives just add it (元気**そう**). Before a noun it becomes **そうな**: おもしろそう**な**ゲーム "a fun-looking game".
points.tip: Two irregulars: いい → よさそう, ない → なさそう (never いそう).
points.yt: Japanese そうです looks like adjective Genki 13

s.en: This cake looks delicious.
Tanaka-san looks busy today.
Kimura-san looks well.
This hotel looks good, doesn't it?
I bought a game that looks fun.

lessons.title: Trying · if it is · frequency
lessons.titleJp: 〜てみる・なら・一週間に三回
vocab: 一週間[いっしゅうかん]

points.title: 〜てみる — try doing
points.pattern: V-て みる
points.gist: do something to see what it's like
points.explain: **てみる** means "do it and see": 着物を着**てみました** "I tried on a kimono." It's for testing an experience — taste it, wear it, go there — to find out how it is. みる conjugates like 見る (てみます, てみたい, てみてください) but is written in kana.
points.tip: てみる means you really did it, to see how it is — not "I made an effort but failed".
points.yt: Japanese てみる try doing Genki lesson 13

s.en: I tried on a kimono in Kyoto.
Please try this sweet.

c.w: 食[た]べてみてください

s.en: Someday I want to try going to a hot spring.
I tried reading a Japanese manga.
Mirage tried making sushi.

points.title: なら — if it's …
points.pattern: N なら 〜
points.gist: picks up a topic: "if it's X (we're talking about)…"
points.explain: **なら** grabs something that's already in the conversation and comments on it: "if it's X…". Someone wants ramen? ラーメン**なら**、あの店がいいですよ "If it's ramen, that place is good." It's great for recommending and narrowing down, and it often hints at a contrast: 日本語**なら**話せます "Japanese, I can speak (other languages, no)."
points.tip: なら reacts to what's on the table. Don't use it out of nowhere — something must already be mentioned or obvious.
points.yt: Japanese なら grammar noun topic Genki lesson 13

s.en: If it's ramen you want, that shop is good.
