As for sports, I like tennis.
Japanese? That one I can speak.
If it's Saturday, I'm free.
If you're going to Kyoto, you should see Kinkakuji.

c.w: 見[み]たほうがいいですよ

points.title: 一週間に三回 — how often
points.pattern: [period] に [number] 回
points.gist: how many times in a period: three times a week
points.explain: To say how often, give the **period + に**, then the **number of times** with 〜回 (かい): 一週間**に**三回 "three times a week", 一日**に**二回 "twice a day". Here に works like "per". Ask with **何回**: 一か月に何回…?
points.tip: Watch the readings: 一回 = いっかい, 一週間 = いっしゅうかん, 一か月 = いっかげつ, 一日 = いちにち (ついたち is "the 1st of the month").
points.yt: Japanese frequency 一週間に三回 how many times 回

s.en: I go to the gym three times a week.

c.w: 一週間[いっしゅうかん]

s.en: Please take this medicine twice a day.
How many times a month do you watch movies?
I call my mother once a week.

c.w: 一週間[いっしゅうかん]

s.en: Kimura-san goes to Okinawa twice a year.

lessons.title: Wanting things · maybe
lessons.titleJp: ほしい・〜かもしれません

points.title: ほしい — want (a thing)
points.pattern: N が ほしいです
points.gist: says you want an object
points.explain: **ほしい** is an **い-adjective** meaning "wanted", so the thing you want is marked with **が**: 新しいくつ**が**ほしいです "I want new shoes." It conjugates like any い-adjective: ほしく**ない**, ほし**かった**. Use ほしい for **things** and 〜たい for **actions**.
points.tip: Like たい, ほしい is for your own wishes, or for asking "you". For other people, report it: 木村さんは車がほしいと言っていました.
points.yt: Japanese ほしい want something Genki 2 lesson 14

s.en: I want new shoes.
What do you want for your birthday?
I don't want a car.
I'd always wanted a dog.
Kimura-san said he wants a new smartphone.

points.title: 〜かもしれません — maybe
points.pattern: [short form] かもしれません · N / na-A かもしれません
points.gist: it might be …; maybe (a real possibility, not a sure thing)
points.explain: **かもしれません** means "might, maybe". Attach it to a **short form**: 明日は雪が降る**かもしれません** "It might snow tomorrow." Nouns and な-adjectives drop だ: 病気**かもしれません**. It's a weaker guess than でしょう ("probably") — just a possibility.
points.tip: No だ before it: 暇かもしれません, not 暇だかもしれません. In casual speech: かもしれない, or just かも.
points.yt: Japanese かもしれない might maybe Genki 2 lesson 14

s.en: It might snow tomorrow.

c.w: 降[ふ]るかもしれません

s.en: Tanaka-san might be sick.

c.w: 病気[びょうき]かもしれません

s.en: I might not be able to go to the party.

c.w: 行[い]けないかもしれません

s.en: This might be Ana's umbrella.

c.w: 傘[かさ]かもしれません

s.en: Kimura-san may have already gone home.

c.w: 帰[かえ]ったかもしれません

lessons.title: Giving and receiving
lessons.titleJp: あげる・くれる・もらう

points.title: あげる — give (away from me)
points.pattern: [giver] は [receiver] に N を あげる
points.gist: give, when the thing moves away from me (or between others)
points.explain: **あげる** is "give" when the gift goes **outward**: from me (or my side) to someone else, or between two other people. The receiver takes **に**: 私は友だち**に**チョコレートを**あげました**. Picture the arrow: me → others = あげる.
points.tip: Never use あげる when someone gives something to YOU — "Ana gave me a book" needs くれる (next point).
points.yt: Japanese あげる くれる もらう giving receiving Genki 14

s.en: I gave my friend chocolate.
What did you give Tanaka-san for his birthday?
Ana gave Kimura-san a book.
I plan to give this to my mother.
Mirage gave his grandmother flowers.

points.title: くれる — give (to me)
points.pattern: [giver] が (私に) N を くれる
points.gist: give, when the thing comes toward me (or my family)
points.explain: **くれる** is "give" when the gift comes **inward** — to me, or to someone on my side such as my family: 母が私にセーターを**くれました**. The arrow points at me. 私に is often left out, because くれる already says "to me".
points.tip: The giver usually takes が: 田中さん**が**くれました. And "I gave you…" is あげる, never くれる.
points.yt: Japanese くれる vs あげる explained

s.en: My mother gave me a sweater.
Tanaka-san gave me this pen.
Who gave you that?
Ana gave my little sister a present.
My friend gave me a souvenir from Okinawa.

points.title: もらう — receive
points.pattern: [receiver] は [giver] に / から N を もらう
points.gist: receive, get something from someone
points.explain: **もらう** tells the same event from the **receiver's** side: "I got it from…". The receiver is the topic, and the giver is marked with **に** or **から**: 私は先生**に**本を**もらいました** "I got a book from my teacher." So "Ana gave me a book" can be アナさんが本をくれました, or 私はアナさんに本をもらいました.
points.tip: With もらう, に means "from", not "to"! The receiver comes first: 私は田中さんにもらいました = "I got it from Tanaka-san."
points.yt: Japanese もらう receive に から giving receiving

s.en: I got a book from my teacher.
Who did you get that bag from?
Ana got a letter from her grandmother.
On Valentine's Day I got chocolate from Kimura-san.
My older brother got a watch from our parents.

lessons.title: Suggesting · amounts
lessons.titleJp: 〜たらどうですか・も・しか

points.title: 〜たらどうですか — why don't you…?
points.pattern: V-た + ら どうですか
points.gist: a friendly suggestion: why don't you …?
points.explain: Take the **past short form**, add **ら**, and ask **どうですか** — "how would it be if you…?" → "why don't you…?": 薬を飲ん**だらどうですか**. It's a light suggestion for friends and equals. Casually: 〜たらどう？ or just 〜たら？
points.tip: It can sound pushy toward people above you. And it's only for things the OTHER person does — to invite someone to do something with you, use 〜ませんか.
points.yt: Japanese たらどうですか suggestion Genki 2 lesson 14

s.en: Why don't you go to the hospital?

c.w: 行[い]ったらどうですか

s.en: Why don't you ask the teacher?

c.w: 聞[き]いたらどうですか

s.en: Why don't you rest a little?

c.w: 休[やす]んだらどうですか

s.en: Why don't you give Ana some flowers?
Why not try this on?

points.title: Number + も — as many as
points.pattern: [number + counter] も
points.gist: stresses that an amount is surprisingly large
points.explain: Put **も** right after a number to say "as many as" — the amount is **bigger than expected**: コーヒーを五杯**も**飲みました "I drank five whole cups of coffee!" The verb stays positive; も just adds the surprise.
points.tip: This も sits on the number, not the noun: 本を十冊も読みました. Compare 本も読みました, which only means "I read books too."
points.yt: Japanese number も as many as emphasis Genki 14

s.en: Today I drank five whole cups of coffee.
I waited at the station for two whole hours.
Kimura-san has five brothers and sisters!
Over summer break I read ten books.
I took 300 photos on the trip.

c.w: 三百枚[さんびゃくまい]

points.title: Number + しか〜ない — only
points.pattern: [number + counter] しか + negative
points.gist: only (and that's not much)
points.explain: **しか** after a number means "only", but it needs a **negative** verb — literally "nothing except…": 千円**しかありません** "I only have 1,000 yen." The feeling is the opposite of number + も: the amount is **smaller than you'd like**.
points.tip: Don't forget the negative ending: 三時間しか寝ませんでした — never 三時間しか寝ました.
points.yt: Japanese しか ない only grammar Genki 2 lesson 14

s.en: I only have 1,000 yen in my wallet.
I only slept three hours last night.
Only two people came to the party.
I can still only read 100 kanji.
There's only one apple in the fridge.

lessons.title: Let's (casual) and plans
lessons.titleJp: 〜よう・〜ようと思っています

points.title: The volitional — casual “let's…”
points.pattern: V-よう / V-おう
points.gist: the casual way to say “let's…” or “shall I…?”
points.explain: The volitional is the casual twin of 〜ましょう. **る-verbs** swap る for **よう** (見る → 見よう). **う-verbs** move the last sound to the **o**-row and add **う** (行く → 行こう, 飲む → 飲もう). Irregulars: する → **しよう**, 来る → **来よう** (こよう). Add **か** to ask “shall we / shall I…?”: 持とうか.
points.tip: 帰る and 入る look like る-verbs but are う-verbs: 帰ろう, 入ろう — never 帰よう. And keep it for friends; with a boss, use 〜ましょう.
points.yt: Game Gengo volitional form よう おう

s.en: Let's watch a movie together tonight!
It's raining, so let's go home by taxi.
That looks heavy, so shall I carry your bag?
What shall we do this weekend?

points.title: 〜ようと思っています — plans on your mind
points.pattern: V-よう と思っています
points.gist: “I'm thinking of doing…” / “I plan to…”
points.explain: Put the volitional in front of **と思っています** to talk about a plan you've been turning over for a while: 留学しようと思っています = “I'm thinking of studying abroad.” The ている shows the idea is ongoing, so it also works for other people: アナさんは…と思っています. Use **〜ようと思います** (no ている) for a decision you're making right now.
points.tip: 行こうと思っています (my plan) is not 行くと思います (my guess that someone will go). The volitional is what turns it into a plan.
points.yt: ToKini Andy Genki 2 lesson 15 volitional と思っています

s.en: I'm thinking of going to Hokkaido next year.
Ana is thinking of studying abroad in Japan.

c.w: 留学[りゅうがく]しよう

s.en: I'm thinking of moving to Osaka in the spring.
What are you thinking of doing in the future?

lessons.title: Getting ready · describing more
lessons.titleJp: 〜ておく・名詞を説明する文

points.title: 〜ておく — doing it in advance
points.pattern: V-て おく
points.gist: do something now so it's ready for later
points.explain: おく means “to put, to leave”. After a て-form it means doing something **ahead of time** so things are ready: ホテルを予約しておきます = “I'll book the hotel in advance.” It can also mean **leaving** something as it is for now: 窓を開けておいてください = “Please leave the window open.”
points.tip: おく is a normal う-verb: おきます, おいて, おいた, おこう. In fast casual speech 〜ておく often shrinks to 〜とく (買っとく).
points.yt: Japanese ておく doing something in advance

s.en: I'll book the hotel for the trip ahead of time.

c.w: 予約[よやく]しておきます

s.en: I have an exam tomorrow, so I'll study tonight.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]しておきます

s.en: It's hot, so please leave the window open.

c.w: 開[あ]けておいてください

s.en: Shall I buy the drinks for the party in advance?

c.w: 買[か]っておきましょうか

points.title: Long descriptions in front of a noun
points.pattern: [short-form sentence] + N
points.gist: a whole sentence placed before a noun describes it
points.explain: Any short-form sentence can sit **right before a noun** and describe it, like an English “that / who…” clause, only in front. Inside that description the doer takes **が**, not は: 母**が**作ったケーキ = “the cake my mom made.” To read it, jump to the noun at the end of the block first, then read the description.
points.tip: No は and no です/ます inside the description: 私が撮った写真, not 私は撮りました写真.
points.yt: Japanese relative clauses noun modifying clause

s.en: This is the cake my mother made.
The town where my grandmother lives is very quiet.

c.w: 祖母[そぼ]が住[す]んでいる

s.en: Did you see the photos I took in Kyoto?

c.w: 私[わたし]が京都[きょうと]で撮[と]った

s.en: I want to go to a place where you can eat great ramen.

c.w: おいしいラーメンが食[た]べられる

lessons.title: Favors
lessons.titleJp: 〜てあげる・〜てくれる・〜てもらう
vocab: to give (someone) a ride, to see off

points.title: 〜てあげる — doing something for someone
points.pattern: V-て あげる
points.gist: I (or my side) do a favor for someone else
points.explain: あげる (to give) after a て-form means **giving an action** as a favor: the kindness flows **away** from you. 妹に絵本を読んであげました = “I read a picture book to my little sister (for her).” The person helped usually takes **に**, unless the verb already marks them another way (田中さん**の**宿題を手伝ってあげた).
points.tip: Saying 〜てあげます straight to a superior sounds condescending (“I'll do you the favor”). To offer help to a teacher or boss, use 〜ましょうか.
points.yt: Japanese てあげる てくれる てもらう explained

s.en: I made dinner for my mother.

c.w: 作[つく]ってあげました

s.en: Mirage helped Tanaka with her homework.

c.w: 手伝[てつだ]ってあげました

s.en: Every night I read picture books to my little sister.
It was raining, so I lent Kimura my umbrella.

points.title: 〜てくれる — someone does something for me
points.pattern: Person が V-て くれる
points.gist: someone does a favor for me (or my side)
points.explain: くれる means “give **to me**”, so 〜てくれる is someone **giving their action to me** or to people on my side. The helper is the subject (が / は), and 私に is usually left out because it's obvious: 田中さんが駅まで送ってくれました = “Tanaka kindly gave me a ride to the station.” It adds a warm “thank you” feeling.
points.tip: 〜てくれる never points away from you. You helped someone → 〜てあげる. Someone helped you → 〜てくれる.
points.yt: てくれる vs てもらう Japanese favors

s.en: Tanaka kindly drove me to the station.

c.w: 送[おく]ってくれました

s.en: My friend taught me this game.

c.w: 教[おし]えてくれました

s.en: My mom made me a bento every day.

c.w: 作[つく]ってくれました

s.en: I caught a cold, so Ana lent me her notes.

points.title: 〜てもらう — getting someone to do something
points.pattern: Person に V-て もらう
points.gist: I receive a favor from someone
points.explain: もらう means “to receive”, so 〜てもらう is **receiving an action**. Now **I** am the subject, and the helper takes **に** (“from”): 木村さんに写真を撮ってもらいました = “I had Kimura take my picture.” It often hints that **you asked** for the favor, while 〜てくれる sounds more like they offered.
points.tip: Watch the helper's particle: が with てくれる, に with てもらう. Same event, two camera angles.
points.yt: Japanese てもらう meaning explained

s.en: I had Kimura take my picture.

c.w: 撮[と]ってもらいました

s.en: I had my teacher look over my essay.
I got my older brother to fix my bicycle.

c.w: 直[なお]してもらいました

s.en: Ana had a Japanese friend read the menu for her.

c.w: 読[よ]んでもらいました

lessons.title: Asking politely · hoping
lessons.titleJp: 〜ていただけませんか・〜といいですね
vocab: to be visible, can be seen

points.title: 〜ていただけませんか — could you possibly…?
points.pattern: V-て いただけませんか
points.gist: the most polite way to ask for a favor
points.explain: Requests form a ladder: 〜て**くれない**? (friends) → 〜て**くれませんか** → 〜て**もらえませんか** → 〜て**いただけませんか** (most polite). The top step uses いただく, the humble version of もらう: literally “couldn't I receive the favor of you doing…?” Use it with teachers, strangers, staff — anyone you want to be extra polite to.
points.tip: Keep the て-form in front: 書いていただけませんか, not 書きいただけませんか. With close friends the top step sounds stiff; use 〜てくれない？
points.yt: ていただけませんか polite request Japanese

s.en: Could you please speak a little more slowly?

c.w: 話[はな]していただけませんか

s.en: Could you look over the Japanese email I wrote?

c.w: 見[み]ていただけませんか

s.en: Could you lend me your dictionary for a moment?

c.w: 貸[か]してもらえませんか

s.en: Could you take a picture of us?

c.w: 撮[と]っていただけませんか

points.title: 〜といいですね / 〜といいんですが — I hope…
points.pattern: short form + といいですね / といいんですが
points.gist: hoping for something you can't control
points.explain: Put a short-form sentence before **といい** (“it would be good if…”) to express a hope. **〜といいですね** is a hope **for the other person**: 合格するといいですね = “I hope you pass.” **〜といいんですが** is a hope **for yourself**, with a little worry: “…but we'll see.”
points.tip: Use it for things outside your control. For your own effort just say what you'll do (頑張ります), not 頑張るといいんですが.
points.yt: といいですね といいんですが Japanese hope

s.en: I hope you pass next week's exam.

c.w: 合格[ごうかく]するといいですね

s.en: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow…

c.w: 降[ふ]らないといいんですが

s.en: I hope your cold gets better soon.

c.w: 治[なお]るといいですね

s.en: I hope we can see Mount Fuji from the hotel…

c.w: 見[み]えるといいんですが

lessons.title: When · apologizing
lessons.titleJp: 〜とき・〜てすみませんでした

points.title: 〜とき — when…
points.pattern: short form + とき
points.gist: a clause + とき tells when the main event happens
points.explain: とき means “time”, so [clause]とき = “(at) the time when…”. Before it you can put a verb, an adjective (暇なとき) or a noun + の (子どものとき). The **tense inside** matters: 日本へ**行く**とき = before getting there; 日本へ**行った**とき = after arriving.
points.tip: Ask: has the とき-action already happened when the main action happens? Yes → た-form. Not yet → dictionary form.
points.yt: Japanese とき when 行くとき 行ったとき

s.en: When I'm free, I often play video games.
When I went to Kyoto, I wore a kimono.
When I was about to go to Japan, I bought a new suitcase.
When I was a child, I lived in Brazil.

points.title: 〜てすみませんでした — sorry for…
points.pattern: V-て / V-なくて すみませんでした
points.gist: apologizing for something you did (or didn't do)
points.explain: Put the reason for the apology in the て-form before **すみませんでした**: 遅れてすみませんでした = “Sorry for being late.” For something you **failed** to do, use the negative て-form **〜なくて**: 電話しなくてすみませんでした = “Sorry for not calling.” With friends, 〜てごめん(ね) does the same job.
points.tip: Apologizing for not doing something takes 〜なくて, not 〜ないで: 返事しなくてごめん.
points.yt: Japanese apology てすみませんでした なくて

s.en: I'm sorry I was late this morning.
Sorry for not calling yesterday.
Sorry I broke your precious cup.
I'm sorry I didn't reply to your email.

lessons.title: I heard that
vocab: 天気予報[てんきよほう]
就職[しゅうしょく]する

points.title: 〜そうです — I hear that…
points.pattern: short form + そうです
points.gist: passing on information you heard or read
points.explain: End a short-form sentence with **そうです** to report something you heard: 雪が降るそうです = “I hear it's going to snow.” Name your source with **〜によると** (“according to…”). Unlike the “looks like” そう, the **whole short form** stays: 高いそうです, 静かだそうです, 医者だそうです.
points.tip: 高そうです = “looks expensive”; 高いそうです = “I hear it's expensive.” That little い changes everything.
points.yt: Japanese そうです hearsay vs appearance

s.en: According to the weather forecast, it will snow tomorrow.

c.w: 天気予報[てんきよほう]

s.en: I hear Kimura got a job at a game company.

c.w: 就職[しゅうしょく]したそうです

s.en: I hear Tanaka's older brother is a doctor.

c.w: 医者[いしゃ]だそうです

s.en: According to Ana, the exam was really hard.

c.w: 難[むずか]しかったそうです

points.title: 〜って — casual quoting
points.pattern: short form + って
points.gist: the casual version of と, と言っていた and そうです
points.explain: Among friends, **って** replaces quoting と: 遅れるって言っていた = “(He) said he'd be late.” At the very end of a sentence it means **“I hear / they say”**, like そうです. After a noun it can also pick a topic you're asking about: こたつって何？ = “What's a kotatsu?”
points.tip: って is for friends and family. In polite speech go back to と言っていました or そうです.
points.yt: Japanese って casual quote explained

s.en: Ana says she's coming to the party too.
Tanaka said he'd be a little late.
They say the new ramen shop in front of the station is really good.
What's a kotatsu?

points.title: 〜たら — if / when (once that happens)
points.pattern: V-たら, …
points.gist: once A happens (or if A happens), then B
points.explain: Take the past short form and add **ら**: 着いた → 着いた**ら**, 高かった → 高かった**ら**, 雨だった → 雨だった**ら**. It means **“if A”** or **“when A has happened”**, and B always comes **after** A: 駅に着いたら電話してください = “Call me when you get to the station.”
points.tip: Future events still take the た-form: 明日雨だったら… = “if it rains tomorrow…”. The た here is about order, not the past.
points.yt: Japanese たら conditional explained

s.en: Please call me when you get to the station.

c.w: 電話[でんわ]してください

s.en: If it rains tomorrow, let's play games at home.
If I win the lottery, I want to live in Okinawa.
If it's expensive, I'll buy it at another store.

points.title: 〜なくてもいいです — you don't have to
points.pattern: V-なくても いいです
points.gist: there's no need to do it
points.explain: Take the ない-form, turn ない into **なくて**, and add **もいいです**: 行かない → 行か**なくてもいいです** = “You don't have to go.” Literally “even if you don't, it's fine.” It's the friendly opposite of 〜なければいけません (must).
points.tip: Don't mix it up with 〜てはいけません. 来なくてもいい = no need to come; 来てはいけない = you're not allowed to come.
points.yt: Japanese なくてもいい don't have to

s.en: You don't have to take off your shoes here.

c.w: 脱[ぬ]がなくてもいいです

s.en: Tomorrow is a day off, so you don't have to come to the office.

c.w: 来[こ]なくてもいいです

s.en: It's free, so you don't have to pay.

c.w: 払[はら]わなくてもいいです

s.en: If you're busy, you don't have to reply.

c.w: しなくてもいいですよ

lessons.title: Seems like · before/after
lessons.titleJp: 〜みたいです・〜前に・〜てから
vocab: to go to bed, to sleep

points.title: 〜みたいです — it seems… / it's like…
points.pattern: short form / N + みたいです
points.gist: a guess from what you see or hear; or “just like a…”
points.explain: **みたいです** after a short form gives your guess from evidence: だれもいないみたいです = “It seems nobody's here.” Nouns and な-adjectives drop だ: 雨みたい, 暇みたい. After a noun it can also mean **“just like a…”**: このホテルはお城みたいです = “This hotel is like a castle.”
points.tip: No だ before みたい: 雨みたいです, not 雨だみたいです. And unlike “looks like” そう, it takes the full short form: 寝ているみたい.
points.yt: Japanese みたい seems like explained

s.en: It seems nobody is home.
It seems Tanaka caught a cold.
It looks like it rained last night.
This hotel is like a castle!

points.title: 〜前に — before doing…
points.pattern: V-dictionary + 前に · N の前に
points.gist: B happens before A
points.explain: Put the **dictionary form** before 前に: 寝る前に = “before going to bed.” The verb stays in the dictionary form even in a past story, because at that moment the action **hadn't happened yet**. With nouns, use の: 映画の前に.
points.tip: Never 寝た前に. Before 前に the verb is always plain present: 日本に来る前に、日本語を勉強しました.
points.yt: Japanese 前に before doing explained

s.en: I brush my teeth before going to bed.
Before coming to Japan, I studied Japanese for two years.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]しました

s.en: Please wash your hands before eating.
Let's eat something before the movie.

points.title: 〜てから — after doing…
points.pattern: V-て から, …
points.gist: first A, and only after that, B
points.explain: **〜てから** = “after doing A”, and it stresses the order: B waits until A is done. 宿題をしてから、ゲームをします = “I'll play games after I do my homework.” A plain て just lists steps; てから says “not before.”
points.tip: Two different から: 食べてから = after eating; 食べるから = because I'll eat. Check what comes before it: て-form means “after.”
points.yt: Japanese てから after doing explained

s.en: I'll play games after I do my homework.
After I graduate, I want to work in Japan.

c.w: 卒業[そつぎょう]してから

s.en: I went to bed after taking a shower.
Let's go shopping after we eat lunch.

lessons.title: Transitive × intransitive
vocab: to go off, to go out

points.title: Transitive × intransitive pairs
points.pattern: N を V (transitive) × N が V (intransitive)
points.gist: someone does it (を) vs. it happens (が)
points.explain: Many verbs come in pairs. The **transitive** one has a doer acting on something marked **を**: 窓を開ける = “(I) open the window.” The **intransitive** one just says what **happens**, and the thing takes **が**: 窓が開く = “the window opens.” Learn them as pairs: 開ける/開く, 閉める/閉まる, 入れる/入る, 出す/出る, 消す/消える, 壊す/壊れる, 落とす/落ちる.
points.tip: Let the particle choose the verb: を → transitive (電気を消す); が → intransitive (電気が消える).
points.yt: Japanese transitive intransitive verb pairs 開ける 開く

s.en: I opened the window.
Suddenly the door opened.
I turn off the lights before going to bed.
The lights went out because of the typhoon.

points.title: Intransitive + ている — the state left behind
points.pattern: N が V (intransitive)-ている
points.gist: a state that's still there after a change
points.explain: With an intransitive verb, **〜ている** describes the **result** that is still in place, not an action in progress: 窓が開いています = “The window is open” (it opened, and it stays open). Look around a room and you can describe it all this way: 電気がついている, エアコンが壊れている.
points.tip: Don't use the transitive verb here: 窓を開けています means someone is opening it right now. “Is open” is 窓が開いています.
points.yt: Japanese intransitive verb ている state

s.en: The window is open, so it's cold.
The air conditioner in this room is broken.
The classroom lights are still on.
There's a wallet lying on the street.

points.title: 〜てしまう — done completely / oops
points.pattern: V-て しまう
points.gist: finishing something off, or doing something you regret
points.explain: しまう means “to put away”. After a て-form it has two flavors: **completion** (漫画を全部読んでしまいました = “I read the whole manga”) and **regret** (傘を忘れてしまいました = “I (stupidly) left my umbrella”). With mistakes and accidents it's almost always regret.
points.tip: It's just て-form + しまう, so get the て-form right first: 読んでしまう, 忘れてしまう. The past しまいました is the usual way to report a mishap.
points.yt: Japanese てしまう regret completion

s.en: I left my umbrella on the train.

c.w: 忘[わす]れてしまいました

s.en: I read that whole manga in one day.

c.w: 読[よ]んでしまいました

s.en: I (accidentally) ate my little sister's cake.

c.w: 食[た]べてしまいました

s.en: I overslept and was late for class.

c.w: 遅刻[ちこく]してしまいました

points.title: 〜ちゃう / 〜じゃう — the casual version
points.pattern: V-ちゃう / V-じゃう
points.gist: how 〜てしまう sounds in everyday talk
points.explain: In casual speech 〜て**しまう** shrinks to **〜ちゃう**, and 〜で**しまう** to **〜じゃう**: 忘れてしまった → 忘れ**ちゃった**, 飲んでしまった → 飲ん**じゃった**. Same two meanings (all done / oops), just friendlier.
points.tip: Follow the て-form: て → ちゃ, で → じゃ. So 行ってしまう → 行っちゃう, but 読んでしまう → 読んじゃう.
points.yt: Japanese ちゃう じゃう casual てしまう

s.en: Oh no, I forgot my wallet!
I drank all the juice.
The last train already left.
I beat this game in three days.

points.title: 〜と — whenever A, B (automatically)
points.pattern: V-dictionary / V-ない + と, …
points.gist: whenever A happens, B follows naturally
points.explain: **[dictionary form] と** means B follows A **every time, automatically** — like nature, a machine, or directions: 春になると、桜が咲きます = “When spring comes, the cherry trees bloom.” The B part reports a fact; it can't be a wish, request or invitation.
points.tip: No 〜てください or 〜ましょう after と. For “when you arrive, please call,” use たら: 着いたら電話してください.
points.yt: Japanese と conditional whenever natural result

s.en: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
If you press this button, a ticket comes out.
Whenever I drink coffee, I can't sleep.
Turn right at the second corner and you'll see the station.

points.title: 〜ながら — while doing…
points.pattern: V-stem + ながら, V
points.gist: one person doing two things at the same time
points.explain: Take the ます-stem and add **ながら**: 聞きます → 聞き**ながら**. The ながら action is the **background**; the main action comes at the end: 音楽を聞きながら勉強します = “I study while listening to music.” Both actions belong to the **same person**.
points.tip: Put the main activity last. ご飯を食べながらテレビを見る = mainly watching TV, eating on the side.
points.yt: Japanese ながら while doing

s.en: I study while listening to music.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]します

s.en: Let's talk while we walk through the park.
Please don't use your phone while driving.

c.w: 運転[うんてん]しながら
使[つか]わないでください

s.en: Kimura works part-time while going to university.

c.w: アルバイトしています

points.title: 〜ばよかったです — I should have…
points.pattern: V-ば よかったです
points.gist: regret: “if only I had…”
points.explain: Make the **ば-form** by changing the final **u** sound to **e** and adding **ば**: 行く → 行けば, 買う → 買えば, 食べる → 食べれば, する → すれば, 来る → 来れば. Then add **よかったです**: literally “it would have been good if…”. もっと勉強すればよかったです = “I should have studied more.”
points.tip: For something you shouldn't have done, use the negative: ない → なければ. 食べなければよかった = “I shouldn't have eaten it.”
points.yt: Japanese ばよかった should have regret

s.en: I should have studied more.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]すればよかったです

s.en: I should have brought an umbrella.

c.w: 持[も]ってくればよかったです

s.en: I shouldn't have eaten that much.

c.w: 食[た]べなければよかったです

s.en: I should have bought the tickets earlier.

c.w: 買[か]えばよかったです

lessons.title: Honorific language
lessons.titleJp: 尊敬語・お〜になる・お〜ください

points.title: Special honorific verbs
points.pattern: いらっしゃる · 召し上がる · おっしゃる · ご覧になる …
points.gist: verbs that raise the person who does the action
points.explain: **Honorific verbs** (尊敬語) are for the actions of people you respect — customers, your boss, a teacher — **never for yourself**. The common ones replace the verb completely: いる/行く/来る → **いらっしゃる**, 食べる/飲む → **召し上がる**, 言う → **おっしゃる**, 見る → **ご覧になる**, する → **なさる**, くれる → **くださる**, 知っている → **ご存じです**. いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, なさる, くださる take **〜います** in the ます-form: いらっしゃいます.
points.tip: Only raise **others**. Using いらっしゃる or 召し上がる about yourself is a classic slip — it sounds like you're bowing to yourself.
points.yt: Japanese honorific verbs sonkeigo いらっしゃる 召し上がる

s.en: The company president is in the meeting room.
What would you like for dessert?

c.w: 召[め]し上[あ]がりますか

s.en: What did the teacher say?
Has the department manager already seen this email?

c.w: ご覧[らん]になりましたか

points.title: お + stem + になる
points.pattern: お V-stem に なる
points.gist: the honorific formula for most other verbs
points.explain: Verbs without a special honorific form follow a formula: **お + ます-stem + になる**. 帰ります → **お帰りになります**, 待ちます → **お待ちになります**, 書きます → **お書きになります**. The meaning doesn't change at all — it just shows respect to the person doing it.
points.tip: The formula doesn't fit verbs that have a special form: it's ご覧になる, not お見になる; 召し上がる, not お食べになる.
points.yt: Japanese お〜になる honorific sonkeigo

s.en: The president has already gone home.

c.w: お帰[かえ]りになりました

s.en: Which bus will you be taking?

c.w: お乗[の]りになりますか

s.en: Did the professor write this book?

c.w: お書[か]きになったんですか

s.en: What time will the guest be going out?

c.w: お出[で]かけになりますか

points.title: お〜ください — please (respectfully)
points.pattern: お V-stem ください · ご N ください
points.gist: the polite request you hear from staff everywhere
points.explain: **お + ます-stem + ください** is a respectful “please do…”, a step above 〜てください. You'll hear it constantly in shops, stations and hotels: **お待ちください** (please wait), **お座りください** (please have a seat). する-nouns take ご instead: **ご注意ください** (please be careful).
points.tip: Verbs with a special honorific use it instead: ご覧ください (please look), not お見ください.
points.yt: Japanese おまちください keigo requests shop

s.en: Please wait a moment.
Please have a seat here.
Please write your name and address here.
Please watch your step.

c.w: ご注意[ちゅうい]ください

lessons.title: Thanks and expectations
lessons.titleJp: 〜てくれてありがとう・〜てよかった・〜はず

points.title: 〜てくれてありがとう — thanks for…
points.pattern: V-て くれて ありがとう
points.gist: thanking someone for a specific thing they did
points.explain: Join 〜てくれる (someone did me a favor) with ありがとう: 来てくれてありがとう = “Thanks for coming.” For a teacher or boss, lift it to 〜て**くださって**ありがとうございました — くださる is the honorific くれる.
points.tip: It's くれて, not もらって, because the other person is the one doing the favor: 手伝ってくれてありがとう.
points.yt: Japanese てくれてありがとう thank you for doing

s.en: Thanks for coming to pick me up.
Thanks for helping me move.

c.w: 手伝[てつだ]ってくれて

s.en: Thank you for teaching us for a whole year.

c.w: 教[おし]えてくださって
ありがとうございました

s.en: Thanks for waiting for me in the rain.

points.title: 〜てよかったです — I'm glad…
points.pattern: V-て / V-なくて よかったです
points.gist: relief or happiness about how things turned out
points.explain: **[て-form] よかったです** = “I'm glad that…”, “good thing…”: 日本に来てよかったです = “I'm glad I came to Japan.” Use **〜なくて** for something that luckily did **not** happen: 雨が降らなくてよかった = “Good thing it didn't rain.” Adjectives work too: 簡単でよかった.
points.tip: Don't confuse it with 〜ばよかった. 行ってよかった = I went, and I'm glad; 行けばよかった = I didn't go, and I regret it.
points.yt: Japanese てよかった glad that

s.en: I'm glad I came to Japan.
Good thing it didn't rain.
I'm glad I got to meet you, Kimura.
I'm glad the exam was easy.

points.title: 〜はずです — should be (I expect)
points.pattern: short form + はずです
points.gist: a confident expectation based on facts
points.explain: **はずです** shows what you **expect to be true** from what you know: 田中さんは今日来るはずです = “Tanaka should be coming today” (he said so). Nouns take の and な-adjectives keep な: 休みのはず, 静かなはず. **〜はずでした** = “was supposed to…” — and usually it didn't happen.
points.tip: はず is a logical expectation, not advice. “You should study” is 勉強したほうがいいです, never 勉強するはずです.
points.yt: Japanese はず should be expected

s.en: Tanaka should be coming today.
That store should be open until nine.

c.w: 開[あ]いているはずです

s.en: It should be warm in Okinawa now.

c.w: 暖[あたた]かいはずです

s.en: The train was supposed to arrive at three (but it didn't).

lessons.title: Humble language
lessons.titleJp: 謙譲語・お〜する・ございます

points.title: Special humble verbs
points.pattern: 申す · 参る · おる · 伺う · いただく …
points.gist: lowering your own actions to show respect
points.explain: **Humble verbs** (謙譲語) are for **your own** actions (and your company's) when you speak to someone you respect. Instead of raising them, you lower yourself: 言う → **申す**, 行く/来る → **参る**, いる → **おる**, する → **いたす**, 訪ねる/聞く → **伺う**, 食べる/もらう → **いただく**, 見る → **拝見する**. They're everywhere in job interviews, offices and hotels.
points.tip: The deciding question is **whose action** it is. The customer's → honorific (いらっしゃる). Mine → humble (参る).
points.yt: Japanese humble verbs kenjougo 参る 申す

s.en: My name is Mirage.
I came from Brazil.
I'll come to your office at ten tomorrow.
I work at a hotel in Tokyo.

c.w: 働[はたら]いております

points.title: お + stem + する
points.pattern: お V-stem する · ご N する
points.gist: the humble formula: I do something for you
points.explain: For verbs without a special humble form, use **お + ます-stem + する**: 持ちます → **お持ちします** (I'll carry it for you), 呼びます → **お呼びします**. する-nouns take ご: **ご案内します** (I'll show you the way), **ご連絡します**. Use it when **your** action is done for, or affects, the other person.
points.tip: Don't swap the formulas: お持ちになる = the customer carries; お持ちする = I carry it for the customer.
points.yt: Japanese お〜する humble kenjougo

s.en: I'll carry your luggage.
I'll show you to your room.

c.w: ご案内[あんない]します

s.en: I'll contact you by email tomorrow.

c.w: ご連絡[れんらく]します

s.en: Shall I call a taxi for you?

c.w: お呼[よ]びしましょうか

points.title: ございます & でございます — extra polite
points.pattern: あります → ございます · です → でございます
points.gist: the very polite “be / have” of shops and hotels
points.explain: In formal service talk, **あります → ございます** and **です → でございます**. They don't raise or lower anyone — they simply make the whole sentence sound very polite. A close relative is **よろしいでしょうか**, the polite いいですか.
points.tip: You'll hear these far more than you'll say them. As a customer, plain です/ます is perfectly polite.
points.yt: Japanese ございます でございます keigo shop hotel

s.en: The restroom is over there.
We also have a slightly bigger size.

c.w: もう少[すこ]し大[おお]きい

s.en: Would this seat be all right?
Breakfast is from seven to ten.

points.title: 〜ないで — without doing…
points.pattern: V-ない で, V
points.gist: doing B without doing A (or instead of A)
points.explain: **〜ないで** links a “not doing” to the main action: 朝ご飯を食べないで学校に行きました = “I went to school without eating breakfast.” It can also mean **instead of**: バスに乗らないで歩きました = “I walked instead of taking the bus.”
points.tip: Not the same as 〜ないでください (please don't). Here ないで joins two actions inside one sentence.
points.yt: Japanese ないで without doing

s.en: I went to school without eating breakfast.
I walked home instead of taking the bus.

c.w: 歩[ある]いて帰[かえ]りました

s.en: Ana fell asleep without brushing her teeth.
Kimura drinks his coffee without sugar.

points.title: 〜か — a question inside a sentence
points.pattern: [question in short form] か + 分かりません / 知っています …
points.gist: “I don't know where…”, “tell me what…”
points.explain: You can tuck a question into a bigger sentence: put it in the **short form** and end it with **か**. 電車は何時に来ますか → **電車が何時に来るか**分かりません = “I don't know what time the train comes.” Keep the question word (何, どこ, だれ, いつ, どれ). After nouns and な-adjectives, だ drops out.
points.tip: Inside the tucked-in question, the subject usually takes が, not は: 店が何時に開くか.
points.yt: Japanese embedded questions か 分かりません

s.en: I don't know what time the train comes.
Do you know where Tanaka lives?
Please tell me what you want for your birthday.
I can't decide which one to buy.

points.title: 〜かどうか — whether or not
points.pattern: short form + かどうか
points.gist: a yes/no question inside a sentence
points.explain: When the tucked-in question is a **yes/no** question (no question word), end it with **かどうか** = “whether or not”: アナさんが来るかどうか分かりません = “I don't know whether Ana is coming.” Same rules as before: short form, and no だ after nouns and な-adjectives.
points.tip: Question word inside → just か (どこに行くか). No question word → かどうか (行くかどうか).
points.yt: Japanese かどうか whether or not

s.en: I don't know whether Ana is coming to the party.
Please check whether the store is open.
I'll try asking whether there are any seats.
Could you check whether this kanji is correct?

c.w: 見[み]ていただけませんか

points.title: 〜という N — an N called…
points.pattern: Name という N
points.gist: introducing a name the listener may not know
points.explain: **X という N** = “an N called X”. Use it when the name might be new to your listener: さくらという喫茶店 = “a café called Sakura.” Literally “the N that people call X”: the name comes first, the category noun last.
points.tip: Keep the category noun on a first mention — it tells what kind of thing it is: ポチという犬 (a dog), ポチという店 (a shop).
points.yt: Japanese という called named

s.en: I went to a café called Sakura.
Do you know a game called Dragon Quest?
I'm reading a novel called Kokoro.
My friend lives in a town called Kamakura.

points.title: 〜やすい / 〜にくい — easy / hard to…
points.pattern: V-stem + やすい / にくい
points.gist: how easy or hard something is to do
points.explain: Attach **やすい** (easy) or **にくい** (hard) to the ます-stem: 書きます → **書きやすい** (easy to write with), 歩きます → **歩きにくい** (hard to walk in). The result is an ordinary い-adjective, so it conjugates like one: 分かりやすくない, 使いにくかった.
points.tip: The thing that is easy or hard is the subject: この辞書は使いやすい = this dictionary is easy to use. Not 私は使いやすい.
points.yt: Japanese やすい にくい easy to hard to

s.en: This pen is really easy to write with.
These shoes are hard to walk in.
Kimura's explanations are easy to understand.
The old app was hard to use.

c.w: 使[つか]いにくかったです

points.title: The passive — having something done to you
points.pattern: A は B に V-られる
points.gist: A has something done to them by B
points.explain: **Form:** る-verbs: る → **られる** (食べられる); う-verbs: u → **a + れる** (読む → 読まれる, 言う → 言わ**れる**); する → **される**, 来る → **来られる**. **Roles:** the one the action happens **to** is the topic, and the **doer** takes **に** — just like もらう, you “receive” the action from them: 私は先生にほめられました = “I was praised by my teacher.”
points.tip: る-verb passives look exactly like potentials (食べられる). Look for a doer + に: 犬に食べられた = eaten by the dog.
points.yt: Japanese passive form られる explained

s.en: I was praised by my teacher.
My little brother was bitten by a dog.
This song is often listened to by young people.
A stranger asked me for directions.

points.title: The “suffering” passive
points.pattern: 私は B に (N を) V-られる
points.gist: something happened, and it bothered me
points.explain: Japanese often uses the passive to show you were **affected badly** by someone else's action: 電車で足を踏まれました = “Someone stepped on my foot on the train” (and it annoyed me). It even works with verbs that have no object: 雨に降られました = “I got caught in the rain.” The one who suffers is the topic; the troublemaker takes **に**.
points.tip: Your belongings and body parts keep を, and you stay the topic: 弟にケーキを食べられた = my brother ate my cake (on me).
points.yt: Japanese suffering passive adversative

s.en: I got caught in the rain yesterday.
Someone stepped on my foot on the train.
My little brother ate my cake (on me).
My bicycle got stolen at the station.

lessons.title: Has been done · during · I want you to
lessons.titleJp: 〜てある・〜間に・〜くする・〜てほしい

points.title: 〜てある — done and left that way
points.pattern: N が V (transitive)-て ある
points.gist: someone did it on purpose, and the result is still there
points.explain: **Transitive verb in て-form + ある** describes a state someone **set up on purpose**, usually as preparation: 窓が開けてあります = “The window has been opened (by someone, for a reason).” The thing takes **が**, and the doer isn't mentioned. Compare 窓が開いています, which just reports that it's open.
points.tip: Only transitive verbs go with てある: 開けてある, 書いてある, 予約してある. Intransitive verbs show their state with ている (開いている).
points.yt: Japanese てある vs ている

s.en: It's hot, so the window has been left open.
The hotel is already booked.

c.w: 予約[よやく]してあります

s.en: Today's homework is written on the board.
The drinks have been put in the fridge to chill.

points.title: 〜間に — while… (at some point)
points.pattern: V-ている / N の + 間に
points.gist: something happens at some point inside a stretch of time
points.explain: **[A] 間に [B]** = B happens **at some point during** period A: 母が寝ている間に、ケーキを作りました = “While my mom was asleep, I made a cake.” Verbs before 間に are usually in **〜ている**, and nouns take **の** (夏休みの間に). Unlike ながら, the two actions can belong to **different people**.
points.tip: 間 without に means B lasts the whole time (授業の間、ずっと寝ていた). 間に means B happens once, somewhere inside.
points.yt: Japanese 間に while during あいだに

s.en: While my mom was asleep, I made a cake.

c.w: 寝[ね]ている間[あいだ]に

s.en: I want to go to Kyoto during summer vacation.

c.w: 夏休[なつやす]みの間[あいだ]

s.en: While I was in the restroom, someone stole my bag.

c.w: 行[い]っている間[あいだ]に

s.en: A package arrived while I was out.

c.w: 出[で]かけている間[あいだ]に

points.title: Adjective + する — to make something…
points.pattern: い-adj → 〜くする · な-adj / N → 〜にする
points.gist: changing something on purpose
points.explain: You know 〜くなる / 〜になる (to become). Swap なる for **する** and someone **makes** the change happen: 音を**小さくする** = “to turn the volume down”, 部屋を**きれいにする** = “to tidy the room.” い-adjectives take **く**; な-adjectives and nouns take **に**.
points.tip: なる = it changes; する = someone changes it. 部屋が暖かくなった (it got warm) vs. 部屋を暖かくした (I warmed it up).
points.yt: Japanese くする にする adjective make something

s.en: Please turn down the TV.

c.w: 小[ちい]さくしてください

s.en: I tidied my room before the guests came.
It's summer, so I cut my hair short.
Could you make it a little cheaper?

c.w: 安[やす]くしていただけませんか

points.title: 〜てほしい — I want you to…
points.pattern: Person に V-て ほしい
points.gist: wanting someone else to do something
points.explain: ほしい means “to want (a thing)”. After a て-form it means **wanting someone else to do** something, and that person takes **に**: 母にこの写真を見てほしいです = “I want my mom to see this photo.” For “I want them **not** to…”, use **〜ないでほしい**.
points.tip: 〜たい is for your own actions (行きたい = I want to go); 〜てほしい is for someone else's (来てほしい = I want you to come).
points.yt: Japanese てほしい want someone to do

s.en: I want my mom to see this photo.
I want my roommate to be quieter at night.

c.w: 静[しず]かにしてほしいです

s.en: I don't want anyone to be late tomorrow.

c.w: 遅[おく]れないでほしいです

s.en: My mom wants me to become a doctor.

points.title: Forming the causative: させる / せる
points.pattern: る-verb → させる · う-verb → a + せる
points.gist: to make or let someone do something
points.explain: **る-verbs:** る → **させる** (食べる → 食べ**させる**). **う-verbs:** u → **a + せる** (読む → 読ま**せる**, 待つ → 待た**せる**). **する → させる**, **来る → 来させる** (こさせる). The result is a normal る-verb: 食べさせます, 食べさせて, 食べさせた.
points.tip: う-verbs ending in う use わ, not あ: 買う → 買わせる, 言う → 言わせる.
points.yt: Japanese causative form させる せる

s.en: The teacher made the students read the textbook.
My mother made me eat vegetables.
I'm sorry for keeping you waiting so long.
The manager had Kimura clean the meeting room.

c.w: 掃除[そうじ]させました

points.title: Making × letting — who does what
points.pattern: Causer は Doer に / を V-させる
points.gist: the same form means “make” or “let”; context decides
points.explain: The **causer** (parent, boss, teacher) is the topic. The **doer** — the one who actually does the action — takes **に**, or **を** when the verb has no object of its own (子どもを遊ばせる). The same form covers **make** and **let**: if the doer didn't want to, it's “make”; if they wanted to, it's “let”.
points.tip: Find the doer by asking “who actually writes / plays / works?” It's the に (or を) person, never the topic.
points.yt: Japanese causative make let に を

s.en: The teacher made the students write the kanji fifty times.
Tanaka lets her kids play in the park every day.
My boss made me work on Sunday.
Ana made everyone laugh.

points.title: 〜させてあげる / 〜させてくれる — letting, as a favor
points.pattern: V-させて あげる / くれる / ください
points.gist: allowing someone to do what they want
points.explain: Add a favor verb and the causative clearly means **let**: 〜させて**あげる** = I let someone do it; 〜させて**くれる** = someone lets **me** do it. 父は車を運転させてくれました = “My dad let me drive his car.” And the very useful 〜させてください = “Please let me…”.
points.tip: 〜させてください is a polite way to volunteer: 今日は私に払わせてください = “Please let me pay today.”
points.yt: させてくれる させてあげる させてください Japanese

s.en: My father let me drive his car.

c.w: 運転[うんてん]させてくれました

s.en: I let my little sister play my new game.
Please let me pay today.

c.w: 払[はら]わせてください

s.en: I had a fever, so my boss let me go home early.

c.w: 帰[かえ]らせてくれました

lessons.title: Commands · if · although · like
lessons.titleJp: 〜なさい・〜ば・〜のに・〜のように

points.title: V-stem + なさい — do it!
points.pattern: V-stem + なさい
points.gist: a firm command from parents or teachers
points.explain: **ます-stem + なさい** is a firm but not rude command used by people in charge: parents to kids, teachers to students. 早く寝**なさい**！ = “Go to bed now!” You'll also see it in test instructions: 正しい答えを選びなさい = “Choose the correct answer.”
points.tip: Never use it to people above you — or even to friends. It makes you sound like their parent.
points.yt: Japanese なさい command

s.en: Go to bed now!
Eat your vegetables too.
Stop playing games and study!

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]しなさい

s.en: Choose the correct answer.

points.title: 〜ば — if…, then…
points.pattern: V-ば (u → e + ば) · い-adj → 〜ければ
points.gist: a condition that leads to a result
points.explain: You met the ば-form in 〜ばよかった. On its own it means **“if A, then B”**, and it puts the weight on **what's needed** for the result: この薬を飲めば治ります = “If you take this medicine, you'll get better.” Verbs: u → **e + ば** (飲む → 飲めば, する → すれば). い-adjectives: い → **ければ** (安い → 安ければ). Negative: ない → **なければ**.
points.tip: ば is great for advice and general truths: 毎日練習すれば上手になります. For a one-time “when this happens, do that” request, たら sounds more natural.
points.yt: Japanese ば conditional form

s.en: If you take this medicine, you'll get better.
If you practice every day, you'll get good at it.

c.w: 練習[れんしゅう]すれば
上手[じょうず]になります

s.en: If the tickets are cheap, I'll go too.
If you don't hurry, you won't make the last train.

points.title: 〜のに — even though…
points.pattern: short form + のに
points.gist: A, and yet B — with surprise or frustration
points.explain: **〜のに** joins two facts that clash and adds a feeling of **surprise, disappointment or complaint**: たくさん勉強したのに、試験に落ちました = “I studied so much, and I still failed the exam.” Nouns and な-adjectives take **な**: 日曜日**な**のに, 暇**な**のに.
points.tip: のに always carries feeling, and it's for real facts only — not for plans, requests or invitations.
points.yt: Japanese のに although frustration

s.en: I studied so much, and I still failed the exam.
It's Sunday, and yet I have to work.

c.w: 働[はたら]かなければいけません

s.en: I invited him, but Tanaka didn't come.
This restaurant is expensive, and yet it's not very good.

points.title: 〜のような / 〜のように — like…
points.pattern: N のような N · N のように V / Adj
points.gist: comparing with something: “like a…”, “such as…”
points.explain: **N のような** + noun describes **what kind** of thing: 父のような人 = “a person like my father.” **N のように** + verb or adjective describes **how**: 日本人のように話す = “speak like a Japanese person.” It also gives examples: 東京のような大きい町 = “big cities like Tokyo.”
points.tip: Before a noun → ような; before a verb or adjective → ように. It's the same switch as きれいな花 vs. きれいに書く.
points.yt: Japanese のような のように like

s.en: I want to become a person like my father.
Ana speaks Japanese like a native speaker.

c.w: 日本人[にほんじん]のように

s.en: Today is warm, like spring.
I want to live in a big city like Tokyo.

c.w: 東京[とうきょう]のような

points.title: The causative-passive — being made to do
points.pattern: Doer は Causer に V-させられる
points.gist: I was made to do something I didn't want to
points.explain: Causative + passive = **being made to do** something, usually against your will. **Form:** る-verbs → **させられる** (食べさせられる); う-verbs → **a + される** (待つ → 待た**される**, 歌う → 歌わ**される**); する → **させられる**; 来る → **来させられる**. **Roles:** the unlucky doer is the topic, and the person who forced them takes **に**: 私は母に野菜を食べさせられました.
points.tip: う-verbs ending in す can't use the short version: 話す → 話させられる. Read it from the end: させ (made to) + られ (it happened to me).
points.yt: Japanese causative passive させられる

s.en: My mom made me eat vegetables.

c.w: 食[た]べさせられました

s.en: I was made to wait an hour at the station.
At the drinking party, my boss made me sing.
As a kid, I was made to take piano lessons.

points.title: 〜ても — even if…
points.pattern: V-て も · い-adj → くても · N / な-adj → でも
points.gist: the condition doesn't change the result
points.explain: Add **も** to a て-form and you get **“even if…”**: 雨が降っても行きます = “I'll go even if it rains.” い-adjectives: 高**くても**; nouns and な-adjectives: 週末**でも**, 暇**でも**. With a question word it means **“no matter…”**: 何回読んでも = “no matter how many times I read it.”
points.tip: 〜たら = if A, then B. 〜ても = even if A, still B. Same condition, opposite expectation.
points.yt: Japanese ても even if

s.en: I'll go even if it rains.
Even if it's expensive, I want to buy this game.
No matter how many times I read it, I don't understand.
Kimura gets up at six, even on weekends.

points.title: 〜ことにする — deciding to do
points.pattern: V-dictionary / V-ない + ことにする
points.gist: announcing a decision you've made
points.explain: **[dictionary form] ことにする** = “to decide to do”. Use the past **ことにしました** to report a decision: 来年、日本に留学することにしました = “I've decided to study in Japan next year.” To decide **not** to do something, use the ない-form: 出かけないことにしました.
points.tip: ことにする is your own choice. When someone else decides for you (your company, your school), Japanese uses a different phrase — that comes later.
points.yt: Japanese ことにする decide to

s.en: I've decided to study in Japan next year.

c.w: 留学[りゅうがく]することにしました

s.en: It's raining today, so I've decided not to go out.

c.w: 出[で]かけないことにしました

s.en: For our trip, we decided to go to Hokkaido.

c.w: 行[い]くことにしました

s.en: Starting today, I've decided to quit sweets.

c.w: やめることにしました

points.title: 〜ことにしている — making it a rule
points.pattern: V-dictionary / V-ない + ことにしている
points.gist: a habit you decided on and keep
points.explain: **ことにしている** = “I make it a rule to…”: a decision that turned into a **habit** you keep on purpose. 毎朝三十分歩くことにしています = “I make a point of walking thirty minutes every morning.” The ている shows the decision is still in force.
points.tip: ことにしました = I decided (once); ことにしています = it's my rule (ongoing).
points.yt: Japanese ことにしている make it a rule

s.en: I make a point of walking thirty minutes every morning.

c.w: 三十分[さんじゅっぷん]
歩[ある]くことにしています

s.en: I make it a rule not to eat sweets at night.

c.w: 食[た]べないことにしています

s.en: Ana makes it a rule to keep her diary in Japanese.

c.w: 書[か]くことにしています

s.en: I make it a rule to go to bed before midnight.

c.w: 十二時[じゅうにじ]前[まえ]
寝[ね]ることにしています

points.title: V まで — until something happens
points.pattern: V-dictionary + まで
points.gist: the action goes on until an event
points.explain: You know N まで (三時まで). Now put a **dictionary-form verb** before まで: 雨がやむ**まで**待ちましょう = “Let's wait until the rain stops.” The main action keeps going **up to** that event. The verb before まで stays in the dictionary form even in past stories.
points.tip: まで ≠ までに. まで = keep doing until then (待つ, 遊ぶ); までに = get it done by then.
points.yt: Japanese まで until verb

s.en: Let's wait here until the rain stops.
I ended up playing games until morning.
I'll keep asking until I understand.
I lived with my parents until I graduated.

points.title: Stem + 方 — how to…
points.pattern: V-stem + 方 (かた)
points.gist: “the way of doing” → how to…
points.explain: Attach **方** (かた, “way”) to the ます-stem and you get a noun meaning **how to do it**: 作り**方** (how to make), 読み**方** (how to read), 買い**方** (how to buy). Because it's a noun, the old object takes **の**, not を: 寿司の作り方 = “how to make sushi.”
points.tip: の, not を: この漢字の読み方, never この漢字を読み方. For する-verbs use 仕方 (しかた): 勉強の仕方.
points.yt: Japanese 方 how to do かた

s.en: Please teach me how to make sushi.
I don't know how to read this kanji.
I asked the station staff how to buy a ticket.
Tanaka's way of speaking is easy to understand.

lessons.title: Coming to be able to · making an effort to
lessons.titleJp: 話せるようになる・話すようにする

points.title: 〜ようになる — coming to (be able to) do
points.pattern: V-dict / V-potential + ようになる · V-なくなる
points.gist: a change that happened over time: now you can, or now you do
points.explain: よう means 'the way things are', so ようになる is 'to come to be that way'. It reports a **change that happened over time**: with a potential verb it is a new ability (読めるようになった), with a dictionary-form verb a new habit. The reverse change is **〜なくなる** (no longer). Compare ようにする (next point): なる = a change you notice, する = an effort you make.
points.tip: With verbs the よう is required: 読めるになった is wrong. For a habit that stopped, 〜なくなった is the natural choice.
points.yt: ようになる ようにする difference Japanese grammar N3

s.en: I've finally become able to read the news in Japanese.

c.w: 読[よ]めるようになりました

s.en: Lately my son has started eating vegetables.

c.w: 食[た]べるようになりました

s.en: Since I bought a smartphone, I no longer read paper books.

c.w: 読[よ]まなくなりました

points.title: 〜ようにする — making a point of doing
points.pattern: V-dict / V-ない + ようにする · ようにしている · ようにしてください
points.gist: a conscious effort or habit you keep up
points.explain: With **する** the change doesn't just happen — you make it happen. 〜ようにしている is a habit you work at ('I make a point of…'), and 〜ないようにする means 'try not to'. Compare: 野菜を食べるようになった = I've come to eat vegetables (a change); 野菜を食べるようにしている = I make sure I eat vegetables (an effort).
points.tip: ようにする is an ongoing effort, not a one-time decision — for 'I decided to…' use ことにする. 〜ようにしてください is a soft way to state a rule.
points.yt: ようにする ようにしている Japanese grammar make sure to

s.en: I make a point of taking the stairs every day.

c.w: 使[つか]うようにしています

s.en: I try not to eat sweets at night.

c.w: 食[た]べないようにしています

s.en: Please make absolutely sure you aren't late tomorrow.

c.w: 遅[おく]れないようにしてください

lessons.title: It has been decided
lessons.titleJp: 働くことになりました

points.title: 〜ことになる — it has been decided
points.pattern: V-dict / V-ない + ことになる · ことになっている
points.gist: a decision made by circumstances or other people, not by you alone
points.explain: こと turns the verb into 'the matter of doing it', and なる says it **came about**. So 大阪で働くことになりました = 'it's been decided that I'll work in Osaka' — by the company, by circumstances, or by a group. **ことになっている** means 'that's the rule / the arrangement'. Compare ことにする (next point), where *you* are the one deciding.
points.tip: People often use ことになりました even for their own big news (a wedding, a move) — it sounds modest, as if things simply worked out.
points.yt: ことになる ことになっている Japanese grammar

s.en: It's been decided that I'll work in Osaka from next month.

c.w: 働[はたら]くことになりました

s.en: In Japanese homes, you're supposed to take off your shoes at the entrance.

c.w: 脱[ぬ]ぐことになっています

s.en: It's been settled: Ana is going to study at a Japanese university next year.

c.w: 留学[りゅうがく]することになりました

points.title: 〜ことにする — I decided (vs. ことになる)
points.pattern: V-dict / V-ない + ことにする · ことにしている
points.gist: a decision you make yourself; ことにしている = your personal rule
points.explain: With **する** you are the decider: 毎朝走ることにしました = I've decided to run every morning. **ことにしている** is a personal rule you keep, while ことになっている is a rule someone else set. Quick test — who decided? You → ことにする. The company, the school, circumstances → ことになる.
points.tip: ことにしている (my rule) is firmer than ようにしている (I try to): one is a decision, the other an effort.
points.yt: ことにする ことになる difference Japanese

s.en: This year I've decided to go running every morning.

c.w: 走[はし]ることにしました

s.en: I have a rule of not looking at my phone before bed.

c.w: 見[み]ないことにしています

s.en: Since I'm being transferred, I've decided to move near the new office.

c.w: 転勤[てんきん]することになった
新[あたら]しいオフィス
引[ひ]っ越[こ]すことにしました

lessons.title: In order to
lessons.titleJp: 働くために・忘れないように

points.title: 〜ために — in order to · for the sake of
points.pattern: V-dict + ために · N の ために
points.gist: a purpose you act on directly, or who something is for
points.explain: ために states a **purpose you act on directly**: 日本で働くために日本語を勉強しています. Both halves share the same doer, and the verb before ために is a deliberate action in dictionary form. After a noun, Nのために means 'for (the sake of) N'. Compare ように (next point), used when the goal is a result you **can't directly control**.
points.tip: ために doesn't take potential or ない forms: 話せるために is wrong — say 話せるように.
points.yt: ために ように difference Japanese grammar purpose

s.en: I study Japanese every day in order to work in Japan.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]しています

s.en: I'm saving money for a trip.
My father works late every night for the sake of our family.

points.title: 〜ように — so that…
points.pattern: V-potential / V-ない / non-volitional V + ように
points.gist: the hoped-for result when you can't directly make it happen
points.explain: ように points at a **hoped-for result**: 忘れないようにメモします = I'll make a note so that I don't forget. It goes with potential forms, ない forms and verbs nobody controls (分かる, 聞こえる, 治る). Rule of thumb: ために + a deliberate action ('in order to do'), ように + a state you want to end up in ('so that…').
points.tip: The two halves of a ように sentence can have different subjects: 子供にも分かるように話します (I speak so that even kids understand). With ために they must match.
points.yt: ように so that Japanese grammar N3

s.en: I'll make a note on my phone so I don't forget.
Please speak loudly so you can be heard all the way to the back seats.
I practise every night so that I can speak Japanese.

c.w: 練習[れんしゅう]しています

lessons.title: The four ways to say "seems"
lessons.titleJp: 降りそう・降るそう・降ったようだ・らしい
vocab: 天気予報[てんきよほう]
to open, to be built (also: can do)

points.title: 〜そうだ — looks… / I hear…
points.pattern: stem + そう (looks) · plain form + そうだ (I hear)
points.gist: two different そう: what you see vs. what you were told
points.explain: Attach そう to a **stem** and it means 'looks like / about to' — your own eyes judge: 雨が降りそうです (it looks like rain), おいしそう. Attach そうだ to a **full plain form** and it means 'I hear' — someone told you: 雨が降るそうです (I hear it'll rain). Same sound, different source: what you see vs. what you're told.
points.tip: いい becomes よさそう and ない becomes なさそう. Careful: かわいそう means 'poor thing', not 'looks cute'!
points.yt: そうだ hearsay vs appearance Japanese grammar

s.en: It looks like it's going to rain any minute.
According to the weather forecast, it's going to rain tomorrow.

c.w: 天気予報[てんきよほう]

s.en: This movie doesn't look very interesting.

c.w: 面白[おもしろ]くなさそうです

points.title: 〜ようだ — it seems (my conclusion)
points.pattern: plain form + ようだ · N の ようだ · な-adj な ようだ
points.gist: a conclusion you draw from clues — measured, slightly formal
points.explain: ようだ is **your own conclusion from clues**: the streets are wet, so 雨が降ったようです (it seems it rained). It sounds measured and a little formal. Compare そう: 降りそう is what things **look like** right now; 降ったようだ is what you **work out** from evidence. まるで〜のようだ means 'just like…'.
points.tip: Connect it properly: 学生のようだ (noun + の), 静かなようだ (な-adjective + な). Forgetting の or な is the most common slip.
points.yt: ようだ みたいだ らしい そうだ difference N3

s.en: It seems there's nobody in the room next door.
Tanaka-san seems to have caught a cold.
It's warm today — it's just like spring.

points.title: 〜みたいだ — seems / like (casual)
points.pattern: plain form + みたい · N + みたい (no の) · N みたいな N
points.gist: the conversational version of ようだ
points.explain: みたい means the same as ようだ — **seems, looks like, like** — but it's the everyday spoken version. The grammar difference: みたい attaches straight to nouns and な-adjectives, **no の or な**: 子供みたい, 静かみたい. Use ようだ in writing and formal speech, みたい in conversation (it's fine with です).
points.tip: Say 子供みたい, never 子供のみたい. Before a noun use みたいな: 田中さんみたいな人 = a person like Tanaka-san.
points.yt: みたい Japanese grammar casual seems like

s.en: Kimura-san seems busy today.

c.w: 忙[いそが]しいみたいです

s.en: Ana speaks Japanese like a Japanese person.

c.w: 日本人[にほんじん]みたいに

s.en: I think I dropped my key somewhere.

c.w: 落[お]としたみたいです

points.title: 〜らしい — apparently · typical of
points.pattern: plain form + らしい · N + らしい
points.gist: what you've heard or read (apparently), or 'a true N'
points.explain: らしい means **apparently**: you pass on something you heard or read, keeping a little distance from it. It's close to hearsay そうだ but vaguer ('word is…'). After a noun it can also mean **typical of, a true N**: 春らしい天気 = real spring weather. Map of all four: そう (looks / I hear) · ようだ (I conclude) · みたい (casual ようだ) · らしい (apparently).
points.tip: N らしい is not N みたい: 男らしい = manly (a true man); 男みたい = looks like a man (but isn't one).
points.yt: らしい ようだ みたい difference Japanese

s.en: Apparently a new café has opened in front of the station.
Apparently Tanaka-san is quitting the company next month.
It's a warm, truly spring-like day today, isn't it?

lessons.title: The moment of the action
lessons.titleJp: 食べるところ・食べているところ・食べたところ

points.title: 〜ところ — about to · in the middle of · just did
points.pattern: V-dict ところ · V-ている ところ · V-た ところ
points.gist: pinpoints where you are on the timeline of one action
points.explain: ところ means 'point' — here, a point in time. The verb form in front picks the moment: **食べるところ** = about to eat, **食べているところ** = right in the middle of eating, **食べたところ** = have just eaten. It's a snapshot, perfect for answering 'What are you doing right now?'.
points.tip: 〜ているところ is only 'at this very moment'. Plain 〜ている can also mean a long-term state or a habit.
points.yt: ところ Japanese grammar るところ ているところ たところ

s.en: I'm just about to make dinner.
I'm in the middle of writing a report right now.

c.w: 書[か]いているところです

s.en: I've just this moment got home.

points.title: 〜たばかり — only just (it feels recent)
points.pattern: V-た ばかり · V-た ばかり の N
points.gist: something happened a short while ago — as the speaker feels it
points.explain: たばかり means **only just**, and the time can be long if it **feels** recent to you: 先月入ったばかり (I only joined last month). Compare たところ: a precise snapshot of right now, minutes ago. ばかり can also come before a noun: 買ったばかりの靴 = shoes I've only just bought.
points.tip: With a time word like 先週 or 去年, use たばかり: 先週来たばかりです. 先週来たところです sounds wrong.
points.yt: たばかり たところ difference Japanese

s.en: I only came to Japan last month.
I dropped the smartphone I'd only just bought.

c.w: 落[お]としてしまいました

s.en: I only ate a little while ago, but I'm already hungry.

lessons.title: While still · during
lessons.titleJp: 温かいうちに・休みの間に・会議の最中に

points.title: 〜うちに — while still (before it changes)
points.pattern: V-ている / V-ない / い-adj / な-adj な / N の + うちに
points.gist: do it inside a window of time, before the situation changes
points.explain: うちに means 'inside the time while X is still true' — so **act before it changes**: 温かいうちに食べて (eat while it's hot, before it gets cold). With a ない form it means **before X happens**: 暗くならないうちに. Compare 間に (next point): 間に just marks a period of time, うちに adds 'while you still can'.
points.tip: With 〜ているうちに it can also mean 'while doing it, before I knew it': 話しているうちに仲良くなった. And 'while it's hot' is never 温かい前に.
points.yt: うちに Japanese grammar while still N3

s.en: Please drink the soup while it's hot.
Let's head home before it gets dark.
I was playing video games, and before I knew it, it was morning.

c.w: 朝[あさ]になってしまいました

points.title: 〜間 vs 〜間に — the whole time vs. at some point
points.pattern: V-ている / N の + 間 (whole period) · 間に (one event inside it)
points.gist: 間 = all through the period; 間に = something happened inside it
points.explain: Both mark a stretch of time; the main verb decides which. **間** (no に) goes with something that **lasts the whole period**: 夏休みの間、ずっと働いていた. **間に** goes with a **one-time event** somewhere inside it: 夏休みの間に引っ越した. Compare うちに: 間に is neutral timing, うちに adds 'before things change'.
points.tip: Check the main verb: continuous (ずっと〜ていた, 待っていた) → drop に; a single event (来た, 終わった) → keep に.
points.yt: 間 間に difference Japanese grammar

s.en: I was at my parents' place for the whole summer vacation.
While I was asleep, my mother cleaned my room for me.

c.w: 掃除[そうじ]してくれました

s.en: The whole time I was waiting, I was playing games on my phone.

c.w: 待[ま]っている間[あいだ]

points.title: 〜最中に — right in the middle of
points.pattern: V-ている + 最中に · N の + 最中に
points.gist: at the height of an activity, something (usually unwelcome) interrupts
points.explain: 最中 means 'the very middle, the height of'. 〜最中に sets up an **interruption**: you were deep in something when something else happened, usually at a bad time: 会議の最中に電話が鳴った. Compare 間に: any point in a period; 最中に is **right at the busiest moment**.
points.tip: The main clause is usually one sudden event (鳴った, 消えた, 来た), not a long state.
points.yt: 最中に Japanese grammar N3

s.en: My phone went off right in the middle of the meeting.

c.w: 鳴[な]ってしまいました

s.en: Right while I was taking a shower, the lights went out.

c.w: 浴[あ]びている最中[さいちゅう]

s.en: In the middle of the match, it started raining hard.

lessons.title: It's not that… · there's no way
lessons.titleJp: 嫌いなわけではない・できるわけがない

points.title: 〜わけだ — so that's why · no wonder
points.pattern: plain form + わけだ (な-adj な / N な・の)
points.gist: a conclusion that clicks into place: 'that explains it'
points.explain: わけ means 'reason, logic', and わけだ says **the facts add up**: you learn something and it explains what you saw. 十年も日本に住んでいたなら、上手なわけだ = if you lived in Japan ten years, no wonder you're good. Compare はずだ (N4): はず is an **expectation before** you check; わけだ is the **conclusion after** the pieces fit.
points.tip: わけだ usually reacts to new information, so it often follows なるほど or 〜んですか.
points.yt: わけだ Japanese grammar no wonder

s.en: Ana practises three hours every day — no wonder she's good.

c.w: 練習[れんしゅう]している
上手[じょうず]なわけです

s.en: The air conditioner was broken — that's why the room was so hot.

c.w: 暑[あつ]かったわけです

s.en: If you study two hours a day, that means fourteen hours a week.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]すれば
一週間[いっしゅうかん]
十四時間[じゅうよじかん]
勉強[べんきょう]するわけです

points.title: 〜わけではない — it's not that…
points.pattern: plain form + わけではない (な-adj な / N な)
points.gist: denies a conclusion someone might draw — a soft, partial 'no'
points.explain: わけではない cancels a **wrong conclusion**: 嫌いなわけではない = it's not that I dislike it (there's another reason). It softens; it doesn't claim the opposite. With いつも or 全部 it means **not necessarily**: 高い物がいつもいいわけではない. Compare わけがない (next point), a strong 'no way'.
points.tip: 嫌いじゃない = I don't dislike it (a flat fact). 嫌いなわけじゃない = it's not that I dislike it (hinting at another reason).
points.yt: わけではない Japanese grammar it's not that

s.en: It's not that I dislike natto, but I don't eat it every day.

c.w: 嫌[きら]いなわけではありません

s.en: Expensive things aren't always good.

c.w: いいわけではありません

s.en: Not every Japanese person is good at keigo.

c.w: 上手[じょうず]なわけではありません

points.title: 〜わけがない — there's no way
points.pattern: plain form + わけがない (な-adj な / N の・な)
points.gist: flat, emotional denial: it's impossible, it makes no sense
points.explain: わけがない means 'there's no reason for it' → **no way!** It's a strong, often emotional rejection: そんなことができるわけがない. Compare わけではない: one particle turns a gentle 'not necessarily' into a firm 'impossible'. In casual speech it's often shortened to わけない.
points.tip: Read the particle: わけ**が**ない = no way; わけ**では**ない = it's not that…. They give very different answers.
points.yt: わけがない はずがない difference Japanese

s.en: There's no way you can memorise a hundred kanji in one day.

c.w: 覚[おぼ]えられるわけがありません

s.en: There's no way someone as kind as Kimura-san would get angry.

c.w: 怒[おこ]るわけがありません

s.en: You haven't practised at all — there's no way you can win.

c.w: 練習[れんしゅう]していない
勝[か]てるわけがないですよ

points.title: 〜はずがない — it can't be (the facts rule it out)
points.pattern: plain form + はずがない (な-adj な / N の)
points.gist: a logical 'impossible' based on what you know
points.explain: はず is an **expectation built on facts** (N4: 来るはずです = he should come). はずがない turns it around: **given the facts, it can't be**: 鍵をかけたから、開いているはずがない. Compare わけがない: both mean 'no way', but はずがない sounds like a **reasoned judgment**, わけがない more emotional and dismissive.
points.tip: はずがない is not ないはずだ: 来るはずがない = he can't possibly come; 来ないはずだ = I expect he won't come (milder).
points.yt: はずがない Japanese grammar N3

s.en: I locked it, so the door can't be open.

c.w: 開[あ]いているはずがありません

s.en: Tanaka-san is in Osaka now, so he can't be coming here.

c.w: 来[く]るはずがありません

s.en: This game only came out last week, so it can't be cheaper already.

c.w: 安[やす]くなっているはずがありません

lessons.title: The more…
lessons.titleJp: 勉強すればするほど面白い

points.title: 〜ば〜ほど — the more…, the more…
points.pattern: V-ば V-dict ほど · い-adj-ければ い-adj ほど · な-adj なら な-adj なほど
points.gist: two things rise (or fall) together
points.explain: Say the same word twice — first in the ば form, then in the dictionary form + ほど: 練習すればするほど上手になる = the more you practise, the better you get. The second half tells **what changes along with it**. Compare plain 〜ば (N4): 練習すれば上手になる just means 'if you practise, you'll improve' — ほど adds the sliding scale.
points.tip: With する-verbs, repeat only する: 練習すればするほど sounds much more natural than 練習すれば練習するほど.
points.yt: ばほど the more the more Japanese grammar

s.en: The more I study Japanese, the more interesting it gets.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]すれば
面白[おもしろ]くなります

s.en: The closer to the station, the higher the rent.
The more I thought about that problem, the less I understood it.

c.w: 分[わ]からなくなりました

points.title: 〜ほど / 〜くらい — so much that · to the point of
points.pattern: V / adj + ほど · くらい · A は B ほど〜ない
points.gist: measures how far something goes, often with a vivid example
points.explain: ほど and くらい measure **how far** something goes, often with a vivid example: 泣きたいほど痛かった = it hurt so much I wanted to cry. くらい (or ぐらい) is more casual; ほど sounds stronger. In **AはBほど〜ない** ('A is not as … as B') only ほど works. Compare ば〜ほど: there two things move together; here ほど just measures degree.
points.tip: Say 今年は去年ほど暑くない, not 去年くらい暑くない — the 'not as … as' pattern needs ほど.
points.yt: ほど くらい degree Japanese grammar

s.en: Yesterday my feet hurt so much I couldn't walk.
I laughed so hard my stomach hurt.
This summer isn't as hot as last year.

lessons.title: Compound particles
lessons.titleJp: 日本について・留学生として
vocab: 留学生[りゅうがくせい]

points.title: 〜について — about, concerning
points.pattern: N について · N についての N
points.gist: names the topic you talk, think, write or ask about
points.explain: について marks **what something is about**: 日本の歴史について話しましょう. It goes with verbs of talking, thinking and researching (話す, 書く, 調べる, 考える). Before a noun it becomes **についての**: 日本についての本. Compare に対して (next point): について is the *subject matter*, に対して the *target* of an attitude.
points.tip: Use について for content, not for people you behave toward: 'polite to customers' is お客さんに対して丁寧, not について.
points.yt: について に対して difference Japanese

s.en: We talked about Japanese history in class.
I looked up temples in Kyoto online.
I'm writing a report on Japanese video games.

points.title: 〜に対して — toward · whereas
points.pattern: N に対して · N に対する N · plain form + のに対して
points.gist: the target an attitude or reaction is aimed at; also 'whereas'
points.explain: に対して aims an attitude or reaction **at a target**: 先生に対して失礼だ (rude toward the teacher), 質問に対して答える (answer a question). After a clause, **のに対して** means **whereas**, setting two facts side by side. Compare について: what you talk *about* vs. who or what you *face*.
points.tip: Before a noun use に対する: 子供に対する態度 (attitude toward children). のに対して sounds written; in chat people just use けど.
points.yt: に対して Japanese grammar N3

s.en: Shop staff in Japan are always polite to customers.

c.w: お客[きゃく]さんに対[たい]して

s.en: The teacher answered my question right away.

c.w: 質問[しつもん]に対[たい]して
答[こた]えてくれました

s.en: Whereas it's sunny in Tokyo, it's raining in Osaka.

c.w: 晴[は]れているのに対[たい]して

points.title: 〜によって — depending on · by · because of
points.pattern: N によって · N による N
points.gist: what something varies with, who did it (formal passive), or the cause
points.explain: によって links a result to **what it depends on or comes from**: **depending on** (人によって違う), **by** a doer in formal passives (〜によって書かれた), and **because of** in news-style sentences (大雪によって). Don't mix it up with **によると** (N4), which names a *source of information*: 天気予報によると = according to the forecast.
points.tip: 人によって, 国によって, 日によって are everywhere — the main verb is usually 違う or 変わる.
points.yt: によって によると difference Japanese

s.en: Favourite foods differ from person to person.
This novel was written by a seventeen-year-old high school student.

c.w: 十七歳[じゅうななさい]

s.en: Many trains stopped because of the heavy snow.

points.title: 〜として — as (in the role of)
points.pattern: N として · N としての N
points.gist: the role, status or capacity in which someone acts
points.explain: として means **in the role of, as**: 留学生として日本に来ました = I came to Japan as an exchange student. It names a role, a status or a purpose. Compare **にとって** ('for, from the viewpoint of'): 私にとって大切 = important *to me*; 友達として = *as* a friend.
points.tip: Don't use として for 'in my opinion / for me' — that's にとって. として is about a role, not a viewpoint.
points.yt: として にとって difference Japanese

s.en: Next year I'm going to Japan as an exchange student.

c.w: 留学生[りゅうがくせい]

s.en: Kimura-san took part in the meeting as an interpreter.
I paint on weekends as a hobby.

lessons.title: Thanks to · because of (blame)
lessons.titleJp: 田中さんのおかげで・雨のせいで
vocab: cancellation (中止になる = be called off)

points.title: 〜おかげで — thanks to
points.pattern: N の おかげで · plain form + おかげで
points.gist: credits a cause for a good result, with gratitude
points.explain: おかげ is 'help, blessing', so おかげで carries **gratitude**: 先生のおかげで合格しました = I passed thanks to my teacher. The result should be **good**. Compare せいで (next point): same grammar, but it **blames** a cause for something bad. Plain から / ので give a reason with no feeling attached.
points.tip: おかげさまで alone is a set reply to 'How are you?' or 'How did it go?' — 'thankfully, fine' — even if the listener didn't help at all.
points.yt: おかげで せいで difference Japanese grammar

s.en: Thanks to Tanaka-san, I was able to pass the exam.

c.w: 合格[ごうかく]できました

s.en: Thanks to the medicine I took, my fever went down.
Thanks to the station being close, I can sleep in every morning.

points.title: 〜せいで — because of (blame)
points.pattern: N の せいで · plain form + せいで · 〜のせいだ
points.gist: blames a cause for a bad result
points.explain: せい means **fault**, so せいで points a finger: 雨のせいで試合が中止になった = the game was called off because of the rain. The result is **bad**, and the cause takes the blame. Compare おかげで: identical grammar, opposite feeling. At the end of a sentence, 〜のせいだ = 'it's X's fault'.
points.tip: おかげで with a bad result is sarcasm: 君のおかげで遅れたよ = thanks a lot, you made me late.
points.yt: せいで Japanese grammar blame

s.en: The match was called off because of the rain.

c.w: 中止[ちゅうし]になりました

s.en: Because I played games until late at night, I overslept.

c.w: 寝坊[ねぼう]してしまいました

s.en: It's my fault the project failed.

lessons.title: Asking permission with the causative
lessons.titleJp: 考えさせてください・発表させていただきます
vocab: to rest, to take time off
自己紹介[じこしょうかい]

points.title: 〜させてください — please let me…
points.pattern: causative て-form + ください
points.gist: asks for permission to do something yourself
points.explain: The causative (N4: 行かせる = make or let someone go) + てください literally says **'please let me do it'**. You're asking to do something **yourself**: 私に払わせてください = let me pay. Compare plain 〜てください: 払ってください asks the *other person* to pay! The doer flips.
points.tip: Forms: 行く → 行かせて, 食べる → 食べさせて, する → させて, 来る → 来(こ)させて. With friends drop ください: ちょっと考えさせて.
points.yt: させてください causative permission Japanese

s.en: Please let me do this job.
Please let me think about it a little.

c.w: 考[かんが]えさせてください

s.en: I have a fever, so please let me go home early today.

c.w: 帰[かえ]らせてください

points.title: 〜させていただきます — I will (humbly) do…
points.pattern: causative て-form + いただきます · いただけませんか
points.gist: a very polite way to announce or request your own action
points.explain: いただく is the humble もらう, so 〜させていただく = 'I humbly receive permission to do'. **〜させていただきます** announces your own action politely, as if the listener allowed it: 発表させていただきます. **〜させていただけませんか** asks for that permission: 休ませていただけませんか (could I take a day off?). Compare 〜ていただけませんか, where the *other person* does the action.
points.tip: This is business and ceremony language — with friends it sounds stiff, and putting it on every verb sounds over the top.
points.yt: させていただきます meaning keigo Japanese

s.en: I'll now begin my presentation.

c.w: 始[はじ]めさせていただきます

s.en: I'm not feeling well — could I possibly take tomorrow off?

c.w: 休[やす]ませていただけませんか

s.en: Allow me to briefly introduce myself.

c.w: 自己紹介[じこしょうかい]させていただきます

lessons.title: Text connectors
lessons.titleJp: しかし・だから・つまり・ところで・それに
vocab: 一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]
to be sunny, to clear up

points.title: しかし — however
points.pattern: Sentence。しかし、Sentence。
points.gist: opens a new sentence that goes against the previous one
points.explain: しかし is a **formal, written 'however'** that opens a new sentence. でも is the everyday spoken version, and けれども / だけど sit in between. Compare が / けど (N5): they join two halves *inside* one sentence; しかし starts a *new* sentence.
points.tip: Don't open a chat message with しかし — it sounds like a newspaper. With friends use でも.
points.yt: しかし でも けれども difference Japanese conjunctions

s.en: I studied as hard as I could. However, I failed the exam.

c.w: 一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]
勉強[べんきょう]しました。
落[お]ちてしまいました

s.en: This shop is famous. However, its prices aren't high.
I want to go to Japan. But this year I don't have the money.

points.title: それで / だから — so, that's why
points.pattern: Sentence。だから / それで、Sentence。
points.gist: the next sentence is a result of the previous one
points.explain: Both mean **so**, but they feel different. **だから** is the speaker's own push — it can lead into opinions, requests and orders: だから早く寝てください. **それで** simply reports what **naturally followed**: 電車が止まった。それで遅れた. Compare から / ので (N5): same logic, but inside one sentence.
points.tip: それで can't lead into a request or a 'let's…' — use だから there. In polite speech, ですから is the polite だから.
points.yt: それで だから difference Japanese

s.en: Yesterday the trains stopped. So I was late for school.
Tomorrow is the exam. So please go to bed early tonight.
Ana is from Brazil. That's why she can speak Portuguese.

c.w: ブラジル出身[しゅっしん]です。

points.title: つまり — in other words
points.pattern: Sentence。つまり、restatement。
points.gist: sums up or rephrases what was just said
points.explain: つまり means **in other words**. It doesn't add a new fact or a consequence; it **restates** the idea more simply or spells out what it really means. Compare だから: だから gives a *result* (it rained → so I stayed home); つまり gives the *same idea in new words* (my mother's brother → that is, my uncle).
points.tip: つまり often pairs with ということです: つまり、来られないということですね = so you mean you can't come?
points.yt: つまり meaning Japanese conjunction

s.en: He's my mother's younger brother. In other words, he's my uncle.
The shop is open Monday to Friday. In other words, it's closed on weekends.
This train stops at every station. In other words, it's a local train.

c.w: 普通[ふつう]電車[でんしゃ]です

points.title: ところで — by the way
points.pattern: ところで、new topic
points.gist: switches to a new topic
points.explain: ところで tells the listener **we're changing the subject now** — often to the thing you really wanted to talk about. Don't confuse it with **ところが** ('but then, unexpectedly'), which continues the same story with a twist. If something just said *reminded* you of a new topic, そういえば ('that reminds me') fits better.
