points.tip: ところで vs ところが — one sound, two jobs: で = new topic, が = surprise twist in the same story.
points.yt: ところで そういえば difference Japanese

s.en: It's really hot today, isn't it? By the way, are you going anywhere for summer vacation?
By the way, how has Tanaka-san been lately?
It was sunny in the morning. But then, unexpectedly, it started raining in the afternoon.

points.title: それに — besides, on top of that
points.pattern: Sentence。それに、another point in the same direction。
points.gist: adds another reason or fact pointing the same way
points.explain: それに **adds another point** that pushes in the same direction: 安いです。それに、おいしいです (it's cheap — and on top of that, tasty). Compare **それから** ('and then'): それから is about **order in time**, それに about **piling up reasons**. In writing, さらに is a formal 'furthermore'.
points.tip: Both points should push the same way (good + good, or bad + bad). For a contrast you need しかし or でも.
points.yt: それに それから difference Japanese

s.en: This apartment is spacious. On top of that, it's close to the station.
I'm tired today. Besides, it's raining too, so I don't want to go out.

c.w: 出[で]かけたくないです

s.en: Kimura-san is a good cook. And on top of that, she's very kind.

lessons.title: Even · precisely
lessons.titleJp: 時間さえあれば・今年こそ・子供でも
vocab: likewise; it's me who should (thank you)

points.title: 〜さえ — even (the bare minimum)
points.pattern: N さえ · N で / に さえ · N さえ〜ば (as long as)
points.gist: picks the most basic example: not even that, or 'if only that'
points.explain: さえ picks an **extreme, minimal example** to show how far things go: 水を飲む時間さえなかった = I didn't even have time to drink water. It replaces が / を and follows other particles (子供にさえ, 日本人でさえ). With ば it means **as long as / if only**: 時間さえあれば. Compare も: 時間もない is a plain 'no time either'; さえ stresses 'not even the bare minimum'.
points.tip: Drop を and が next to さえ: 水さえ, not 水をさえ. Other particles stay: 先生にさえ.
points.yt: さえ さえば Japanese grammar N3

s.en: I was so busy I didn't even have time to eat lunch.

c.w: 昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べる

s.en: I hear even Japanese people can't read this difficult kanji.

c.w: この難[むずか]しい漢字[かんじ]

s.en: If only I had the time, I could study Japanese more.

c.w: 勉強[べんきょう]できます

points.title: 〜こそ — precisely this one
points.pattern: N こそ · 今年こそ · こちらこそ
points.gist: spotlights one item: this, and nothing else
points.explain: こそ shines a **spotlight** on one word: 'this one, precisely'. 今度こそ = this time for sure (after failing before); こちらこそ = no, it's *me* who should thank you. Compare さえ: さえ picks a *minimal* example ('even that'), こそ the *most important* one ('that, above all').
points.tip: こそ is positive emphasis, so it rarely highlights something bad. Like さえ, it replaces は, が and を.
points.yt: こそ Japanese grammar emphasis

s.en: I failed last year, so this year I really want to pass.

c.w: 合格[ごうかく]したいです

s.en: It's precisely small daily practice that matters.
No — it's me who should thank you.

c.w: ありがとうございました

points.title: 〜でも — even · or something · any-
points.pattern: N でも · question word + でも
points.gist: 'even N' (a surprising example), or a soft 'N or something'
points.explain: でも after a noun has three everyday jobs. **Even**: 子供でも分かる (even a child gets it). **Or something** (a soft suggestion): お茶でも飲みませんか. With question words it means **any-**: 何でも, いつでも, 誰でも. Compare さえ: さえ is stronger and more dramatic, でも light and conversational.
points.tip: Don't confuse it with sentence-initial でも ('but'). Position tells you: after a noun = even / or something; at the start = but.
points.yt: でも even or something Japanese grammar

s.en: This game is easy, so even kids can play it.
Let's take a little break — how about some tea or something?
If there's anything you don't understand, ask me any time.

lessons.title: Tendencies
lessons.titleJp: 子供っぽい・遅れがち・風邪気味
vocab: 運動不足[うんどうぶそく]

points.title: 〜っぽい — -ish, -like
points.pattern: N / い-adj stem / V-stem + っぽい
points.gist: has the feel of something (casual, often a little critical)
points.explain: っぽい means **-ish, kind of like**: 子供っぽい (childish), 黒っぽい (blackish), 忘れっぽい (forgetful). It's casual, and about people it's often a little critical. Compare らしい: 大人らしい = a true adult (praise); 子供っぽい = acting like a kid when you're not one. It conjugates like an い-adjective: 子供っぽくない.
points.tip: After a verb stem it means 'easily, by nature': 忘れっぽい = forgetful, 怒りっぽい = short-tempered.
points.yt: っぽい Japanese grammar meaning

s.en: My big brother is thirty, but he's a bit childish.

c.w: 三十歳[さんじゅっさい]
子供[こども]っぽいです

s.en: My dad has become forgetful lately.

c.w: 忘[わす]れっぽくなりました

s.en: Ana was wearing a blackish coat.

points.title: 〜がち — tend to (and it's a problem)
points.pattern: V-stem / N + がち · がちな N
points.gist: something that happens too often, usually unwelcome
points.explain: がち says **this tends to happen, and it's not great**: 冬は運動不足になりがちです. It attaches to a verb stem or a noun (遅れがち, 病気がち). Compare っぽい: 忘れっぽい describes a **person's nature**; 忘れがち describes a **tendency** in a situation. It acts like a な-adjective: 遅れがちな電車.
points.tip: Don't use がち for good habits: 'I tend to study a lot' isn't 勉強しがち. For neutral habits use よく〜します.
points.yt: がち Japanese grammar tend to

s.en: In winter, people tend not to get enough exercise.

c.w: 運動不足[うんどうぶそく]

s.en: When I'm busy, I tend to skip breakfast without meaning to.
On rainy days, the buses tend to run late.

points.title: 〜気味 — a touch of, slightly
points.pattern: N / V-stem + 気味 (ぎみ) · 気味だ · 気味の N
points.gist: a slight symptom or feeling right now
points.explain: 気味 (ぎみ) means **a slight touch of**: 風邪気味 = coming down with a cold, 疲れ気味 = a bit worn out. It describes a **mild state right now**, usually not a pleasant one. Choosing among the three: っぽい = it has the *feel* of X; がち = it *often happens*; 気味 = there's *a little of it at the moment*.
points.tip: After another word it's read ぎみ (風邪気味, 太り気味). On its own it's きみ, as in 気味が悪い (creepy).
points.yt: 気味 がち っぽい difference Japanese

s.en: I've got a bit of a cold today, so I'll go to bed early.
Work has been busy lately, and I'm a bit worn out.

c.w: 疲[つか]れ気味[ぎみ]です

s.en: I ate too much over New Year, so I've put on a little weight.

c.w: 太[ふと]り気味[ぎみ]です

lessons.title: Real speech (contractions)
lessons.titleJp: 食べちゃった・行かなきゃ・言ったじゃん
vocab: 今週中[こんしゅうちゅう]

points.title: 〜ちゃう / 〜じゃう — the casual てしまう
points.pattern: 〜てしまう → 〜ちゃう · 〜でしまう → 〜じゃう
points.gist: did it completely, or (oops) ended up doing it
points.explain: In speech てしまう shrinks: **てしまう → ちゃう**, **でしまう → じゃう** (past: 食べちゃった, 飲んじゃった). It keeps both meanings: **done completely** and **oops, it happened**. Compare とく (next point): ちゃう is about a finished or regretted result, とく about preparing ahead.
points.tip: If the て-form ends in で (飲んで, 遊んで), use じゃう: 飲んじゃった, never 飲んちゃった.
points.yt: ちゃう じゃう てしまう casual Japanese

s.en: I ate all the cake.
Oops, I left my phone at home.
I ended up hanging out with friends until morning.

points.title: 〜とく — the casual ておく
points.pattern: 〜ておく → 〜とく · 〜でおく → 〜どく
points.gist: do it in advance, or leave it as it is
points.explain: ておく shrinks to **とく** (and でおく to **どく**): 買っておく → 買っとく, 読んでおく → 読んどく. Same meaning: **do it in advance**, or **leave it that way**. Compare ちゃう: ちゃう is about something done or regretted; とく is about getting ready.
points.tip: It conjugates like a normal う-verb: 買っとく, 買っといて (please do it ahead), 買っといた (I already did).
points.yt: とく ておく casual Japanese contraction

s.en: I'll buy the drinks before the party, okay?
It's hot, so leave the window open.
Read this book before the test.

points.title: 〜てる — the casual ている
points.pattern: 〜ている → 〜てる · 〜でいる → 〜でる
points.gist: drop the い: is doing, or is in a state
points.explain: In speech the い of ている almost always disappears: 見ている → **見てる**, 読んでいる → **読んでる**. The meaning doesn't change: an action **in progress** (今ご飯食べてる) or a **resulting state** (結婚してる = is married). Compare とく: listen for the vowel — 読んでる (is reading) vs 読んどく (will read in advance).
points.tip: It's fine in polite speech too: 知ってます, 待ってます are completely normal. Don't confuse 寝てた (was sleeping) with 寝た (slept).
points.yt: てる ている casual Japanese

s.en: What are you doing right now?
Tanaka-san is already married, you know.

c.w: 結婚[けっこん]してるよ

s.en: Ana has been reading manga the whole time.

points.title: 〜なきゃ / 〜なくちゃ — gotta, have to
points.pattern: 〜なければ(いけない) → 〜なきゃ · 〜なくては(いけない) → 〜なくちゃ
points.gist: casual 'I have to', usually with the ending dropped
points.explain: The long 'must' forms get squashed: なければいけない → **なきゃ**, なくてはいけない → **なくちゃ**. Dropping the いけない part is normal: もう行かなきゃ = I gotta go. なきゃ and なくちゃ mean the same; なくちゃ sounds a bit softer. Compare ちゃう: both have ちゃ, but なくちゃ has the ない inside it.
points.tip: Build it from the ない form: 行かない → 行かなきゃ. 行かきゃ is wrong.
points.yt: なきゃ なくちゃ Japanese casual must

s.en: I have an early start tomorrow, so I gotta go to bed.
I have to hand in the report this week.

c.w: 今週中[こんしゅうちゅう]

s.en: I need to get a passport before I go to Japan.

c.w: 取[と]らなきゃいけない

points.title: 〜じゃん — …right? · see?
points.pattern: plain form / N / adj + じゃん
points.gist: casual 'isn't it?' — pushing for agreement, or 'see, I told you'
points.explain: じゃん comes from じゃないか ('isn't it?'), but it is **not negative**. It pushes the listener to agree — いいじゃん = that's nice, right? — or points out the obvious: だから言ったじゃん = see, I told you. It attaches directly to plain forms, nouns and adjectives. Compare ね: ね shares a feeling softly, じゃん is pushier.
points.tip: Only with friends — never with teachers or bosses. And 上手じゃん means 'you're good!', not 'you're not good'.
points.yt: じゃん meaning casual Japanese

s.en: Hey, these clothes look great!
See, I told you!
Your Japanese has got really good!

c.w: 上手[じょうず]になったじゃん

lessons.title: Can't not · it's not that I don't
lessons.titleJp: 休むわけにはいかない・食べられないことはない

points.title: 〜わけにはいかない — I can't (it wouldn't be right)
points.pattern: V-dict + わけにはいかない · V-ない + わけにはいかない
points.gist: you're able to, but duty or common sense won't allow it
points.explain: わけにはいかない means **I can't, because it wouldn't be right** — the block is duty, manners or responsibility, not ability: 試験だから、休むわけにはいかない. With a ない form it flips: 行かないわけにはいかない = I can't *not* go, I have no choice. Compare the potential: 行けない = something stops me; 行くわけにはいかない = I could, but I mustn't.
points.tip: Don't use it for real inability: 'I can't swim' is 泳げない, never 泳ぐわけにはいかない.
points.yt: わけにはいかない Japanese grammar

s.en: I have an important meeting, so I can't take today off.

c.w: 休[やす]むわけにはいきません

s.en: It's my friend's secret, so I can't tell anyone.

c.w: 話[はな]すわけにはいきません

s.en: My senior invited me, so I can't not go.

c.w: 行[い]かないわけにはいきません

points.title: 〜ないことはない — it's not that I can't
points.pattern: V-ない / い-adj-くない + ことはない
points.gist: a hesitant 'yes': possible, but not easily or not gladly
points.explain: Two negatives make a **weak, reluctant yes**: 行けないことはない = it's not that I can't go — I could, but it's not easy or I'm not keen. It's a hedge for when you don't want to give a plain yes. Compare わけではない: わけではない denies a *conclusion* ('it's not that I dislike it'); ないことはない admits a *possibility* ('I could, I suppose').
points.tip: Don't confuse it with dictionary form + ことはない = 'there's no need to': 心配することはない = no need to worry.
points.yt: ないことはない Japanese grammar

s.en: It's not that I can't eat spicy food, but I don't really like it.

c.w: 食[た]べられないことはないです

s.en: If we hurry now, we can probably still make the last train.

c.w: 間[ま]に合[あ]わないことはないです

s.en: It's not that this movie isn't interesting, but it's a bit long.

c.w: 面白[おもしろ]くないことはないです

lessons.title: As soon as · the moment
lessons.titleJp: 窓を開けたとたん・分かり次第

points.title: 〜たとたん — the moment X happened
points.pattern: V-た + とたん（に）
points.gist: right when X happened, something unexpected happened
points.explain: とたん means **that very instant**. 〜たとたん says that right after X, **something sudden or surprising** happened — something you didn't plan: ドアを開けたとたん、猫が飛び出した. Compare 次第 (next point): a planned future 'as soon as… I'll'. Everyday 〜てすぐ just means 'right after', with no surprise.
points.tip: The second half can't be your own plan: 着いたとたん電話します is wrong — say 着いたらすぐ電話します or 着き次第電話します.
points.yt: たとたん Japanese grammar the moment

s.en: The moment I opened the window, a strong wind blew in.
Just as I got home, it started to rain.
The moment I started the game, the power went out.

c.w: 停電[ていでん]になりました

points.title: 〜次第 — as soon as (I'll…) · depends on
points.pattern: V-stem + 次第 · N 次第だ (depends on N)
points.gist: a polite, planned 'as soon as X, I will Y'
points.explain: 次第 (しだい) after a verb stem means **as soon as X happens, I'll do Y** — a promise or plan, typical in business: 分かり次第、連絡します. It's formal and always points to the **future**. Compare たとたん: a past surprise vs. a future plan. After a noun, 次第 means **depends on**: 天気次第です.
points.tip: 次第 can't describe the past: 'I called as soon as I arrived' is 着いてすぐ電話した, not 着き次第電話した.
points.yt: 次第 Japanese grammar as soon as

s.en: I'll contact you as soon as I know the details.

c.w: ご連絡[れんらく]します

s.en: Let's set off as soon as we're ready.

c.w: 出発[しゅっぱつ]しましょう

s.en: Whether we go hiking depends on tomorrow's weather.

c.w: 天気[てんき]次第[しだい]です

lessons.title: Airport and immigration
vocab: 入国審査[にゅうこくしんさ]

points.title: At the immigration counter
points.pattern: 〜は何ですか・〜です
points.gist: short answers to the officer's standard questions
points.explain: Officers usually ask two or three questions, so keep your answers short: a noun + **です** is perfect. **観光です** (sightseeing) and a length of stay like **三週間です** cover most of it. Have your hotel name and address ready on paper or on your phone.
points.tip: Don't joke or chat at the counter, and never answer "business" if you are a tourist — answer exactly what is asked, calmly and politely.
points.yt: Japanese immigration questions at the airport phrases for travelers

s.en: (you hear) What is the purpose of your visit?
The purpose is sightseeing.
(you hear) Your passport, please.
(you hear) How many days will you stay?

c.w: 滞在[たいざい]しますか

s.en: I'll stay for three weeks.

c.w: 三週間[さんしゅうかん]

s.en: (you hear) Where will you be staying?
At a hotel in Shinjuku.

points.title: Fingerprints and customs
points.pattern: 〜てください・何もありません
points.gist: follow the officer's instructions and answer the customs question
points.explain: At the fingerprint scanner and camera you mostly **listen**: 〜てください means "please do…", so catch the verb just before it (置いて = put, 見て = look). At customs, **何もありません** ("nothing") answers the declaration question if you carry nothing special. Many travellers fill in the customs form online beforehand (Visit Japan Web) and just show a QR code.
points.tip: Carry prescription medicine in its original box with a copy of the prescription — some medicines that are normal at home are restricted in Japan, so check before you fly.
points.yt: Japan airport arrival customs Visit Japan Web walkthrough

s.en: (you hear) Do you have anything to declare?
No, I have nothing to declare.
(you hear) Please put your index fingers here.
(you hear) Please look at the camera.
(you hear) Please open this suitcase.
This is my own medicine.
These are souvenirs for my friends.

points.title: Leaving the airport
points.pattern: 〜はどこですか・〜まで
points.gist: find the trains, buses, money exchange and the way out
points.explain: Signs at Japanese airports are bilingual, but asking is faster when you're tired: **X は どこですか** works for anything. **乗り場** means "the place where you board" — for trains, buses and taxis alike. **〜まで** ("as far as") is how you name your destination when you buy a ticket.
points.tip: Start every question to staff with すみません — it means both "excuse me" and "sorry", and it opens the conversation politely.
points.yt: Narita Haneda airport to Tokyo train bus Japanese phrases

s.en: Where is the exit?
Where do I get the train?
Where can I change money?
One ticket to Shinjuku, please.
Does this bus go to Tokyo Station?

c.w: 東京駅[とうきょうえき]

s.en: (you hear) The bus leaves from stop number 5.
(you hear) The next one is at 10:15.

c.w: 十時[じゅうじ]十五分[じゅうごふん]です

points.title: IC cards and tickets
points.pattern: 〜までいくらですか・〜に〜チャージします
points.gist: buy tickets, top up your card and fix gate problems
points.explain: Suica, PASMO and ICOCA are rechargeable **IC cards**: touch in, touch out, and the fare is taken automatically. Topping up is called **チャージ** and is done with cash at any ticket machine. If the gate beeps and closes, go to the staffed window next to it — it's usually just a low balance.
points.tip: Have your card in your hand before you reach the gate, and step aside if you need to search your bag — stopping in the gate blocks a whole line of commuters.
points.yt: how to use Suica PASMO IC card Japan station Japanese phrases

s.en: Where is the ticket machine?
How much is it to Shibuya?
I'll put 2,000 yen on my Suica.
Is this card OK on the subway too?

c.w: 大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]ですか

s.en: The gate won't open.
(you hear) Your balance is too low.
(you hear) Please pay the difference at the fare adjustment machine.

c.w: 精算[せいさん]してください

points.title: Platforms and transfers
points.pattern: 〜は何番線ですか・〜で乗り換えます
points.gist: find your platform and change lines
points.explain: Platforms have numbers — **〜番線** — and lines have colours and letters (G for Ginza, JY for Yamanote). Before boarding, check the train type: **各駅停車** (かくえきていしゃ) stops everywhere, while **快速** (かいそく) and **急行** (きゅうこう) skip small stations. Big stations have many exits, so ask for yours by name, like **ハチ公口** or **東口** (ひがしぐち, east exit).
points.tip: Line up at the marks on the platform floor and let everyone get off before you board — pushing in while people are still getting off is a real faux pas.
points.yt: Tokyo subway transfer platform Japanese phrases

s.en: Which platform is the Yamanote Line?

c.w: 何番線[なんばんせん]ですか

s.en: (you hear) It's platform 2, over there.

c.w: 二番線[にばんせん]です

s.en: Does this train stop at Harajuku?
Where do I change to the Ginza Line?
(you hear) Change trains at the next station.

c.w: 乗[の]り換[か]えてください

s.en: (you hear) This train is a rapid service.
Which way is the Hachikō exit?

points.title: Shinkansen and announcements
points.pattern: 〜まで〜を〜枚お願いします
points.gist: buy bullet-train seats and follow the announcements
points.explain: At a ticket machine or counter, give three things: the destination with **まで**, the seat type, and the number of tickets with **〜枚**. Announcements repeat the same frames — **次は〜** ("next is…") and **ドアが閉まります** ("the doors are closing") — so you only need to catch the station name. Your ticket shows the car number (**号車**, ごうしゃ) and the seat, and the platform floor shows where each car stops.
points.tip: Give a small すみません and a glance back before reclining your seat, and take phone calls in the space between cars, not at your seat.

A window seat, please.

points.title: Checking in
points.pattern: 〜で予約しています・〜てもいいですか
points.gist: give your name, confirm the nights and ask about times
points.explain: Most check-ins need only your name and passport: **〜で予約しています** ("I have a booking under…") starts it smoothly. Many hotels keep your bags before check-in and after check-out — ask with **荷物を預けてもいいですか**. Check-in is often 15:00 and check-out 10:00 or 11:00.
points.tip: If you ask for something and hear "それはちょっと…" (a trailing "that's a bit…"), it's a polite **no** — don't keep pushing.

s.en: I have a reservation under the name Mirage.

c.w: 予約[よやく]しています

s.en: Two nights, starting today.
(you hear) Please write your name and address here.

c.w: 何時[なんじ]からですか

s.en: (you hear) Check-out is at eleven.

s.en: May I leave my luggage until three?

c.w: 預[あず]けてもいいですか

points.title: Requests and problems
points.pattern: 〜が〜ません・〜てください
points.gist: ask for things and report what doesn't work
points.explain: To report a problem, name the thing with **が** and add a negative verb: **エアコンがつきません**, **お湯が出ません** — no long story needed. To ask for something, use **〜をください** or **〜てください**. Staff often answer in humble keigo like **伺います** (うかがいます, "I'll come"), so just listen for the key noun.
points.tip: Many rooms only get power when the key card sits in the slot by the door — check that before you report the lights as broken.
points.yt: Japanese phrases hotel front desk problems requests

s.en: The air conditioner won't turn on.
The hot water isn't coming out.
Could I have one more towel?
What is the Wi-Fi password?
I left my key in the room.
(you hear) We'll come to your room right away.
Could you call a taxi, please?

points.title: Ryokan customs
points.pattern: 〜てもいいですか・〜てください
points.gist: shoes, yukata, meal times and futon
points.explain: Ryokan run on a schedule: dinner and breakfast at set times, the futon laid out while you eat, and bath hours posted near the entrance. Use **〜てもいいですか** ("is it OK if I…?") whenever you're unsure — staff appreciate being asked. When you leave, **お世話になりました** is the perfect thank-you.
points.tip: Wrap the yukata **left side over right** — right over left is how the dead are dressed at funerals. And take your slippers off before stepping onto tatami.

points.title: Getting a table
points.pattern: 〜でも大丈夫ですか・〜はありますか
points.gist: say how many you are and understand how to order
points.explain: When you walk in, staff call out **いらっしゃいませ** (welcome) — you don't need to answer, just hold up fingers for the number of people. At ramen and gyūdon shops you often buy a **食券** (meal ticket) from a machine by the door and hand it to the staff. Many places now take orders on a tablet or with a QR code on your phone.
points.tip: Wait to be seated instead of choosing a table yourself; if there's a waiting list by the door, write your name and number of people on it.

Is it OK for just one person?

points.title: Ordering and dietary needs
points.pattern: 〜をください・〜は食べません
points.gist: order food and drinks and explain what you can't eat
points.explain: Point and say **これをください** — it works everywhere, and menus often have photos. Count dishes and drinks with **一つ、二つ、三つ**. For dietary needs, be direct: **肉を食べません** or **〜のアレルギーがあります**; fish stock (dashi) is in many dishes, so vegetarians should ask carefully.
points.tip: In an izakaya a small dish called **お通し** (おとおし) arrives without you ordering it — it's a seat charge of a few hundred yen, not a mistake.

points.title: Paying
points.pattern: 〜をお願いします・〜でお願いします
points.gist: ask for the bill and pay the way you want
points.explain: In most restaurants you pay at the **レジ** (register) by the door, not at the table — take the bill slip with you. Cards and IC cards are widely accepted, but small family places can be cash only, so carry some yen. On the way out, **ごちそうさまでした** ("thank you for the meal") always gets a smile.
points.tip: Don't leave a tip — tipping isn't done in Japan, and staff may run after you to give the money back.

points.title: At the konbini register
points.pattern: 〜は〜ですか・〜はいりません
points.gist: answer the cashier's four standard questions
points.explain: Konbini cashiers ask the same few questions every time: bag, heating, chopsticks, payment. Say yes with **お願いします** and no with **大丈夫です** — both work for every question. Plastic bags cost a few yen, so many people bring their own.
points.tip: Avoid いいです as an answer — it can mean "yes, good" or "no, I'm fine", so the cashier can't tell. 大丈夫です is the clear, polite "no thanks".

At a shrine the usual way to pray is **two bows, two claps, one bow**, after dropping a coin in the offering box. A **御朱印** is a hand-written stamp collected in a special book — hand the book over open at a fresh page.
points.tip: Walk along the sides of the path, not the middle — the centre is said to be for the gods. If your omikuji is bad luck, tie it to the rack there instead of taking it home.

At the counter give the destination with **まで**, the train with **の** and the number of tickets with **一枚**. A Suica on your phone pays ordinary fares, but the Narita Express and the Skyliner also need a reserved-seat ticket, so always check.
points.tip: You fly home from Kansai Airport, so buy a **片道** (one-way) ticket — a round-trip (**往復**) deal only pays off if you come back to Narita. If you land late, check the **終電** (last train) first: after it, only buses and taxis are left.

Most business hotels keep the front desk open all night, and **夜遅くにすみません** ("sorry to come so late") is a warm way to start.
points.tip: Your exit may be behind a different ticket gate — inside Shinjuku the wrong gate can mean ten minutes of walking with your suitcase. Exit signs are **yellow**: follow the yellow boards with your exit's name.

points.gist: check you're welcome, understand the charge and introduce yourself
points.explain: **Golden Gai** is about 200 tiny bars packed into six alleys beside Kabukicho. A few are for regulars only, but many welcome newcomers — look for a price list on the door and ask **初めてですが、大丈夫ですか** before you sit. Most bars add a **チャージ** (cover charge) of about 500–1,500 yen. Then introduce yourself: where you're from, that you travel alone, and how long you're here — **一か月ぐらいいます** ("I'm here for about a month").
points.tip: After two words of Japanese you'll hear **日本語がお上手ですね** — answer modestly with **まだ勉強中です** ("I'm still learning"); it sounds friendlier than simply accepting the praise.

points.explain: Yanaka and Nezu are quiet old-Tokyo streets full of small temples, and **Gotokuji** in Setagaya is covered in thousands of white **招き猫** (beckoning cats) left by visitors. Open your **御朱印帳** at a blank page and hand it over at the temple office with **この御朱印帳にお願いします**; at busy times you may get a pre-written sheet (**書き置き**) instead. If your omikuji is bad (**凶**), tie it to the rack and leave the bad luck behind.
points.tip: A goshuin records a prayer visit — it is not a tourist stamp: pray at the main hall first, then go to the office. Keep a separate notebook for station and museum stamps.

points.title: Morning in a Showa kissaten
points.pattern: 〜はまだありますか・〜てもいいですか
points.gist: order coffee and a set, ask about smoking and chat with the owner
points.explain: A **喫茶店** (kissaten) is an old-style coffee shop from the **Showa** era: velvet chairs, slow hand-made coffee and an owner who has been there for decades. Until about 11 am many serve a **モーニング** — toast and an egg for little more than the price of a coffee — so ask **モーニングはまだありますか**. Some old kissaten are among the last places where smoking is still allowed indoors; look for **喫煙可** on the door if smoke bothers you.
points.tip: Kissaten talk: **ホット** means hot coffee and **アイス** iced coffee, so the classic order is **ブレンドをホットで**. Compliment the place (**すてきなお店ですね**) and the owner may tell you its whole history.

points.title: Freepass, ropeway and Mt. Fuji

December is a great month for Fuji: cold, dry air gives clear views, so ask **今日は富士山が見えますか** before you ride up.
points.tip: Fuji often hides in cloud by midday, so take the ropeway in the morning and save the boat for the afternoon. **見えます** means "can be seen" — don't confuse it with **見ます** ("I look").

points.gist: book a room for one, pick a drink plan and extend your time
points.explain: **一人カラオケ** (or ヒトカラ) is completely normal in Japan; big chains like Big Echo and Karaoke-kan happily give one person a room. At the desk you choose the number of hours, a drink plan (**飲み放題** = all you can drink) and sometimes the machine (DAM or JOYSOUND). Ten minutes before your time is up the room phone rings: **延長します** keeps you singing, **大丈夫です** means you're done.
points.tip: Prices are per person per 30 minutes and go up at night and at weekends; late at night ask about the **フリータイム** (free-time) plan — one flat price for many hours, often cheaper than paying by the hour.

points.gist: drop your bag for a domestic flight and catch the right train to Sapporo
points.explain: Domestic flights (**国内線**) are quick: show your booking, drop your bag and walk to the gate — no immigration. **〜たいです** ("I'd like to…") is all you need at the bag-drop counter: **預けたいです** = "I'd like to check it in". From New Chitose Airport, the **快速エアポート** train reaches Sapporo in under 40 minutes.
points.tip: Power banks and lighters must stay in your carry-on, never in the checked suitcase — that's why the agent asks about them.

points.tip: **暖かい** is for warm weather and clothes, **温かい** for warm food and drinks — both are read あたたかい, only the kanji changes.

points.title: Miso ramen your way
points.pattern: 〜でお願いします・〜にしてください
points.gist: use the ticket machine and choose noodle firmness and flavour
points.explain: Many Sapporo ramen shops have a ticket machine by the door: put in money, press the button, and hand the ticket to the staff. Some shops then ask how you like your bowl — noodles **固め** (firm), **普通** (regular) or **柔らかめ** (soft), and flavour **濃いめ** (stronger) or **薄め** (lighter). Sapporo is famous for rich **味噌ラーメン**, often topped with butter and corn, and locals love it as the last stop of a night out.
points.tip: The ending **〜め** means "on the … side": 固め = firmish, 薄め = a bit lighter. If you're unsure, **普通で** ("regular") is always a safe answer.

points.explain: **ジンギスカン** is lamb grilled on a dome-shaped iron pan: meat in the middle, vegetables around the edge catching the juices. Crabs are counted with **杯** (はい・ばい・ぱい), so 一杯 means one whole crab, and many menus only say **時価** (market price) — ask before you order. At the bar, try Sapporo Classic, a beer sold only in Hokkaido.
points.tip: Jingisukan smoke soaks into clothes: many shops offer a plastic bag for your coat or a paper apron — take it!

For fragile gifts, say you're flying home, and staff will pack them extra carefully.
points.tip: Most shops in Otaru close around 6 p.m. — shop first, then head to your ryokan in time for dinner.

points.title: Omicho market: what's fresh today?
points.pattern: 何が〜ですか・〜てもいいですか
points.gist: ask what's in season, buy a crab and eat it on the spot
points.explain: Omicho market (**近江町市場**) has been Kanazawa's kitchen for about 300 years; go in the morning, when the stalls are full and the queues for **海鮮丼** are shorter. December is the season of **香箱がに**, the small female snow crab with orange roe, sold only from November to late December. A short walk away, Kenrokuen's pine trees wear **雪吊り** — cones of rope that stop heavy snow from breaking the branches.
points.tip: Some stalls let you eat on the spot and some don't — ask before you start, and don't walk around while eating in the market.

points.title: The bus to snowy Shirakawa-go

points.gist: get a seat, know the last bus back and respect the village

points.tip: Shirakawa-go gets deep snow in December: wear boots with real grip, and check the time of the last bus back before you start exploring.

points.title: Counter dining in Pontocho
points.pattern: 〜は必要ですか・何が入っていますか
points.gist: get a seat, order obanzai and ask what's in a dish
points.explain: Pontocho is one narrow stone lane of tiny restaurants beside the river; early in the evening many counter places take walk-ins, so just ask at the door — and you may hear the Kyoto welcome **おこしやす** instead of いらっしゃいませ. **おばんざい** are everyday Kyoto side dishes — simmered vegetables, tofu, yuba — often displayed in big bowls on the counter, so you can simply point. **これは何が入っていますか** ("what's in this?") works for any dish you don't recognise.
points.tip: Some old places are **一見さんお断り** — regulars and introductions only. If there's no menu or price list outside, it may be one of them: smile and try the next door.

points.title: Gion manners and a riverside bar
points.pattern: 〜ないでください・〜はありますか
points.gist: follow Gion's rules, then order Kyoto sake by the river
points.explain: Gion is a living neighbourhood: **maiko** are on their way to work, so never block their path or photograph them. Some side alleys are **私道** (private roads) where photography is banned and fines are posted. Afterwards, the bars along the **鴨川** are quiet and grown-up — and Kyoto's own sake comes from **伏見**, in the south of the city.
points.tip: Keep your voice down in the lanes: sound carries between the old wooden houses, and people live upstairs.

points.gist: buy and write a fox ema, and ask how long the climb takes
points.explain: Fushimi Inari's thousands of orange **鳥居** are open day and night, so go at dawn, when the paths are almost empty. Foxes are the messengers of Inari, the god of rice and good business; the shrine's fox-shaped **絵馬** come with a blank face for you to draw, and your wish goes on the back. The walk to the summit and back takes about two to three hours.
points.tip: The shrine never closes, but the counter that sells charms and ema (**授与所**) closes in the late afternoon — buy yours on the way up.

points.explain: In winter many Kyoto temples close around 4:30 p.m., and the last entry (**受付**) is often 30 minutes earlier, so start your day early. Go to Arashiyama's bamboo grove right after sunrise: by mid-morning it is packed, and the buses back to the center fill up fast in the afternoon.
points.tip: After dark, the JR Sagano Line or the Randen tram from Arashiyama is often faster than a packed city bus.

points.pattern: 〜てから〜てください・どのぐらい〜ですか
points.gist: feed the deer the right way and ask about Todaiji
points.explain: Nara Park's deer — more than a thousand of them — are wild, and locals see them as sacred messengers. Buy **鹿せんべい** at the stalls (the only food you should give them) and hand the crackers over quickly: teasing makes deer push and nip. Many deer bow for a cracker — bow back! — before you head to **東大寺**, whose bronze Great Buddha is about 15 metres tall.
points.tip: Keep maps, tickets and paper bags out of reach — deer eat paper. When the crackers are gone, show your empty hands and they lose interest.

Each bath has its own hours and one **closing day** a week, so check the list before you head out. In December, wear the padded **丹前** over your yukata, and open a quiet chat in the bath with **いいお湯ですね**.
points.tip: Dry your hair and body well before you walk to the next bath: the winter wind turns a warm soak into **湯冷め** (a post-bath chill) very fast.

points.title: Reading a handwritten menu
points.pattern: あれは何と読みますか・〜はどれですか
points.gist: decode the wall menu and ask what a dish is
points.explain: Ura-Namba izakaya often have only a **handwritten menu** on the wall, so learn four cooking words: **刺身** (raw slices), **焼き** (grilled), **揚げ** (deep-fried) and **煮込み** (stewed). When the brushwork is too hard to read, point and ask **あれは何と読みますか**. The answers come in Kansai-ben: **めっちゃ** = とても (very), **なんぼ** = いくら (how much), and the endings **や** = だ and **で** = よ. You keep speaking normal polite Japanese, which is exactly right for a visitor.
points.tip: **土手焼き** (どてやき) is beef sinew simmered in sweet miso: despite the 焼き in its name, it isn't grilled. Read the whole dish name, not just the ending.
points.yt: Osaka izakaya Japanese menu words sashimi yaki age nikomi

points.title: Kansai-ben at the counter
points.pattern: あかん = だめ・〜へん = 〜ない・おおきに = ありがとう
points.gist: understand the owner's Kansai-ben and answer in polite standard Japanese
points.explain: Osaka owners love to chat, and a few Kansai words come up all night: **あかん** = だめ (no good), **ほんま** = 本当 (really), **おおきに** = ありがとう (thank you). Negatives end in **〜へん** instead of 〜ない, so **飲まへん？** = 飲まない？, a friendly "won't you have a drink?" just like 〜ませんか. Answer in your polite standard Japanese: copying the dialect too early can sound like teasing.
points.tip: Osaka shopkeepers say **毎度おおきに** ("thanks as always") even on your very first visit. It's a greeting, not a mistake, so just smile and say ごちそうさまでした.

Wait times are shown as **〜分待ち**, and as a solo traveller the **シングルライダー** line can save you a long wait.

points.title: Kushikatsu in Shinsekai
points.pattern: 〜を〜本ください・〜てもいいですか
points.gist: order skewers, follow the sauce rule and find a seat in party season
points.explain: **新世界** (Shinsekai), the retro neighbourhood under Tsutenkaku tower, is the home of **串カツ**: breaded, deep-fried skewers dipped into a shared tin of sauce. The golden rule is **二度づけ禁止**: dip each skewer only once, and scoop extra sauce with the free cabbage. Count skewers with **〜本** (いっぽん, にほん, さんぼん). Late December is **忘年会** season, so many places are packed or booked out for office parties; go early or squeeze in solo at the counter.
points.tip: Once you have bitten a skewer, it never goes back into the shared sauce. That is the one thing that will get you scolded in Shinsekai.
points.yt: Shinsekai kushikatsu no double dipping rule how to eat

s.en: Three kushikatsu skewers, please.

points.title: Chatting at a standing bar
points.pattern: 〜はどうですか・〜と思います
points.gist: chat with salarymen and use the year-end goodbye
points.explain: A **立ち飲み** (standing bar) is cheap, quick and very social, and in late December it fills up with salarymen on their way home from a **忘年会**. Expect simple questions like **大阪はどうですか**, and answer with **〜と思います** ("I think…") plus something nice about the city. Before the New Year, people part with **良いお年を** ("have a good New Year"), and you just say it back.
points.tip: Use **良いお年を** only until December 31. From January 1 the greeting becomes **あけましておめでとうございます**.

points.title: Inside Himeji Castle
points.pattern: いつできましたか・〜は何階までありますか
points.gist: buy a ticket, climb the keep safely and ask about its age
points.explain: **姫路城**, the "White Heron Castle", is Japan's most famous original castle: its main keep has stood for about 400 years. Inside you take your shoes off and carry them in a plastic bag, then climb wooden stairs so steep they are almost ladders. Ask about history with **いつできましたか** ("when was it built?"): できる here means "to be completed".
points.tip: Wear warm socks without holes and keep your bag small: the keep's stairs are narrow and steep, and the wooden floors are icy in December.

In **灘** (Nada), Kobe's historic sake district, many breweries offer **試飲** (tastings): **辛口** is dry, **甘口** is sweet. December is new-sake season, so look for **新酒** and a fresh green cedar ball hanging over the brewery door.

points.gist: Mirage describes an ordinary weekday, from getting up to studying Japanese at night.

points.tip: でも at the start of a sentence means "but" — it links back to the sentence before it.

points.gist: Tanaka-san queues for ramen in Shinjuku with a friend, then they go manga shopping.

points.title: My first week in Tokyo
points.pattern: 〜曜日に + V-ました
points.gist: Mirage's diary of his first seven days in Tokyo, from Narita to a solo night at an izakaya.
points.explain: The text moves day by day, so the **day of the week** at the start of each sentence is your bookmark: 月曜日, 火曜日, 水曜日… Read it, then jump to the verb at the end to see what happened that day. Watch the two "to" particles: **に** for arriving (空港に着きました) and **へ** for heading somewhere (ホテルへ行きました).
points.tip: 初めて means "for the first time" (an adverb), not "first" in a list — 最初 is the word for "the first one".
points.yt: Japanese N5 reading diary past tense days of the week

s.en: Last week I came to Japan for the first time.
On Monday I arrived at Narita Airport.

c.w: 成田空港[なりたくうこう]

s.en: From the airport I went by train to a hotel in Asakusa.
On Tuesday I went to Sensō-ji.
The temple was really big.
Wednesday was rainy.
I rested at the hotel all day.

c.w: 一日中[いちにちじゅう]

s.en: On Thursday I bought old games in Akihabara.
On Friday night I went to an izakaya by myself.
My first week in Japan was really fun.

c.w: 一週間[いっしゅうかん]

q.q: Where did Mirage stay?
What did he do on Wednesday?
opts: He rested at the hotel because it rained

q.q: Who did he go to the izakaya with?
opts: With a friend from the hotel

readings.title: The cat café
vocab: 写真[しゃしん]を撮[と]る

points.title: The cat café
points.pattern: V-て V・V-ていました・V-たい
points.gist: Mirage and Ana spend a Sunday afternoon at a cat café — and one cat chooses Mirage.
points.explain: Watch the **て-form**: 入って…洗いました is "went in and then washed" — て links actions in the order they happen. **〜ていました** shows what was going on at that moment, like a snapshot: one cat sleeping, another playing. The last line uses **〜たい** ("want to") for a wish.
points.tip: 十匹 is read じゅっぴき and 一匹 いっぴき — the counter 匹 changes its sound (ひき / びき / ぴき) depending on the number.
points.yt: Japanese te form reading practice N5 te imasu

s.en: On Sunday I went to a cat café with Ana.
We went in and first washed our hands.
There were ten cats inside.
A black cat was sleeping near the window.
A small cat was playing with a toy.
Ana took lots of photos.
I sat on the sofa and drank coffee.
Then one cat climbed onto my lap.
The cat was very warm.

c.w: 温[あたた]かかったです

s.en: I want to come again with Ana.

q.q: What did they do right after going in?
What was the black cat doing?
What happened while Mirage drank his coffee?
opts: A cat climbed onto his lap

readings.title: The konbini night shift
vocab: 週[しゅう]に三回[さんかい]

points.title: The konbini night shift
points.pattern: relative clause + N・V-ています
points.gist: A night at the station konbini where Kimura-san works, with its regular customers and 3 a.m. deliveries.
points.explain: Look for the **relative clause** in sentence 4: 夜中のコンビニに来る describes 人 — "the people who come to the konbini at night". In Japanese the description always comes **before** the noun, so when you meet a plain verb followed by a noun, read it as "the … who/that …". 働いています is an ongoing habit: "he works (these days)".
points.tip: 来る here is the plain form of 来ます and is read くる, not きる — the reading of 来 changes with the form (きます, くる, こない).
points.yt: Japanese relative clauses reading practice N5 N4

s.en: Kimura-san is a university student.

c.w: 大学生[だいがくせい]です

s.en: Three times a week he works at the konbini in front of the station.

c.w: 週[しゅう]に三回[さんかい]

s.en: He works from ten at night until six in the morning.
The people who come to the konbini in the middle of the night are interesting.

c.w: 夜中[よなか]のコンビニに来[く]る

s.en: Around one o'clock, the same old man always comes.
Every night the old man buys a sweet-bean bun and milk.
At three, a truck brings new bento boxes.
Kimura-san lines them up on the shelves.
After work he is very sleepy.
But Kimura-san likes the night konbini.

q.q: How often does Kimura-san work at the konbini?
What does the old man buy every night?
What happens at three o'clock?
opts: A truck brings new bento boxes

readings.title: A rainy day in Kyoto
vocab: 観光客[かんこうきゃく]

points.title: A rainy day in Kyoto
points.pattern: V-たかった・short form + から・V-ていました
points.gist: Heavy rain spoils Mirage's plan in Kyoto, and a quiet temple turns out to be even better.
points.explain: Sentence 3 has a **reason clause**: 雨が強かったから — "because the rain was heavy". The から clause always comes first and the result after it, the reverse of English "…, because…". **行きたかった** is the past of 行きたい: "wanted to go (but didn't)". Quotes sit inside 「」 and are closed by **と** + 言いました / 答えました.
points.tip: でしょう at the end of the old woman's line asks for agreement ("…, don't you think?") — it isn't a question you must answer with facts.
points.yt: Japanese reading practice kara because tai form N5

s.en: Mirage's second day in Kyoto was rainy from the morning.
He wanted to go to Fushimi Inari.

c.w: 伏見稲荷[ふしみいなり]

s.en: Because the rain was heavy, he changed his plans.
He asked the hotel staff and went to a temple nearby.
Rain was falling on the quiet garden.
There were almost no tourists.

c.w: 観光客[かんこうきゃく]

s.en: Mirage sat on the veranda and listened to the sound of the rain.
On the way back, he ate hot udon at a small shop.
The old woman at the shop said, "Kyoto in the rain is nice too, isn't it?"

c.w: 「雨[あめ]の京都[きょうと]もいいでしょう」

s.en: Mirage smiled and answered, "It's really beautiful."

c.w: 「本当[ほんとう]にきれいです」

q.q: Why did Mirage change his plans?
What did he do at the temple?
opts: He sat and listened to the rain

q.q: What did the old woman at the udon shop say?
opts: That the rain would stop soon
That Kyoto in the rain is nice too

points.title: Cooking curry with a friend
points.pattern: short forms・V-てから・V-たい
points.gist: Mirage writes in his diary about making Japanese curry at Tanaka-san's place.
points.explain: This is a diary, so it uses **short (plain) forms**: 作った, 買った, 甘い, 最高だった. It isn't rude — it's simply the style of personal writing. Follow the recipe through the **て** and **てから** links: each one is the next step. In sentence 9, 二人で食べた is a relative clause: "the curry we ate together".
points.tip: The plain past of です after a noun is だった (最高だった), and the plain form of 作りたいです is just 作りたい.
points.yt: Japanese plain form diary reading practice N5

s.en: Yesterday I made curry at Tanaka-san's house.
First, the two of us went to the supermarket and bought vegetables and meat.
Tanaka-san cut the onions, and I cut the carrots.
Tanaka-san said "My eyes hurt!" and laughed.
We fried the meat and vegetables, and then added water.
We waited about twenty minutes and put in the curry roux.

c.w: 二十分[にじゅっぷん]ぐらい

s.en: The room filled with a lovely smell.
Japanese curry is a little sweet.
The curry we ate together was the best.

c.w: 二人[ふたり]で食[た]べた

s.en: Next time I want to cook a Brazilian dish.

q.q: Who cut the onions?
What did they do before adding the water?
opts: They fried the meat and vegetables
They went back to the supermarket

q.q: What does Mirage want to do next time?

readings.title: The game tournament
vocab: 準決勝[じゅんけっしょう]

points.title: The game tournament
points.pattern: potential・V-てくれる/もらう・V-たら
points.gist: Mirage enters a fighting-game tournament in Osaka and makes a rival — and a friend.
points.explain: Three N4 patterns carry this story. **Potential** forms say what was (not) possible: 寝られませんでした "couldn't sleep", 勝てました "was able to win". **〜てくれる / 〜てもらう** show a favour: Kenta 言ってくれました (did it for Mirage) and Mirage 教えてもらいました (received the teaching — the giver is marked with に). **〜たら** in Kenta's quote means "if".
points.tip: With 〜てもらう, the person marked with に is the one who does the favour — ケンタさんに教えてもらいました means Kenta taught Mirage, not the other way round.
points.yt: Japanese N4 reading practice potential form te morau te kureru

s.en: Last month, Mirage took part in a game tournament in Osaka.
Before the tournament he was so nervous he couldn't sleep at all.

c.w: 寝[ね]られませんでした

s.en: At the venue, a Japanese player kindly said to him, "Shall we practise together?"

c.w: 「一緒[いっしょ]に練習[れんしゅう]しませんか」

s.en: His name was Kenta.
Kenta taught Mirage a powerful move.

c.w: 教[おし]えてもらいました

s.en: Mirage was able to win the first round easily.
His opponent in the semifinal was — Kenta!

c.w: 準決勝[じゅんけっしょう]

s.en: Kenta said, "If you beat me, I'll buy you ramen."

c.w: 「僕[ぼく]に勝[か]ったら、ラーメンをおごるよ」

s.en: It was a heated match right to the end.
Mirage lost, but Kenta treated him to ramen anyway.

q.q: Why couldn't Mirage sleep before the tournament?
What did Kenta do for Mirage before the matches?
How did the story end?
opts: Mirage won and paid for ramen
Mirage lost, but Kenta bought him ramen anyway

points.title: The autumn festival
points.pattern: V-てくれる/もらう・potential・V-たら・より
points.gist: Kimura-san takes Mirage to a neighbourhood autumn festival, yukata and portable shrine included.
points.explain: Count the favours: Kimura-san 誘ってくれました, his mother 貸してくれました, and Mirage 手伝ってもらいました — **くれる** when someone does something for "me", **もらう** when "I" receive it. **夜になったら** means "when night came": 〜たら for something that happened once a condition was met. **思ったより** is "than I thought".
points.tip: 結べなかった (couldn't tie) is the potential of 結ぶ in the negative past — when a potential verb takes an object, that object is often marked with が instead of を.
points.yt: Japanese N4 reading practice festival te kureru tara

s.en: One weekend in October, Kimura-san invited me to the town's autumn festival.

c.w: 誘[さそ]ってくれました

s.en: Kimura-san's mother lent me a yukata.
I couldn't tie the sash by myself, so she helped me.

c.w: 手伝[てつだ]ってもらいました

s.en: In front of the shrine, lots of food stalls stood in a row.
We bought takoyaki and shaved ice.
When night came, we heard the sound of big drums.
People from the town carried the mikoshi on their shoulders through the streets.
Kimura-san asked, "Mirage, do you want to try carrying it too?"

c.w: 「ミラージュも担[かつ]いでみる？」

s.en: The mikoshi was much heavier than I thought.
I was really happy that I could take part in a Japanese festival.

q.q: Who lent Mirage a yukata?
What did they buy at the stalls?
How was carrying the mikoshi?
opts: It was cancelled because of rain

points.title: Lost in Osaka
points.pattern: passive・V-てしまう・V-たら・V-てくれる
points.gist: On his first day in Osaka, Mirage's phone dies — and a local grandmother walks him to his hotel.
points.explain: Sentence 3 has a light **passive**: 声をかけられました — "I was spoken to" (by a stranger, marked with に). **〜たら** appears twice for "when…": 困っていたら (while I was stuck), 着いたら (when we arrived). The grandmother speaks **Osaka dialect**: ほな = じゃあ ("well then") and 行こか = 行こうか ("shall we go?").
points.tip: 飴 (あめ, candy) and 雨 (あめ, rain) sound almost the same — the kanji and the context tell you which one. Osaka grandmothers handing out "アメちゃん" are famous.
points.yt: Japanese N4 reading passive form tara Kansai dialect

s.en: On the day I arrived in Osaka, my phone battery died.

c.w: 大阪[おおさか]に着[つ]いた
切[き]れてしまいました

s.en: I couldn't look at the map, so I couldn't find my hotel.

c.w: 見[み]つかりませんでした

s.en: While I was standing there lost in front of the station, an old lady I didn't know spoke to me.
She listened to me patiently.
Then she said, "Well then, shall we go together?"

c.w: 「ほな、一緒[いっしょ]に行[い]こか」

s.en: We walked together to the hotel for about fifteen minutes.

c.w: 十五分[じゅうごふん]ぐらい

s.en: On the way, she gave me a candy.
When we reached the hotel, she waved and went home.

c.w: 帰[かえ]っていきました

s.en: I couldn't even ask her name.
People in Osaka are really kind.

q.q: Why couldn't Mirage find his hotel?
opts: His phone battery died, so he couldn't see the map
He had forgotten the hotel's name

q.q: What did the old lady give him on the way?
What was Mirage NOT able to do?

points.title: A letter to my teacher
points.pattern: passive・ようになる・ように・V-てもらう
points.gist: Back in Brazil, Mirage writes to his Japanese teacher about what three weeks in Japan taught him.
points.explain: A letter mixes past events and present feelings, so check each sentence ending: **ほめられました** is passive ("I was praised"), **わかるようになりました** means "I came to understand" (a change over time), and **話せるように** means "so that I can speak". 先生に教えてもらった言葉 is one long noun: "the words I had my teacher teach me".
points.tip: Don't confuse ように (so that, aiming at a goal) with ようになる (to come to, a change) — the second one always ends in なる / なりました.
points.yt: Japanese N4 reading practice letter passive you ni naru

s.en: Dear Yamada-sensei, how are you?

c.w: 山田[やまだ]先生[せんせい]

s.en: Last week I came back to Brazil from my three-week trip to Japan.

c.w: 三週間[さんしゅうかん]
日本旅行[にほんりょこう]

s.en: In Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka I was able to use a lot of Japanese.

c.w: 東京[とうきょう]、京都[きょうと]、大阪[おおさか]
使[つか]うことができました

s.en: At first, I didn't understand fast Japanese at all.
But as I talked every day, little by little I started to understand.

c.w: わかるようになりました

s.en: At a ryokan in Kyoto I was praised: "Your Japanese is very good!"

c.w: 「日本語[にほんご]がお上手[じょうず]ですね」

s.en: I was a little embarrassed, but very happy.

c.w: 恥[は]ずかしかったです

s.en: When I got lost in Osaka, a kind person helped me.

c.w: 助[たす]けてくれました

s.en: The words you taught me were really useful.

c.w: 先生[せんせい]に教[おし]えてもらった
役[やく]に立[た]ちました

s.en: I'll keep working hard so that I can speak even better on my next trip.

q.q: How long was Mirage's trip?
What happened at the ryokan in Kyoto?
What does he say about the words his teacher taught him?

wagotabi.note: Wagotabi does not publish a lesson-by-lesson syllabus. This map is built from the game's Steam patch notes, store pages and reviews (researched Nov 2026). Topics are paraphrased; areas marked 'approx' have an unverified exact order. The game follows travel situations, not Genki order.

areas.name: Airport (tutorial)
topics: first hiragana, introduced only as words need them
immigration and luggage situations
finding and boarding the right bus, buying a ticket
asking where something goes

areas.name: Road to Takamatsu · Takamatsu
topics: first quiz battles against the rival
animals and everyday nouns
the question particle か
first kanji inside words (e.g. 家, 花)
a side quest that unlocks the kanji card game
drills: kanji match with your first kanji

areas.name: Sanuki · Marugame · Konpirasan
topics: dakuten and the kana keyboard groups
more nouns and set phrases
first verbs and particles in short dialogues

areas.name: Okayama Castle
topics: な-adjectives before a noun (the な link)
a castle master battle for the region's seal

areas.name: Kōrakuen
topics: connecting clauses with から (because), ので (because, softer) and けど (but)

areas.name: Road to Kurashiki · Kurashiki
topics: weather words and the verb 描く (to draw/paint)
temperature adjectives (暑い, 寒い, 温かい)

areas.name: Kibitsu · Bizen · Hinase · Shizutani
topics: numbers
よろしくお願いします in introductions
floors with 階 and 何階 (which floor?)

areas.name: Daisen
topics: the て-form
polite requests with 〜てください
fruit vocabulary

側 (side) for positions

areas.name: Tottori Dunes
topics: telling the time (clock puzzle)

topics: newest levels (2026); exact topics are not documented publicly
